A lightweight quadruped manipulator platform integrating a custom-designed Lite Arm and a Unitree Go1 is developed, together with a hybrid task-space representation that enables rough-terrain loco-manipulation while preserving task-consistent end-effector behavior.

A systematic ablation study validates the effectiveness of the proposed objective hierarchy.

title: FLoTS-SLAM: Optical Flow-Derived Uncertainty for Monocular Dynamic SLAM with Two-Stage Optimization
authors: Haorui Du,Lipu Zhou
abstract:
Monocular simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) remains challenging in
dynamic environments. Thus, real-time dynamic object identification in
such environments is a critical problem. Recent approaches estimate per-pixel
uncertainty from rendering residuals or multiview feature inconsistency to
identify dynamic regions. These methods lack direct motion
evidence, and their accuracy may degrade when reconstruction is inaccurate or
features are ambiguous. In addition, such uncertainty merely downweights
pixels in bundle adjustment (BA), so inaccurate uncertainty estimates can
still impair camera pose estimation and 3D reconstruction. Accordingly, we
present a monocular RGB SLAM system for dynamic scenes. Specifically, a
motion uncertainty estimation method is proposed to derive
uncertainty from the residual between optical flow and
camera motion induced flow, directly reflecting object motion. The estimation
varies with frame alignment accuracy, reducing false detections and yielding accurate
pixel-level masks of dynamic regions. To make BA more robust, we estimate camera poses from high confidence pixels. These poses are then used to reproject
dynamic pixels during joint refinement of poses and depth, reducing
the influence of object motion on both pose and depth updates. Moreover, we
provide a quantitative evaluation of dynamic masks and analyze how
these masks affect the downstream tracking and reconstruction of dynamic
objects. Our approach improves the mean dynamic mask IoU by 35% over a
state-of-the-art baseline on DAVIS, and reduces the average ATE by
59% on Bonn and 19% on TUM relative to the SLAM backbone used in our system.
The source code will be made publicly available.
introduction:
Monocular simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is a
fundamental problem in robotics, with broad applications in autonomous
navigation [1], augmented reality
[2], and virtual reality
[3].
However, dynamic objects disrupt the geometric consistency across views and may
introduce erroneous correspondences. Such correspondences
degrade camera pose estimation and 3D reconstruction, reducing SLAM accuracy
and robustness in real-world scenes. Dynamic environments therefore remain a
challenge for reliable SLAM. This paper focuses on monocular SLAM
in such environments.

Identifying dynamic objects underpins subsequent camera tracking and 3D scene
reconstruction. Moving object segmentation (MOS) models
[4, 5, 6] can identify dynamic objects in video, but these models typically have prohibitive inference costs for real-time tasks.
Earlier dynamic SLAM methods instead use lightweight semantic segmentation or
object detection models [7, 8, 9], which infer motion from
semantic categories rather than actual motion. As a result, they fail to
recognize moving objects from unseen classes. For known classes, they may
mistake static objects for dynamic ones and moving ones for static.
Open-vocabulary segmentation [10] broadens object coverage but
leaves this semantic basis unchanged. Fig. 1 illustrates
the potential errors of the detection-based method NGD-SLAM [11].

Recent works [13, 14] estimate per-pixel uncertainty for
dynamic regions, independent of object categories. This uncertainty is
predicted from DINO [15] features with a shallow
multilayer perceptron (MLP), supervised online by the discrepancy between
input images and current renderings. The estimates degrade when the
map is inaccurate. DROID-W [12] avoids this dependence
on reconstruction accuracy by using multiview feature inconsistency.
However, the feature inconsistency provides indirect evidence of motion
and may be unreliable in semantically complex or weakly textured regions,
as shown in the second row of Fig. 1.

Optical flow captures interframe motion directly, and several
SLAM systems use it to detect dynamic regions
[16, 8, 17]. In these systems, however, the flow comes
from a dedicated estimator, adding computational overhead and increasing
per-frame processing time [18].
In addition, the identification scheme for
marking a pixel as dynamic is fixed in advance
[16, 19, 20]. Consequently, pose and depth errors
may cause static pixels to be misclassified as dynamic.

Apart from dynamic object identification, how the estimated uncertainty is used in
optimization also affects system robustness. Existing uncertainty-aware
systems [13, 12] apply uncertainty estimates in
bundle adjustment (BA) as per-pixel weights, and refine poses and depths
jointly under that weighting. However, motion residuals from dynamic pixels
that are not fully suppressed still impact both depth estimates and keyframe
poses. All pixels are used in BA, so inaccurate uncertainty at any pixel can affect
the estimation.

Motivated by the above observations, we present a monocular RGB SLAM system for dynamic scenes built on FLow-derived uncertainty and Two-Stage optimization (FLoTS-SLAM).
Optical flow measures motion directly and is obtained from the existing
correspondence predictions of the system tracker without additional computation.
To identify dynamic objects accurately, we design a motion uncertainty
estimation method based on optical flow residuals.
In addition, uncertainty weighting alone may not fully suppress the influence
of dynamic pixels on pose and depth estimation, and removing these pixels
would reduce the number of constraints for optimization. We therefore perform
optimization in two stages to improve robustness.
In the first stage, depth is fixed and poses are estimated from high confidence pixels.
In the second stage, poses and depth are jointly refined,
using the first-stage poses to predict where dynamic pixels would appear if the scene were static.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose a motion uncertainty estimation method
to improve the accuracy of dynamic object identification. It
derives uncertainty from the residual between optical flow and
camera motion induced flow, and adapts to frame alignment accuracy.

We propose a motion uncertainty estimation method
to improve the accuracy of dynamic object identification. It
derives uncertainty from the residual between optical flow and
camera motion induced flow, and adapts to frame alignment accuracy.

We introduce a two-stage optimization method to reduce the influence of
object motion on pose and depth updates, and improve tracking
robustness.

We conduct extensive experiments.
FLoTS-SLAM attains state-of-the-art camera localization on Bonn
and TUM, reducing the average ATE of its DROID-SLAM backbone by 59%
and 19%. We also introduce
Dynamic Mask IoU (DM-IoU) to quantitatively evaluate dynamic identification
across methods. On DAVIS, our method improves the mean DM-IoU by 35%
over a state-of-the-art baseline.

We will make the source code publicly available to facilitate future research.

camera motion induced flow, and adapts to frame alignment accuracy.

2. We introduce a two-stage optimization method to reduce the influence of
object motion on pose and depth updates, and improve tracking
robustness.

3. We conduct extensive experiments.

and 19%. We also introduce

across methods. On DAVIS, our method improves the mean DM-IoU by 35%
over a state-of-the-art baseline.

4. We will make the source code publicly available to facilitate future research.

title: HexaShell: A Thin Harness for Exploring the Limits of VLM Agents as Robot Coding Agents
authors: Hongcheng Gao,Alex Zhou,Jay Zhu,Zelin Zheng,Shijia Ge,Xiping Li,Di Wu,Yazhe Wang,Jianshu Zeng,Xuan Shangguan,Yongli Wang,Yexing Wan,Lingyu He,Zhiqi Jia,Sihang Wu,Xiao He

abstract: Agents built on vision language models (VLMs) now compete with learned policies on robot manipulation leaderboards. We ask how far a coding agent can go when it controls a robot instead of a computer, and where it stops. Our system, HexaShell, keeps the harness thin: it only turns the agent’s commands into robot motion. The agent drives a robot with two arms through one command line. It sees three RGB cameras and knows their calibration. After each failed attempt, the agent reads the log, finds the cause, and writes or fixes small programs called tools. In this way it keeps what it learns as code, as a coding agent does when it fixes a failing test. The tools may use only what the robot observes. They use triangulation to find where objects are, relative to each other and to the gripper. If two cameras see the same point, the point lies where the two camera rays meet. If a point lies on a known plane, such as the table or the top of a block, it lies where its ray meets that plane. When the head camera is not enough, the robot moves a wrist camera to get a second view. We build the tools on only ten layouts of one seed per task, then freeze them and test them on ten new layouts of the same seed. We use Codex with GPT-6-Astra at medium reasoning effort. On all 42 RoboDojo tasks, HexaShell reaches a success rate of 39.7% and a progress score of 48.0, averaged in the same way as the leaderboard. This is a new state of the art on RoboDojo. The limit is contact, not reasoning: pushing reaches 92.5% and memory tasks 65.0%, but tight insertion only 8.3%. When the agent fails, it usually sees the failure but cannot make the motion work. We open source the tools evolved so far at https://github.com/HexaFuture/HexaShell.
introduction:
Robot manipulation leaderboards have been led by learned policies. Vision language action models and world action models learn from large sets of demonstrations and output the robot’s actions directly [35, 4, 7]. Agents built on vision language models have now started to compete. On RoboDojo [14], the model we use reaches 22.5% without tools of its own, choosing gripper targets through a fixed harness written by the benchmark’s authors [69].

Coding agents suggest another route. In a software repository, a coding agent reads the code, runs it, reads the error and fixes the code, and the fix stays. Recent work has begun to let coding agents write and revise robot tools and programs [26, 25, 40, 34]. We ask how far a coding agent can go when it works on a robot in the same way, and where it stops. Our system, HexaShell, keeps the harness thin. The agent gets one command, robo, three RGB images with their calibration, and a manual of one page. The harness turns commands into joint motion and does nothing else. What the agent learns is kept as tools, small programs that add commands to robo and may use only what the robot observes. An acting agent tries a layout with the current tools. After a failure, an optimizer agent of the same model reads the episode as it would read a failing test, writes or fixes a tool with its unit tests, and the layout is tried again (Fig. 3). Both agents are Codex with GPT-6-Astra at medium reasoning effort.

The hard part is turning pixels into positions. In a repository, everything the agent works on is text it can read exactly. On a robot, the agent sees objects as pixels, but every command needs a position in the world, to about a centimetre for a grasp. Vision language models are known to judge such distances poorly [9, 16]. The standard observation has no depth. A monocular depth network can estimate depth from one image, but on RoboDojo scenes Depth Anything V2 [65] is off by a median of 41 mm at the head camera and about 100 mm at the wrists, even after we fix its scale with the table. Our tools use triangulation instead. The cameras are calibrated, and the robot knows where its wrists are. A point that two cameras see lies where their rays meet, and a point on a measured plane, such as the table, lies where its ray meets that plane [27]. When one view is not enough, the robot moves a wrist camera to get another. This is active perception [3], and on a benchmark it has a price: the motion uses action steps, and every task has a step limit.

We build the tools on ten layouts of each task, freeze them, and test them on ten new layouts. On all 42 tasks, HexaShell reaches 39.7% success and a progress score of 48.0 on the leaderboard’s metric, a new state of the art on RoboDojo (Fig. 2). It does best where the right action follows from measured geometry, and it stops at contact: tight insertion stays low. The paper makes three contributions.

A thin harness and a short repair loop for robot coding agents. The harness gives an unchanged coding agent one command line to the robot and makes no decisions for it. All that the agent learns is kept as small tools with unit tests, which the next episode loads. After a failure, a second agent of the same model edits one tool and the same layout runs again. A repair round takes a median of 6.3 minutes, and no robot data, training or change to the model is needed (Section 3).

The finding that triangulation locates objects more reliably than a depth network, and so lifts what a VLM agent achieves on a robot. The model picks a pixel on the target, and the tool turns it into a position. With the same harness, loop and model, on the same layouts, triangulation scores 8.7 points higher than Depth Anything V2; paired by layout, it wins 57 layouts and loses 23 (Table 1). Its second views cost at least 3.6% of the executed steps, and on the layouts where the robot moved a camera to look, triangulation succeeds 39 times against 22 (Section 4.5).

A map of the current limits of VLM agents in the physical world. Over 420 retest episodes, success follows the contact a task needs, not what the agent must read or remember. Pushing reaches 92.5% and memory tasks 65.0%, but tight insertion only 8.3%. On the development layouts, clutter matters little: with 13 to 18 extra objects, HexaShell keeps 95% of its success. How an episode fails also separates a gap in perception, where the agent claims a success that the checker rejects, from a gap in execution, where it runs out of steps (Sections 4.3 and 5).

title: No Eyes, No Problem: What Does Touch Contribute to Blind Baoding Ball Manipulation?
authors: Ayush Deshmukh,Nalin Agarwal,Elle Miller,Sethu Vijayakumar
abstract:
Humans manipulate objects within their hands through touch alone with remarkable ease, but for robots, achieving sustained real-world manipulation without vision remains an open challenge. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can generate sophisticated blind manipulation policies in simulation, transferring them to a real dexterous hand remains hindered by continuously changing contacts, motion-induced tactile information drift, and the gap between simulated and physical dynamics. We study this problem through Baoding ball rotation on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, using only proprioception and binary tactile feedback as observations. We achieve successful zero-shot transfer through a combination of a sensor-aligned, coupling-aware embodiment in simulation, tactile calibration, and two novel episodic domain randomisations: slew-rate action limits and STuck-AT Taxels. On the physical hand, the policy achieves sustained blind Baoding rotation, completing 225 consecutive 𝟏𝟖𝟎∘\mathbf{180^{\circ}} rotations (112.5 full rotations) at ∼0.36​rot/s\sim 0.36\;\text{rot/s} in a single continuous trial without any vision or object-state information. Furthermore, we evaluate the contribution of tactile sensing relative to proprioception alone and identify the hand regions where tactile information is most important.
This is the strongest reported hardware result for Baoding ball manipulation in both rotation count and speed, irrespective of the sensing modality used. By effectively bridging the sim-to-real gap, our framework sets a new benchmark for sustained tactile-driven dexterous manipulation on physical hardware.
introduction:
In-hand manipulation requires continuous control of contact, with fingers making, breaking, and re-establishing contact as the object moves relative to the hand. The hand is simultaneously the actuator and the sensor, so each corrective motion changes the contact state from which the next correction is made. This intermittent contact and discontinuous dynamics make in-hand manipulation difficult to model and control. Most approaches address this challenge by supplying object state externally, through cameras, markers, or privileged simulator information. These observations provide explicit information about object pose and geometry, yet humans can reorient objects in the hand without continuously observing them, relying instead on contact during manipulation.
This raises a fundamental question: can contact alone stand in for explicit object state, as it does for humans?

We take this question literally. Unlike prior systems that rely on
cameras [1, 2],
motion-capture markers [3], or privileged
simulator state distilled into a student
policy [4, 5], our policy receives none
of these; it observes only joint encoders and 16 binary contact
signals, a representation shown to be sufficient in
simulation for single-object
rotation on hardware [6].
While most existing real-world in-hand manipulation studies focus on reorienting a single object via reinforcement learning (RL) [3, 7, 1, 6, 2, 5], we choose to study Baoding ball manipulation as a more challenging instance of in-hand dexterity: two objects circulate simultaneously, interact with each other as well as the fingers, and are manipulated here on only a four-fingered Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite. The phase relationship between the two objects must be maintained without being directly observed.

Prior approaches that attempt Baoding ball rotation have typically used external object-state information or tactile sensing to demonstrate rotation [8, 9, 10]. However, sustained zero-shot transfer of a blind policy from simulation to physical hardware remains an open challenge.
More recently, dexterous Baoding ball rotation was demonstrated in simulation across multiple robotic hands using only proprioception and binary contacts [11]. It was shown that combining RL with self-supervision (e.g. latent multi-step forward dynamics) learned implicit representations of the manipulated object(s) state, which led to superhuman simulated blind dexterity [12]. Yet, these works did not provide any hardware results, so the transferability of these results was unknown.

In this work, we achieve zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of Baoding ball rotation using only proprioceptive and binary contacts as observations, extending upon the simulation results in [12, 11]. We construct a simulation embodiment that reproduces the physical tendon coupling and tactile sensor layout used on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, and introduce per-channel tactile calibration, command slew-rate randomisation and Stuck-AT Taxels (STAT) to improve robustness to hardware discrepancies. We show that a policy trained entirely in simulation can complete 225 consecutive 180∘180^{\circ} rotations (112.5 full rotations) at ∼0.36​rot/s\sim 0.36\;\text{rot/s} in a single continuous trial on a physical Shadow Hand Lite from touch and proprioception alone. Our main contributions are as follows:

A hardware-aligned Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite simulation with matched tactile sensor sites and action mapping that reproduces the physical tendon coupling.

A hardware-aligned Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite simulation with matched tactile sensor sites and action mapping that reproduces the physical tendon coupling.

A per-channel hysteresis-based tactile calibration to mitigate sensor noise.

Two episode-level randomisations, Slew-rate Domain Randomisation (SlewDR) and Stuck-AT Taxels (STAT), that encourage smoother policy outputs and reduce reliance on individual tactile channels.

Rigorous benchmarking of Baoding ball rotation across increasing levels of feedback information and cumulative randomisation ablations.

Zero-shot transfer of a blind Baoding policy to the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, sustaining rotation from proprioception and binary contact, with tactile feedback substantially improving performance and long-horizon recovery.

1. A hardware-aligned Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite simulation with matched tactile sensor sites and action mapping that reproduces the physical tendon coupling.

2. A per-channel hysteresis-based tactile calibration to mitigate sensor noise.

3. Two episode-level randomisations, Slew-rate Domain Randomisation (SlewDR) and Stuck-AT Taxels (STAT), that encourage smoother policy outputs and reduce reliance on individual tactile channels.

4. Rigorous benchmarking of Baoding ball rotation across increasing levels of feedback information and cumulative randomisation ablations.

5. Zero-shot transfer of a blind Baoding policy to the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, sustaining rotation from proprioception and binary contact, with tactile feedback substantially improving performance and long-horizon recovery.

title: AWAM: Active Trajectory-Conditioned View Imagination for Robust Robot Manipulation
authors: Jiawei Geng,Zhenyang Liu,Yuzheng Wu,Yanwei Fu
abstract: Rapid progress in embodied intelligence has enabled increasingly capable robots to follow language instructions and manipulate diverse objects. However, strong results in structured environments do not automatically transfer to open-world conditions, where clutter, occlusion, and changing viewpoints can obscure the spatial relationships required for action. To address this perceptual gap, a virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced. AWAM, an Active World-Action Model actively plans where to observe and imagines what will be seen along the planned trajectory before acting. Task-related virtual camera motion is predicted and used as a structured query into a geometry-conditioned world model, producing a reusable spatial prior for manipulation, which is later compressed into a fixed memory and fused with live observations through cross-attention for diffusion-based action prediction. AWAM achieves competitive success rates with 75.9% on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 76.5% on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4% in real-robot trials. These results support improved robustness to the evaluated occlusions and distribution shifts, addressing part of the gap between structured manipulation and less controlled environments.
introduction:
Embodied intelligence has advanced rapidly through large-scale robot learning, vision–language pretraining, and generative action modeling. Increasingly capable policies can translate language goals and visual observations into manipulation behaviors across diverse tasks (Brohan and others, 2022; Brohan and others, 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025; Chi et al., 2025).

However, much of this progress is evaluated in relatively structured settings in which camera configurations, scene layouts, and task-relevant objects remain sufficiently observable. Occlusion-focused and distribution-shift benchmarks expose a complementary limitation: once deployment becomes less structured, an unfavorable camera pose, clutter, or a shifted layout can hide the target or interaction region and remove the evidence required for control (Li et al., 2026; Fei et al., 2026; Bai et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025c; Liu et al., 2025d). This creates a perceptual bottleneck rather than only an action-modeling bottleneck. More expressive action models alone cannot directly recover scene evidence that is absent or highly ambiguous in the input, so performance gains obtained under well-observed scenes may not transfer to open-world conditions with incomplete visibility.

Several lines of work have begun to address this problem. Physical active perception acquires additional evidence by moving the camera or robot, but introduces extra execution steps and can alter the robot or scene state. Virtual-view methods avoid this cost by selecting or synthesizing complementary observations. Candidate-view approaches choose from predefined cameras (Liu et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2026); TVVE predicts task-conditioned virtual poses and re-renders reconstructed geometry (Bai et al., 2026); and world-action models such as Motus and Fast-WAM exploit predictive visual modeling to strengthen action representations (Bi et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026). These directions establish the value of additional visual context, yet the underlying limitation is not fully resolved: virtual perception is often restricted to isolated views, reconstruction-based rendering cannot reveal surfaces absent from the initial geometry, and predictive world models are commonly organized around action-induced futures rather than deliberate viewpoint queries.

To address these questions, task-conditioned virtual active perception is formulated as trajectory-conditioned view imagination. Instead of selecting a single view or a small set of independent poses, a virtual camera trajectory specifies how perception should evolve to expose task-relevant evidence. Such a trajectory can reorient toward a target, approach fine interaction geometry, or move around an occluder when no single viewpoint is sufficient. Importantly, the predicted trajectory is never physically executed; it serves only as a sequence of virtual queries, thus retrieving the available evidence and learned spatial priors into a representation that better supports control, separating perceptual exploration from robot motion.

Based on this formulation, AWAM is introduced as an Active World-Action Model that realizes the virtual-perception process before closed-loop control. A task-conditioned trajectory predictor first produces virtual camera poses for better observation from the initial RGB-D image and language instruction. The calibrated observations are then back-projected into coarse 3D geometry and rendered along the predicted path. A geometry-conditioned world model fills unsupported regions and produces multi-view latent features, which are compressed into a persistent world memory. During manipulation, live static- and wrist-camera observations retrieve relevant predictive context from this memory, and a diffusion policy generates short-horizon action chunks in closed loop. The resulting design uses world modeling as an internal perceptual mechanism for asking where to look and what would be seen, rather than as a prediction of the robot’s executed future.

Evaluation is conducted across three simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation. Success reaches 75.9% on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 76.5±1.176.5\pm 1.1% on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4% in real-robot trials. On LIBERO-Occ, removing the entire predictive-memory branch reduces average success by 11.5 percentage points, and replacing learned task-conditioned virtual trajectory with sampled viewpoints reduces it by 5.7 points. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of learned virtual camera motion and persistent predictive memory for manipulation under incomplete visibility. The contributions are threefold:

A trajectory-conditioned virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced for manipulation, replacing isolated or physically executed viewpoint acquisition with a continuous sequence of task-directed virtual queries.

A trajectory-conditioned virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced for manipulation, replacing isolated or physically executed viewpoint acquisition with a continuous sequence of task-directed virtual queries.

AWAM is proposed to transform the predicted observation trajectory into geometry-consistent multi-view representations and compress them into persistent world memory as a reusable spatial prior for manipulation under partial observability.

Extensive evaluations across three challenging simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation demonstrate strong performance under occlusion and distribution shifts and confirm the benefits of learned camera motion and predictive memory through ablations.

1. A trajectory-conditioned virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced for manipulation, replacing isolated or physically executed viewpoint acquisition with a continuous sequence of task-directed virtual queries.

2. AWAM is proposed to transform the predicted observation trajectory into geometry-consistent multi-view representations and compress them into persistent world memory as a reusable spatial prior for manipulation under partial observability.

3. Extensive evaluations across three challenging simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation demonstrate strong performance under occlusion and distribution shifts and confirm the benefits of learned camera motion and predictive memory through ablations.

title: Look Before You Act: Bridging Active Perception and Vision-Language-Action Models via Observation-Aligned Data Adaptation
authors: Jiawei Geng,Zhenyang Liu,Yuzheng Wu,Yongchong Gu,Yanwei Fu
abstract: Robots manipulating objects in clutter must decide not only how to act, but also where to look. Although active camera motion can expose an occluded target, it may move the robot into an initial observation–state distribution that differs from the manipulation policy’s training distribution. We identify this problem as first-frame distribution sensitivity: under perturbed starts in LIBERO, naively prepending camera repositioning to π0.5\pi_{0.5} reduces success from 46.3% to 11.5%. We introduce ActiveAlign, a data-adaptation framework that trains a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy from the states at which active perception terminates. A learned viewpoint module first generates a camera trajectory. Offline, ActiveAlign uses closed-loop alignment to connect the trajectory endpoint to an existing demonstration, replays the remaining manipulation trajectory, and retains successful continuations for fine-tuning. At deployment, the same viewpoint module precedes the adapted VLA without modifying its architecture. Across 40 LIBERO tasks, ActiveAlign achieves 70.7% success with π0\pi_{0} and 72.7% with π0.5\pi_{0.5}, outperforming their standard-training baselines by 40.0% and 26.4% respectively. Matched-state and data-matched controls support gains beyond prefix shortening and generic viewpoint augmentation; OpenVLA and GR00T N1 also show the same trend. Success rate under physical occlusion in real world increases from 35/90 to 83/90. These results show that active perception benefits manipulation when policy training is aligned with the observation and robot-state distribution induced by viewpoint selection.
introduction:
Effective manipulation begins with an observation that supports the intended action [1, 2]. A robot asked to retrieve fruit from a container or grasp a cup behind clutter may need to move its camera before it can see a useful approach direction. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [3, 4, 5, 6, 7] provide a powerful interface from visual observations and language to robot actions, but their input is still determined by where the robot looks. Repositioning an existing wrist camera is an appealing way to expose the target before manipulation. The resulting system must therefore solve two connected problems: selecting an informative view and continuing the task from the state produced by that selection.

The most direct composition is to let an active-perception (AP) module improve the view, then hand control to a VLA trained on conventional demonstrations. Our experiments reveal a counterintuitive outcome: this composition can substantially reduce task success. Under a shared perturbed-start LIBERO protocol, π0.5\pi_{0.5} falls from 46.3% to 11.5% average success after camera repositioning, and π0\pi_{0} falls from 30.7% to 7.0%. The qualitative examples in Fig. 1 illustrate the tension: a policy can act from a familiar but occluded view, yet struggle to exploit a view selected to reveal the target. Improving the observation and making it usable by the action policy are distinct requirements.

We study this interface through first-frame distribution sensitivity. Here, the first frame is the observation at the handoff from active perception to manipulation. Wrist-camera motion changes image location, scale, and occlusion together with arm configuration and the relationship to the remaining task. A policy must consequently infer a suitable continuation from a different combination of visual and proprioceptive cues. Action chunking [8, 9] can propagate an early error through the actions executed before the next observation, even when later decisions use fresh images. This motivates examining the joint observation–action interface; a difference between first-frame image distributions alone does not establish the cause of every failure. Our experiments therefore pair the failure observation with controls that separate viewpoint information from robot-state progress and data volume.

The central design insight is that the deployment viewpoint policy is available during data construction. Rather than requiring a manipulation learner to accommodate arbitrary sensing motions, we can expose it to successful continuations from the endpoints of the very module it will encounter at inference. This turns the composition problem into a question about supervision: how can existing demonstrations be made to begin where active perception stops? Demonstration-generation methods such as MimicGen and DemoGen [10, 11] motivate reusing recorded behavior, while the present setting adds a specific constraint: the starting observation and state are chosen by a task-conditioned camera policy. Visual augmentation alone does not supply the actions needed to continue from that state.

ActiveAlign constructs these continuations offline. Given scene RGBD and a language instruction, a learned module predicts a wrist-camera trajectory. In a restored environment, we execute the trajectory and match its endpoint to a nearby end-effector state in an early demonstration prefix. Closed-loop alignment bridges the residual gap, after which the recorded manipulation suffix is replayed. Successful alignment-and-replay trajectories become training data for the VLA. The active approach replaces part of the original demonstration, while the recorded continuation teaches the policy how to proceed after that approach. At deployment, the same viewpoint module runs once before object contact; the adapted VLA then manipulates using fresh observations. The procedure changes training data and policy weights while preserving the VLA architecture.

Replay feasibility is essential to this construction. End-effector proximity does not ensure that object and contact states agree, so nearest-state matching alone cannot validate a continuation. Successful replay filters the candidate endpoints and limits the training distribution to states for which usable supervision can be reconstructed. ActiveAlign consequently applies to resettable simulators and reconstructable physical workcells. This requirement belongs to offline data collection: deployment requires neither scene reset nor expert replay. The resulting scope is pre-manipulation view selection, with longer-horizon tasks testing the lasting value of that initial view rather than continuous response to moving occluders.

Our evaluation follows this reasoning from composition failure to controlled explanation and physical validation. On LIBERO Spatial, a matched-state camera-extrinsics control holds the demonstration step and manipulation suffix fixed and reaches 54.6%, compared with 78.2% for ActiveAlign. Data-matched random views and broad viewpoint jitter reach 58.0% and 61.4%, respectively. These comparisons support a benefit from the informative, deployment-matched observations beyond shorter demonstrations and generic coverage. Across four suites, ActiveAlign improves π0\pi_{0} and π0.5\pi_{0.5} by 40.0 and 26.4 percentage points; OpenVLA and GR00T N1 extend the evidence to different action formulations. Initial-occlusion simulation tasks, diverse physical tasks, and endpoint perturbations further characterize when the construction is useful and where it breaks down.

Our contributions are threefold:

We characterize the failure of naive composition of active perception and VLAs, and test competing explanations through matched-state and data-matched controls.

We introduce observation-aligned demonstration adaptation, connecting active-view endpoints to successful manipulation through prefix matching, closed-loop alignment, and replay filtering.

We evaluate the construction across four VLA backbones, 40 LIBERO tasks, initial occlusion, and physical manipulation, with sensitivity studies that quantify the feasibility–diversity trade-off and endpoint error tolerance.

1. We characterize the failure of naive composition of active perception and VLAs, and test competing explanations through matched-state and data-matched controls.

2. We introduce observation-aligned demonstration adaptation, connecting active-view endpoints to successful manipulation through prefix matching, closed-loop alignment, and replay filtering.

3. We evaluate the construction across four VLA backbones, 40 LIBERO tasks, initial occlusion, and physical manipulation, with sensitivity studies that quantify the feasibility–diversity trade-off and endpoint error tolerance.

title: Beyond Success Rate: Interventional Evaluation of Memory in Vision-Language-Action Systems
authors: Keyuan Luo,Yi Xie,Wanyun Ling,Yuanzhe Li,Ziyue Li,Zhuoqi Zeng
comment: including references and appendices
abstract:
When we say that a robot uses memory, does that memory actually play a role?
Success-rate ablations alone cannot establish the use of task-relevant facts: they
change information and computation together, while aggregate rates can hide
offsetting gains and losses. We propose an Interventional Memory Evaluation
Protocol (IMEP) for vision–language–action (VLA) systems to address four
questions: (1) Does memory provide a net benefit? (2) Under what conditions does
memory help? (3) Do changes to memory alter task outcomes? (4) Are these effects
specific to task-relevant facts? At the retrieval interface, we
compare target-fact substitutions with fact-preserving replacements, minimal
numerical perturbations, and exact replicas, while assessing decision correctness
separately from motor execution success. We evaluate within-episode,
cross-episode, and agentic memory. In cross-episode learned-bank experiments,
a one-unit-in-the-last-place (ULP) intervention, including its installation
procedure, changes 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while changing key facts produces no clear additional effect
over fact-preserving replacements. To examine when memory helps, we introduce
ChainBench, where correct decisions require historical information unavailable in
current observations. The full memory configuration raises task
success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching the oracle-decision condition under
shared recorded executions. These results show that correct history can support
robot decisions, but establishing whether a memory system realizes this benefit
requires fact-specific evidence beyond aggregate success rates.
introduction:
A robot’s current observation may omit information needed to act: an earlier
visual cue, a previous episode’s experience, or a fact retained across tasks.
Vision–language–action (VLA) systems therefore augment policies with memory
banks, event keyframes, or temporal representations
(Shi et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026; Koo et al., 2026), experience retrieval (Sridhar et al., 2026), and external
text records (Zhang et al., 2026b). These mechanisms aim to turn history into
useful evidence for current decisions. Their value is often evaluated through
memory ablations and task success (Shi et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026). Such gains show
improved performance, but do they establish use of task-relevant stored facts
(Figure 1a)?

Three distinctions prevent that inference. First, enabling memory can change
both information and computation. Second, an unchanged success rate can hide
gains on some trials and losses on others (Milani Fard et al., 2016). Third, changing memory can alter
behavior even when a replacement preserves the target fact or introduces only
a small numerical perturbation. History can also support shortcuts, as shown
by causal confusion and copycat behavior in imitation learning
(de Haan et al., 2019; Wen et al., 2020). Behavioral sensitivity alone does not
establish use of task-relevant facts. Conversely, an undetected net gain does not imply
that memory has no effect. Interpretation also depends on whether current
observations already reveal the answer, whether an intervention reaches the
reader, and whether stored facts remain valid.

We introduce the Interventional Memory Evaluation Protocol (IMEP) to
separate net benefit (Q1), conditions for memory to help (Q2), outcome
sensitivity (Q3), and fact specificity (Q4). At a fixed retrieval interface,
IMEP compares replacements that change the target fact with those that preserve
it. On matched units, it records outcome flips alongside aggregate success
and scores decisions separately from execution where observable.
Section 3 defines the protocol; Section 2
discusses related work.

In the evaluated learned banks, memory interventions change outcomes without
establishing fact specificity. Remember Color’s one-unit-in-the-last-place
(ULP) control, including installation, changes 11.9%11.9\% of paired outcomes;
different-fact replacements, as delivered, produce no clear additional effect
over same-fact replacements. No detected learned-bank gain meets a registered net-benefit
criterion. On ChainBench, full memory achieves perfect decision accuracy on
202 chains and raises task success from 39.1%39.1\% to 74.3%74.3\%, matching the
oracle under shared recorded executions. A separate
experiment supports fact specificity for a scripted reader on curated records.

Our contributions are:

IMEP, a four-question protocol using fact-changing and
fact-preserving substitutions, exact repeats, and one-ULP controls, with
separate decision and execution readouts.

ChainBench, a LIBERO benchmark of multi-episode chains requiring
historical facts absent from current observations, with decisions scored
separately from motor execution.

An evaluation of within-episode, cross-episode and agentic
memory, finding outcome sensitivity without established fact specificity in
learned banks, and task success at the motor-execution ceiling for the evaluated
ChainBench configuration under shared recorded executions.

1. IMEP, a four-question protocol using fact-changing and
fact-preserving substitutions, exact repeats, and one-ULP controls, with
separate decision and execution readouts.

2. ChainBench, a LIBERO benchmark of multi-episode chains requiring
historical facts absent from current observations, with decisions scored
separately from motor execution.

3. An evaluation of within-episode, cross-episode and agentic
memory, finding outcome sensitivity without established fact specificity in
learned banks, and task success at the motor-execution ceiling for the evaluated
ChainBench configuration under shared recorded executions.

title: LAW: Unifying Language, Action, and World Modeling for Agentic Physical Intelligence
authors: Jiajun Cao,Kai Tang,Bohua Zhang,Zezhong Qian,Ying Li,Xiaozhu Ju,Xiaobao Wei,Jiaming Liu,Yang Ding,Sixiang Chen,Yiding Sun,Siyuan Qian,Tinghao Wang,Jixian Wu,Yichen Guo,Yi Zhang,Shilong Zou,Yong Dai,Jian Tang,Shanghang Zhang
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Long-horizon manipulation is a sequence of semantic subtasks, not merely a longer sequence of motor commands. After reaching for an object, a robot must decide whether the grasp actually succeeded; after a successful grasp, it must recognize that the task has entered a new stage; before executing the next motion, it must choose among several physically plausible actions according to the current objective [23, 22]. Errors in any of these decisions compound over time. Consequently, local action quality alone does not determine task success. A capable agent must maintain a persistent account of task progress, connect that account to action generation, and revise its decisions when execution departs from expectation [35, 44].

Vision-language-action policies connect semantic representations to control [60, 26, 8], while world-action models learn action-conditioned scene evolution and executable behavior [59, 57, 27, 51]. These models substantially improve action generation, but long-horizon deployment exposes a complementary systems problem: reasoning and control must remain aligned as the task evolves. A language plan generated once at the beginning cannot determine whether its intermediate steps were completed [22], and an action generator conditioned only on the current observation may not know which visual changes matter to the larger goal [41]. Placing a planner before a policy therefore leaves three interfaces underspecified: how execution progress updates the plan, how candidate actions are judged against the current semantic objective, and how relevant history is retained without overwhelming either model.

Our premise is that semantic subtask progress should serve as the temporal interface between language reasoning and world-action modeling. Subtasks provide more than a decomposition of the instruction: they define when the agent should advance its plan, which outcomes a candidate action should optimize, and which observations should remain salient in memory. This view reveals that computations occur at different rates. State assessment should run continuously without blocking control, candidate evaluation should occur whenever the WAM proposes a new action chunk, and planning should operate at the semantic task scale rather than at every control step. The challenge is coordinating reasoning and control, rather than invoking a larger reasoner at every step.

We instantiate this principle in LAW, a closed-loop VLM–WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress, as summarized in Fig. 1. The LAW agent uses a hybrid-expert VLM with role-selected planner, state, and value experts on a shared frozen backbone. The planner predicts the remaining semantic subtasks; conditioned on the current subtask, the WAM generates diverse action chunks; the value expert ranks and fuses them; and execution status is assessed asynchronously to determine subtask completion. Once the current subtask is completed, the planner predicts the next subtask and the agent switches to it; otherwise, the agent continues executing the current subtask. The LAW agent coordinates planning, action selection, and execution monitoring at different frequencies, using feedback to continue or switch subtasks.

To strengthen joint world and action modeling, we introduce Mixture-of-Transformer Experts (MoTE) into the WAM, yielding MoTE-WAM. MoT projects video and action features into a common attention space to exchange cross-modal information, but their subsequent transformations remain modality-specific. MoTE introduces shared experts to further transform these cross-modal representations, alongside video-private and action-private experts that preserve modality-specific computation. The shared experts learn common temporal and physical structure across predicted scene dynamics and robot actions, strengthening video–action joint modeling beyond information exchange through attention alone. Long-horizon execution also requires memory aligned with subtask transitions. Separate hierarchical memory streams for the VLM and WAM retain recent observations and full-resolution states at subtask boundaries, while compressing older history to preserve relevant context across subtasks. To better exploit failed trajectories when training the value expert, we introduce subtask-local value learning, which terminates returns at semantic boundaries. This preserves positive supervision from successfully completed subtasks within failed episodes, rather than assigning zero value to all their actions.

We evaluate LAW on 50 RoboTwin [13] tasks, the RoboDojo [12] capability benchmark, and three long-horizon real-robot tasks containing up to nine semantic subtasks. LAW achieves 94.21% average success on RoboTwin, 2.38 percentage points above Fast-WAM, without robot-data pretraining. Replacing the WAM backbone with OpenWAM-α\alpha further raises the average success rate to 95.56%, establishing a new open-source state of the art on RoboTwin. Despite having only 2B parameters, our VLM outperforms variants using Embodied-R1.5 and GPT-5.5 High within the same LAW framework. On RoboDojo, LAW achieves leading performance across capability dimensions among methods without additional robot-domain or embodied-interaction pretraining. On the three long-horizon real-robot tasks, LAW achieves 65% average success, compared with 28.33% for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 25% for Fast-WAM. We also conduct extensive ablation studies to validate the effectiveness of each component. Our contributions are:

We introduce LAW, a closed-loop VLM–WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress. The LAW agent coordinates planning, asynchronous completion assessment, and value-guided action fusion for long-horizon execution.

We introduce MoTE, dual-stream hierarchical memory, and subtask-local value learning to support progress-aware control: MoTE strengthens joint video–action modeling through shared and modality-specific experts; dual-stream hierarchical memory preserves task-relevant history and subtask-boundary observations; and subtask-local value learning retains positive supervision from completed stages of failed trajectories.

We demonstrate LAW’s effectiveness on RoboTwin, RoboDojo, and long-horizon real-world manipulation through extensive experiments and ablation studies. Integrating OpenWAM-α\alpha achieves 95.56% average success on RoboTwin, establishing a new open-source state of the art and demonstrating LAW’s extensibility to stronger pretrained WAMs.

We introduce MoTE, dual-stream hierarchical memory, and subtask-local value learning to support progress-aware control: MoTE strengthens joint video–action modeling through shared and modality-specific experts; dual-stream hierarchical memory preserves task-relevant history and subtask-boundary observations; and subtask-local value learning retains positive supervision from completed stages of failed trajectories.

title: SkyAgent: Revisable Target Memory for Continuous Aerial Search
authors: Kaibo Yang,Xingyu Wu,Enze Zhu,Yajie Chai,Xuyang Li,Jiahui Cui,Xiaoxuan Liu,Lei Wang,Zhan Chen
abstract:
Continuous aerial search builds target hypotheses from sparse,
viewpoint-dependent observations.
When later evidence contradicts a stored hypothesis, however, the
candidate can remain available to the planner and continue triggering
approach or verification actions.
We call this trajectory-level failure false candidate persistence
(FCP).
We equip SkyAgent with Revisable Target Memory (RTM),
which associates evidence with persistent candidates, discounts
correlated views, and revises each candidate through
Tentative, Confirmed, and Rejected states.
The key interface binds every generated waypoint to its source candidate:
rejection therefore invalidates stale goals, while conservative
reactivation protects temporarily occluded targets. Across four splits from the CityAVOS, UAV-ON, and OpenUAV benchmarks, our SkyAgent equipped with RTM outperforms all competitors, improving SR by 2.90–6.31 points while substantially reducing Behavior-FCP and post-contradiction travel with a low false-rejection rate. Across 35 matched real-world DJI scenarios per method, RTM consistently improves task success and behavioral reliability, further validating its state-to-action correction under physical deployment conditions.
introduction:
In a representative aerial search, a distant rectangular region is logged
as a target candidate.
A later side-angle view reveals that the region is a facade reflection,
not the target.
This revision problem is central to continuous aerial object search: the
physical target is static, but evidence about each candidate shifts
as the vehicle approaches, changes viewpoint, or encounters occlusion
(Ji et al. 2026; Xiao et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2025).
The agent rarely sees decisive evidence in a single frame; a distant
shape, a brief gap in foliage, or an intermittent specular return may be
all that a long trajectory provides.

Existing aerial agents have made progress on two fronts.
Memory-based methods retain observations across frames through
asynchronous maps, octree representations, or filtered
write-in (Zhang et al. 2026a; Zhou et al. 2026; Ji et al. 2026).
Verification-based methods seek additional viewpoints before
committing to a stop or reconsider a selected snapshot before
executing it (Jang and Kim 2026; Cao et al. 2025; Ren et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2026a).
Both fronts focus on the forward direction: building or validating
confidence before a decision is made.
We focus on what happens after: when a later view contradicts
a candidate already sitting in persistent memory, can the system
actually change that memory and cancel the goals it generated?
In the systems we study, the answer is often no—the candidate remains
available to planning even after a closer view proves it wrong.

We define false candidate persistence (FCP) as a trajectory-level
failure: after a candidate receives sufficient reference contradiction,
it stays in the active plan (State-FCP) or again induces approach,
revisit, or confirmation actions (Behavior-FCP).
FCP is not a transient detector error, which is a wrong observation in
a single frame; it is a known-wrong hypothesis that continues to consume
distance, time, and planning cycles through stale memory state.
Figure 1 illustrates this failure and its correction.

The fix is not more storage.
It is different memory semantics: candidates should be revisable
hypotheses, not committed facts.
A candidate must retain both supporting and opposing evidence, discount
redundant adjacent frames, and expose an explicit lifecycle state to
the planner.
Changing a score alone is not enough; when a candidate is rejected,
every pending waypoint it sourced must be invalidated before the next
planning cycle.
At the same time, rejection must not be permanent, because temporary
occlusion and low-quality frames can produce misleading negative evidence.

We equip the SkyAgent execution backbone with
Revisable Target Memory (RTM).
Candidate Evidence Memory associates observations with persistent
candidates, groups them by independent viewpoint, and accumulates
signed evidence.
Revise-and-Suppress maps accumulated evidence to lifecycle states
through a state-dependent transition function and cancels all stale
waypoints on rejection.
The existing fast search policy, event trigger, inspection skills, and
safety-projected controller remain as execution infrastructure;
candidate truth state is managed exclusively through RTM.

Our contributions are three:
(1) we identify false candidate persistence (FCP) as a trajectory-level
failure distinct from transient detection errors, and introduce
complementary state-, behavior-, and cost-level measures that separate a
stored false hypothesis from one that still affects flight;
(2) we propose Revisable Target Memory (RTM), which couples candidate
lifecycle revision to planner binding: rejecting a candidate invalidates
every unexecuted goal it sourced, while conservative reactivation permits
recovery after new independent positive evidence;
(3) we evaluate RTM through natural FCP prevalence, controlled comparisons
and mechanism ablations on three aerial benchmarks, and 35 matched DJI
scenarios per method (Table 1).

title: CoEvolve: Self-Evolving Code Policies from Skills to Strategies for Humanoid Robots
authors: Zicheng Liu,Haochen Wu,Jiawei He,Suyun Zhao,Huan Yang,Cheng Chi,Hao Tang
comment: Under review at ICLR 2027
abstract:
Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Action
Models (WAMs) have expanded the manipulation and whole body capabilities of
individual robots. Yet a single robot remains limited by its embodiment, and
many real world tasks require capabilities that can only emerge through
cooperation. Existing multi robot frameworks largely emphasize task
decomposition, allocation, and replanning, while providing limited support
for adapting executable coordination when physical execution deviates from
the intended behavior. We present CoEvolve, a framework that represents
team coordination as executable code over fixed robot motor skills.
CoEvolve introduces Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution, where a
multimodal foundation model instantiates coordination strategies through
motion primitives, semantic objectives, temporary robot roles, and bounded
execution parameters. Physical verification evaluates each executed
transition, rejected behaviors trigger structured coordination revision from
an accepted checkpoint, and verified experience is retained to guide
subsequent decisions. We evaluate CoEvolve with two simulated Unitree G1
humanoids transporting a freely supported rigid payload through constrained
corridors. Across 15 base task runs with three multimodal backbone families,
CoEvolve completes 8 tasks, with every backbone achieving end to end
success. Additional evaluations yield verified placement on two additional
corridor layouts and after both same-backbone and cross-backbone experience
initialization, while exposing persistent limitations in motion precision and
contact stability. These results support executable coordination as a
practical interface for adapting long horizon multi robot collaboration under
shared physical constraints. Our code will be available at
https://github.com/Innovationlzc/CoEvolve.
introduction:
Recent advances in robot foundation models have equipped individual robots
with increasingly general visuomotor capabilities, enabling them to follow
language instructions and perform diverse manipulation
tasks (Brohan et al., 2022; Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024).
Yet some physical tasks require capabilities that cannot be provided by one
robot alone. Transporting an extended object through a constrained environment, for
example, requires coordinated support, relative motion, corner negotiation,
and placement (De Vincenti and Coros, 2023; Pandit et al., 2025).
Collaboration is therefore not simply the aggregation of individual skills.
Robots that can independently walk, turn, and move laterally must still
determine how to combine these capabilities while carrying a shared object.
We view this formation of team behavior as a form of co-becoming:
effective cooperation is realized through the changing relationship between
individual capabilities and the shared physical state.

This motivates our central question: given fixed individual motor
skills, how can an agent instantiate and revise executable team coordination
as a shared physical task unfolds?
Multi-robot planning methods address task decomposition, allocation, and
collaboration through structured and language-model planning
 (Cai et al., 2025; Mandi et al., 2024; Kannan et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a; Yuan et al., 2026),
while learned coordination methods optimize joint or decentralized policies
through training (Zhang et al., 2026a; Doshi et al., 2026). In parallel, agents improve
textual skills, memory systems, and executable implementations through
feedback and experience
sharing (Yang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025; Weng et al., 2026).
Code as Policies and subsequent robot programming systems also generate and
revise executable behaviors through
interaction (Liang et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026).
We study a complementary challenge: revising coordination when robots are
physically coupled through a shared payload. In this setting, an individual
action can alter both a teammate’s support conditions and the feasibility of
subsequent joint motion. As a result, a valid task plan does not guarantee
that the current coordination pattern remains executable. The key challenge
is therefore to instantiate joint behavior from fixed motor skills and revise
the relevant coordination relation when physical execution deviates, for
example when unequal displacement disrupts formation or a constrained turn
requires temporary support and mover roles.

We introduce CoEvolve, a framework for adapting executable team
coordination during shared physical tasks. Figure 1 summarizes
the motivation and overall interaction loop. CoEvolve separates fixed
individual motor capabilities from the coordination strategy that composes
them for the current task phase. Rather than selecting from a library of
complete strategies, the agent instantiates coordination through motion
primitives, semantic objectives, temporary roles, coordination modes, and
bounded execution parameters. The evaluated setting provides simulator
measurements and route references, while the model determines how these
capabilities should be combined within the resulting physical constraints.

Our Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution mechanism uses physical execution
evidence to determine which aspects of coordination should change. A rejected
transition triggers a revision to the maneuver, the relationship between
robot roles, or the execution parameters. Revised policies are evaluated
after restoration of the latest accepted simulator checkpoint. Verified
outcomes also contribute complementary forms of experience: abstract
coordination records guide subsequent decisions, while accepted executable
examples inform code generation. Foundation model and motor policy weights
remain fixed. The adaptation concerns the task plan, instantiated
coordination strategies, and stored experience rather than the acquisition
of new motor skills.

We evaluate CoEvolve with two simulated Unitree G1 humanoids carrying a
freely supported rigid payload through constrained corridors. The base
evaluation contains eight complete tasks across fifteen runs and three
foundation model families. We further compare against four adapted external
baselines and two component variants, evaluate additional corridor layouts,
and study reuse of verified cooperative experience across foundation model
backbones. These experiments distinguish demonstrated execution capability
from causal component effects: some comparison, scene, and transfer records
differ in runtime configuration, interaction budget, or continuation
conditions. Our contributions are:

We introduce an executable representation of team coordination
that separates fixed individual motor capabilities from the cooperative
strategy instantiated for the current physical situation.

We introduce an executable representation of team coordination
that separates fixed individual motor capabilities from the cooperative
strategy instantiated for the current physical situation.

We propose Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution, which combines
physical verification, structured strategy revision, and reusable
cooperative experience to adapt coordination during execution.

We provide an extensive evaluation across three foundation model
families, adapted multi robot and code policy baselines, additional corridor
layouts, and cross-model experience reuse, while analyzing the execution and
contact limitations that remain.

1. We introduce an executable representation of team coordination
that separates fixed individual motor capabilities from the cooperative
strategy instantiated for the current physical situation.

2. We propose Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution, which combines
physical verification, structured strategy revision, and reusable
cooperative experience to adapt coordination during execution.

3. We provide an extensive evaluation across three foundation model
families, adapted multi robot and code policy baselines, additional corridor
layouts, and cross-model experience reuse, while analyzing the execution and
contact limitations that remain.

title: NestedVLA: Learning to Consolidate and Generate Skills for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Guodong Du,Wanyu Lin
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. . Code:this https URL
abstract:
Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models promise generalist robotic
agents, yet consolidating skills learned across heterogeneous tasks and
environments remains difficult: training data is fragmented across
platforms, joint multi-task training suffers from interference, and model
merging tends to introduce parameter conflicts or require architectural
changes. We instead advocate a paradigm in which skills are first learned
independently and then consolidated post hoc. To this end, we propose
NestedVLA, which replaces parameter aggregation with
parameter generation: a nested hypernetwork, conditioned on the
target task, synthesizes task-adaptive action-expert parameters that compose
with a frozen base VLA. Task-specific compressed VLM residuals are retained
separately. This formulation enables flexible task-conditioned skill reuse
while mitigating interference. Across three RL benchmarks (MetaWorld,
ManiSkill, CALVIN), NestedVLA outperforms the strongest model-merging
baseline by 4141 pp on average, matches per-task fine-tuning within
11 pp on ManiSkill, and substantially closes the gap on CALVIN, pointing
toward a storage-efficient route to skill consolidation. Code is available
at https://github.com/WanyuGroup/NeurIPS2026-NestedVLA.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine visual and language understanding
with embodied control [2, 71, 26, 1, 40]. Independently
fine-tuning a common backbone produces policies specialized for different
robotic benchmarks, but storing one full checkpoint per benchmark duplicates
most parameters. Joint multi-task training can avoid this duplication when
data from all benchmarks can be pooled. We instead study post-hoc
consolidation of policies independently fine-tuned from the same backbone.
We seek to consolidate their task-specific parameter updates into a compact
representation without pooling the original training data.

A natural post-hoc approach is to merge the parameter updates of the
fine-tuned policies into a single checkpoint. In VLA models, however,
independently learned updates can interfere strongly when combined: in our
experiments, simple averaging loses most of the performance of the separate
policies. Our weight-space analysis finds weak alignment across major
parameter groups, an incompatibility that is particularly consequential in
the action expert because it directly governs control
(Appendix E). This observation is consistent with
MergeVLA [16], which likewise identifies dependencies
distributed across action-expert layers as a major obstacle to cross-skill
merging. These findings motivate a consolidation strategy that preserves
policy-specific parameter structure rather than collapsing all updates into
one set of weights.

We propose NestedVLA, a framework that shifts the paradigm from
parameter aggregation to parameter generation. A hypernetwork embedded in
the VLA generates sparse action-expert updates conditioned on the target
task, while compressed task-specific VLM residuals are retained separately.
The selected updates compose with a shared base to instantiate a
task-specific VLA without changing its forward architecture or introducing
routing supervision. We evaluate NestedVLA on MetaWorld [35],
ManiSkill [45], and CALVIN [36] using the open-source
π0.5\pi_{0.5} [40] backbone. NestedVLA outperforms the strongest
model-merging baseline by 4141 pp on average, matches per-task fine-tuning
within 11 pp on ManiSkill, and substantially closes the gap on CALVIN.

title: Expand-and-Prune: Test-Time Candidate-Space Adaptation for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
authors: Fabian Schmidt,Karol Fedurko,Markus Enzweiler,Abhinav Valada
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Accepted to IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) 2027
abstract:
Candidate-based end-to-end driving planners reason over a finite set of trajectory hypotheses. However, for sparse planners, a limited candidate set may provide insufficient support for scene-relevant maneuvers, while fixed downstream candidate budgets do not account for prediction uncertainty.
To address these challenges, we introduce Expand-and-Prune, a test-time framework that jointly adapts candidate support and capacity without updating learned parameters.
The framework expands the native candidate set using semantic driving intent and temporally propagated predictions and then uses uncertainty in intermediate trajectory scores to adaptively prune the resulting candidates.
Across four heterogeneous candidate-based planners and four benchmarks, Expand-and-Prune consistently improves planning performance.
It achieves state-of-the-art results on LangAuto, increasing the Driving Score from 68.268.2 to 75.975.9, while providing further improvement on Bench2Drive, Fail2Drive, and NAVSIMv2, with particularly strong improvements in out-of-distribution scenarios.
Moreover, in its full instantiation, 72.5%72.5\% of selected trajectories originate from the newly introduced intent-guided or temporal candidates, confirming that candidate-space expansion provides useful hypotheses beyond those generated natively by the planner.
The code is available at https://github.com/iis-esslingen/Expand-and-Prune.
introduction:
End-to-end planning has become a prominent paradigm for autonomous driving, directly mapping sensor observations and contextual information to future ego motion [2, 8, 11, 21].
Rather than predicting only a single trajectory, many recent planners capture multimodal driving behavior through a finite set of motion hypotheses.
These candidates may originate from offline precomputed trajectory vocabularies or clustered anchors [14, 17, 34, 27], or be generated and refined online through learned queries, diffusion, or related generative mechanisms [13, 5, 18, 41, 22].
The planner subsequently scores or refines these hypotheses before selecting a trajectory for execution [17, 34, 27].

Despite advances in candidate generation, how motion hypotheses are constructed and how many are propagated downstream remains largely prescribed by the planner’s inference design.
First, for sparse anchor- or proposal-based planners [18, 19], a limited number of hypotheses must cover a broad motion space and may therefore provide only limited support for the maneuver currently favored by the scene.
For example, a generic candidate set may contain only a few hypotheses matching a sharp turn even when the current semantic belief strongly favors that maneuver.
Second, a fixed downstream candidate budget, often implemented through static Top-KK selection, treats confident and ambiguous scenes alike, propagating the same number of hypotheses regardless of how many plausible alternatives remain [34, 27].
Such limitations may become particularly consequential over longer closed-loop horizons and under distribution shift, where the planner may encounter scene configurations and maneuvers that are poorly represented by its training distribution and native candidate set.

Learned scene-adaptive proposal mechanisms [35, 36] can improve candidate generation, but require planner-specific training. Other methods operate at test time [25, 32], either updating model parameters or optimizing trajectories using the planner’s scores as an objective. In contrast, we keep the pretrained planner entirely fixed and adapt its candidate space at inference time, leaving both the model parameters and the scoring procedure unchanged. Thus, we enable adaptation of pretrained planners without specific retraining or modification of their native scoring pipeline.

Building on this principle, we introduce Expand-and-Prune, which dynamically reshapes the planner’s candidate space through complementary expansion and pruning, cf. Fig. 1.
Intent-guided candidate expansion and entropy-adaptive temporal memory augment the native candidate set with semantically and temporally relevant hypotheses.
Uncertainty-aware adaptive pruning regulates downstream candidate capacity.
Expansion therefore adapts where candidate support is allocated, while pruning adapts how many hypotheses receive further computation.
Both mechanisms operate at existing candidate-processing boundaries, enabling their integration into different candidate-based architectures.

We evaluate Expand-and-Prune using LAD-Drive [22] on LangAuto [23] as our primary testbed. Expand-and-Prune achieves state-of-the-art performance, increasing mean Driving Score from 68.268.2 to 75.975.9, with particularly strong improvements on longer routes.
We further evaluate the transferability of our framework across three additional heterogeneous candidate-based planners.
For each architecture, we instantiate the components that are compatible with its native candidate representation and processing pipeline, using the established evaluation settings: BridgeDrive [19] on Bench2Drive [9], and DriveSuprim [34] and SparseDriveV2 [27] on NAVSIMv2 [1].
Across these planners and benchmarks, the proposed adaptations consistently improve planning performance.
We additionally evaluate our candidate-space-adapted BridgeDrive on Fail2Drive [6], where the gains become particularly pronounced in out-of-distribution scenarios.
Candidate-provenance analysis on LAD-Drive further reveals that 72.5%72.5\% of selected trajectories originate from the added intent-guided or temporal candidates, indicating that the additional hypotheses frequently influence the planner’s final decision.

Our main contribution is Expand-and-Prune, a test-time framework for adapting the candidate support and downstream capacity of pretrained candidate-based driving planners without updating their learned parameters or modifying their scoring procedure.
We demonstrate the generality of this principle across sparse diffusion and dense selection-based planners, complemented by analyses of candidate provenance, adaptive capacity, and computational efficiency.

title: SimpleVLN: Towards Simple and Frontier Vision-Language Navigation
authors: Lingyi Hong,Weiren Cai,Jiayu Chen,Xinyu Zhou,Bailin He,Yunfei Guo,Qiao Sun,Boyu Ma,Jianfei Yang,Wenqiang Zhang

abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires embodied agents to ground language in visual observations and make long-horizon decisions. Existing methods often address these demands through task-specific architectures. As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly capable, an important question remains: Have we truly unlocked the potential of native MLLMs for VLN before introducing task-specific architecture? introduction:
Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires embodied agents to follow natural-language instructions in unseen environments (Anderson et al., 2018; Ku et al., 2020), combining visual understanding, language grounding, spatial reasoning, and long-horizon decision making. Existing methods have advanced through task-specific designs for perception and spatial reasoning (Zeng et al., 2026), graph-based modeling (Chen et al., 2022), and hierarchical or dual-system decision making (Wei et al., 2026). These architectures are effective, while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer strong general-purpose visual understanding, reasoning, and instruction following (Bai et al., 2025). However, the performance of augmented MLLM systems reflects both the backbone and task-specific components, leaving the capability of a native MLLM alone unclear. This raises an underexplored question: Have we truly unlocked the potential of native MLLMs for VLN before introducing task-specific architecture? To answer it, we investigate how far native MLLMs can be advanced for VLN without architectural modifications.

Preserving the architecture still requires adapting the MLLM to sequential navigation. We develop SimpleVLN by studying three aspects: formulation, data construction, and optimization (Figure 1). First, at the formulation level, we combine single-turn decision inputs with fixed-budget global–local memory to prevent unbounded context growth while efficiently using navigation history. Action chunking further enables efficient action output by predicting multiple primitive actions per model invocation. Second, for data construction, we combine expert demonstrations with policy-dependent experience collected through DAgger (Ross et al., 2011). We further develop a scalable task-synthesis pipeline to generate large-scale navigation tasks for reinforcement learning. Third, at the optimization level, we investigate a progressive IL–DAgger–RL training pipeline. IL initializes the policy through action imitation, DAgger adapts it to policy-induced states, and RL directly optimizes task-level outcomes, progressively improving navigation accuracy.

Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of these three aspects. We instantiate SimpleVLN across multiple MLLM backbones and model sizes, demonstrating its generality. SimpleVLN achieves 76.7%76.7\% and 80.1%80.1\% SR on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen splits, respectively, substantially outperforming existing methods. These results demonstrate that the navigation capabilities of native MLLMs can be effectively unlocked without task-specific architectural designs.

Our contributions are threefold:
(1) We introduce SimpleVLN, an architecture-preserving framework that adapts native MLLMs to VLN through single-turn decision inputs, managed visual history, and action-chunk prediction, without task-specific architectural modules.
(2) We construct training data from expert demonstrations, policy-dependent DAgger experience, and scalable RL task synthesis, and develop a progressive IL–DAgger–RL pipeline for improving navigation accuracy.
(3) We instantiate SimpleVLN across multiple backbone families and model sizes, achieving strong performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, while extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of its formulation, data construction, and optimization.
