title: ORD-WM: Learning Object-Centric Rigid Dynamics for 3D World Modeling in Robotic Manipulation
authors: Yueyang Weng,Xiaopeng Zhang,Yuxi Ou,Yongjin Mu,Chengzhi Zhao,Yanjie Li
abstract: World models provide robots with a predictive mechanism for reasoning about how actions change object states in manipulation tasks. However, existing image-based and dense 3D world models do not explicitly impose object-level rigid motion, leaving rigid-object geometry preservation to be learned implicitly and making multi-step rollouts susceptible to shape drift or object-level motion inconsistency. To address this, we propose ORD-WM, a 3D world model that learns object-centric rigid dynamics for robotic manipulation. ORD-WM learns a vector-neuron variational autoencoder supervised by signed distance fields, which encodes each object point cloud as a geometry-aware latent representation composed of 3D vector features, and uses an action-conditioned dynamics model to predict object-wise SE(3) motion increments. Rather than generating unconstrained next latent states, ORD-WM analytically applies predicted object-wise rigid transformations to the current latent states, separating persistent object geometry from pose changes. Experiments show that ORD-WM enables stable, geometry-preserving multi-step prediction and supports efficient real-time replanning for closed-loop model predictive control in simulated and real-world manipulation scenarios.
introduction:
Humans can anticipate how physical scenes evolve and how actions change object states, which is fundamental to everyday interaction with the physical world. Endowing robots with a similar predictive ability is an important step toward more capable manipulation: before pushing, grasping, or rearranging objects, a robot should reason about how its actions may move and transform the objects in a scene. World models provide a natural framework for acquiring such capability by learning action-conditioned dynamics and rolling out future states internally, enabling robots to evaluate candidate actions and plan toward desired object configurations without relying solely on trial-and-error interaction in the real world [14, 18].

Recent robotic world models have explored several forms of action-conditioned prediction. Video-based models roll out future visual observations and can capture rich visual changes in robot-object interaction [33].
However, because prediction is performed in image or visual latent space, these models lack an explicit metric 3D state. As a result, visual plausibility alone does not guarantee temporally consistent object geometry or physically plausible interactions during rollout [23, 56].
Dense 3D world models based on point clouds, particles, or Gaussian scene representations move prediction closer to physical space by forecasting the motion of 3D elements [1]. However, when modeling rigid object motion through local element-wise updates, these models must coordinate local motions to produce globally consistent object transformations, which may accumulate into shape distortions or object-level drift during multi-step rollout [22].

For manipulation tasks involving rigid or approximately rigid objects, prediction should preserve object geometry while allowing object poses to change through interaction. Rigid-body simulators [41] offer a useful abstraction for this setting: they represent scenes as collections of bodies with persistent geometry and update object states through constrained body-level motion, rather than by independently moving dense visual or geometric elements. This separation between geometry and motion suggests a natural inductive bias for learned world models of rigid-object manipulation.

Building on this perspective, we propose ORD-WM, a 3D world model that learns object-centric rigid dynamics for robotic manipulation (Fig. 1).
ORD-WM represents a manipulation scene as a collection of geometry-aware object states and evolves them through object-wise rigid motion. To obtain such states, ORD-WM trains a signed-distance-field (SDF)-supervised vector-neuron (VN) [7] variational autoencoder (VAE) [26], denoted SDF-VNVAE. Its encoder maps each object point cloud to a geometry-aware latent state composed of 3D vector features that capture object geometry and can be analytically transformed by rigid motions in latent space. Instead of predicting unconstrained next latent states, ORD-WM predicts object-wise SE(3)11

Together, these design choices yield an object-centric 3D world model in which object geometry is maintained as a persistent latent structure and future states are generated through structured rigid updates. We evaluate ORD-WM on multi-step dynamics prediction and model predictive control (MPC) for object pushing and pick-and-place, showing that its object-centric SE(3)-structured rollout improves geometric consistency and supports downstream model-based control.

title: SCOPE: Selective Certification of Program Edits for Embodied Heuristic Learning
authors: Junyang Shu,Bingqing Wei,Jishuo Li,Zheqi He,Yongtao Wang
abstract:
Embodied heuristic learning must balance strategic adaptation with the
preservation of previously successful behavior. Local repairs may leave
structural failures unresolved, whereas broader revisions can introduce
regressions that are costly to detect through repeated environment interaction.
We introduce SCOPE (Selective Certification Of Program Edits), which uses
failed and successful executions as complementary evidence for program revision.
Frontier-guided program search annotates a shared diagnostic graph with
execution evidence to distinguish supported progress from unresolved checks.
Selective behavioral certification
uses stateful API replay to restore recorded responses and mutations, checking
whether edits preserve selected historical successes. Diagnosis and certification feedback,
supplemented by sparse environment diagnostics, guide consecutive repairs
across configurations. SCOPE outperforms the strongest baseline
in both simulation and real-world tasks. On LIBERO-PRO and Robosuite,
it achieves mean success rates of 80.66% and 84.48%, with respective gains
of 6.51 and 3.48 percentage points.
Our code is available at https://github.com/VDIGPKU/SCOPE.
introduction:
Robot control programs provide an explicit representation of how perception,
decisions, and actions compose into task behavior. Language models can
generate these programs from natural-language instructions, using control
flow and API calls to express policies and situated task
plans (Liang et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2023). Environment feedback then
provides a basis for adapting behavior when execution departs from the
plan (Huang et al., 2023b). This supports embodied heuristic learning,
in which interaction improves task-specific decision rules while
language-model parameters remain fixed. The resulting program must work across
configurations, so learning requires more than solving the latest observed
failure.

Execution-driven systems build on this approach through iterative program search.
CaP-X studies coding agents that compose robot APIs and revise programs
through interactive execution, while RHO optimizes policy repositories
using execution feedback and validation-based candidate
selection (Fu et al., 2026; Elmaaroufi et al., 2026). Reusable knowledge provides
another source of improvement. Playful Agentic Robot Learning acquires code
skills through self-directed exploration, and ASPIRE combines multimodal
execution traces, validated repair knowledge, and evolutionary program
search (Zhang et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). These approaches establish
execution as both a source of learning evidence and a means of evaluating
candidate programs. As revisions accumulate, the effects of each edit on
previously successful behavior become an additional concern.

The difficulty is that a failure reveals where execution broke down, but
the required change may extend beyond that point. A failed lift, for
example, may originate in an unstable grasp, requiring the grasping stage
to be redesigned rather than the lifting height to be adjusted. Local
repairs can leave such structural failures unresolved, whereas broader
revisions can alter decisions that supported success in other
configurations. Success on the current configuration provides no direct
evidence about those earlier behaviors. Repeating environment execution
across historical successes can assess the change, but spends interaction
budget on checking old behavior as well as discovering new behavior.
Effective search therefore needs evidence to guide the extent of a repair
and assess its consequences for prior successes.

Our central insight is that failed and successful executions provide
complementary evidence for program revision. Failed traces guide diagnosis
and revision planning, while successful traces can be replayed to assess
whether earlier behavior is preserved after an edit. By executing a revised
program against the exchanges recorded in a successful trace, we can check
whether it makes the same API requests and consumes the full trace with
normal termination.
Under faithful recording and deterministic execution, with all relevant
external interactions captured at the API boundary, a complete match
certifies success on the recorded instance. A divergence instead identifies
where behavior changes and provides a target for further environment
diagnosis. This turns historical interaction into feedback for subsequent
program edits.

We introduce SCOPE (Selective Certification Of Program Edits), which couples
frontier-guided program search with this selective certification feedback.
SCOPE first constructs a shared diagnostic graph whose checks describe
observable task progress and whose edges encode prerequisites. Execution
evidence annotates the graph to identify a failure frontier consisting of
unresolved checks with supported prerequisites. This frontier and its dependencies
guide repair planning, allowing the model to select among local repair,
stage redesign, and strategy regeneration. Revisions accumulate in a shared
working program across development configurations.

SCOPE accepts the working program whenever it succeeds on a configuration.
If this changes the accepted source, SCOPE
samples historical successes for stateful full-trace API replay.
Replay preserves recorded responses and public-state
mutations, allowing later program decisions to depend on the same effects
as in the original execution. For selected configurations that remain
uncertified, sparse environment diagnostics provide fresh outcomes and
failure evidence. These observations feed back into the same repair loop.
Certification thus informs subsequent search through evidence of preserved
behavior and changed interactions.

We evaluate the frozen programs on held-out configurations in
LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al., 2025) and
Robosuite (Zhu et al., 2020). SCOPE achieves mean success rates of
80.66% and 84.48%, exceeding the strongest baseline on each benchmark
by 6.51 and 3.48 percentage points, respectively. Component ablations
support the roles of failure-frontier guidance, certification feedback,
and explicit revision-level planning. Across the reported settings,
full-trace replay takes 4.62–6.59% of the corresponding original
environment execution time, demonstrating the low cost of obtaining
behavioral evidence from recorded interactions.

Our contributions are:

A program-search framework that uses execution evidence to
localize failure frontiers and plan repairs at different revision
levels, integrating historical-success feedback into consecutive
repair.

A selective certification mechanism based on stateful full-trace
API replay, with an instance-specific success guarantee under the
stated execution assumptions and sparse diagnostics for further repair.

An evaluation on LIBERO-PRO and Robosuite showing improved
mean held-out success over the strongest baseline on each benchmark,
together with real-world experiments demonstrating strong performance
on tasks requiring base–arm coordination, bimanual coordination,
and fine manipulation.

1. A program-search framework that uses execution evidence to
localize failure frontiers and plan repairs at different revision
levels, integrating historical-success feedback into consecutive
repair.

2. A selective certification mechanism based on stateful full-trace
API replay, with an instance-specific success guarantee under the
stated execution assumptions and sparse diagnostics for further repair.

3. An evaluation on LIBERO-PRO and Robosuite showing improved
mean held-out success over the strongest baseline on each benchmark,
together with real-world experiments demonstrating strong performance
on tasks requiring base–arm coordination, bimanual coordination,
and fine manipulation.

title: BeJEPA: A Goal-Conditioned Humanoid Behavior World Model via Unsupervised RL
authors: Liyun Yan,Haoyang Li,Yang Zhang,Jialing Zhu,Zhanxiang Cao,Zihao Zhou,Keqi Zhu,Yizhi Chen,Huang Chuxuan,Shengcheng Fu,Zhong Jiangwei,Qiao Sun,Chen Zhang,Yue Gao
abstract:
Humanoid control requires coordinating whole-body posture with position and heading in the world frame.
Mainstream controllers imitate trajectories in the root frame, but struggle to regain the target world pose after displacement.
We introduce BeJEPA, a goal-conditioned Behavior World Model learned through unsupervised
reinforcement learning from human motion priors and robot interaction.
BeJEPA learns a shared representation of body configuration and world placement
through a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA).
A Dynamic Predictor predicts the next state embedding under an action, while a Successor Predictor
summarizes a goal-conditioned policy’s expected discounted future state embeddings in a single vector.
During joint training, Dynamic grounds the initial representation in observed physical transitions,
while Successor increasingly organizes it around long-term behavior.
Their composition guides policy improvement through one physical prediction and one behavioral summary,
without long imagined rollouts.
In 20-second motion-tracking experiments, BeJEPA with online action refinement using Dynamic outperforms
all evaluated baselines in global body-position error, reducing it on AMASS
by 61.7% relative to BFM-Zero with world-pose inputs and 58.7% relative to SONIC.
Physical deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrates joint attainment of posture, world position,
and heading goals, recovery from the ground, and closed-loop return after disturbances and goal changes.
Project page: https://ylyem9x.github.io/BeJEPA-project/.
introduction:
Whole-body control (WBC) is the physical foundation of humanoid applications, enabling manipulation, expressive motion, and the execution of higher-level commands (Ben et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026).
It translates desired robot states into coordinated actuator commands.
For world-coordinate tasks, the desired body posture must be reached together with the requested base position and heading.
Existing motion-centered controllers can reproduce a posture while remaining displaced from its intended location.
Correcting this displacement requires the robot to step, temporarily departing from the requested posture before reaching it at the right place.
Whole-body control must therefore judge a movement by the goal it helps achieve, even when that movement initially worsens posture matching.

Human motion references show coordinated movement, making imitation a practical starting point for learning WBC (Peng et al., 2018; He et al., 2025; Liao et al., 2026).
However, tracking a given trajectory does not explain how to reach a new goal when no trajectory is provided.
This motivates reinforcement learning (RL), through which the robot can discover intermediate movements and evaluate how they help it reach the goal.
Meta Motivo and BFM-Zero use unsupervised RL to learn reusable behaviors (Tirinzoni et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026).
Given a reward that is linear in the learned state features, these methods can select behaviors to maximize return without specifying intermediate states.
BFM-Zero uses body-relative features, so its learned objective focuses on posture and excludes absolute position and heading.
To control posture and world placement together, the robot must learn how actions change its body and how the resulting behavior brings it closer to the goal.

We introduce BeJEPA, a goal-conditioned Behavior World Model for humanoid control, learned through unsupervised RL from human motion priors and robot interaction.
Its shared representation encodes body configuration, world position, and heading.
A goal-independent Dynamic Predictor models one-step action consequences, while a goal-conditioned Successor Predictor summarizes the policy’s expected future state features.
Early in joint training, Dynamic provides physical supervision that helps preserve useful features despite the unskilled policy’s noisy long-term targets.
As the policy improves, Successor organizes these features around long-term behavior.
Their composition trains the actor to choose movements by their future goal alignment, including steps that temporarily worsen posture matching, without long imagined rollouts.
Dynamic also supports online action refinement for time-indexed tracking.

title: GRASP: Global-Local Representation Alignment and Spatial-Physical Grounding for Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
authors: Zeyuan Ren,Guanxun Zhao,Qi Li,Hao Wang,Wenlong Liao,Keyi Luo,Xijing Zhang,Zhiyuan Zhang,Jingye Cui,Qibin Gu,Zhichen Wang,Yucheng Hu,Liqiao Xia,Nan Bu,Zhengde Ma,Rankun Li,Xue Yang,Wende Xie
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that directly regress joint-space actions avoid the deployment-time cost of inverse kinematics. However, their training objectives remain misaligned with task success, as joint-space losses ignore the unequal physical consequences of joint errors and visual conditioning lacks explicit focus on hand-object interaction regions. To address these issues, we propose a training-phase prior injection framework for fine-grained bimanual manipulation. First, a physics-grounded flow-matching loss maps the implicit clean-action estimate at every noise level through differentiable forward kinematics (FK) and supervises the resulting Tool Center Point (TCP) pose and inter-arm relative pose, with a bounded noise-level weighting that compensates gradient decay. Second, we introduce a global prediction query group distilled from a frozen DINOv3 teacher through future-frame feature prediction, together with a local interaction query supervised by Grounding DINO at the attention level. Both teachers are removed at inference, and the deployment pipeline is that of a standard joint-space flow policy, adding only the learned query pathway. Simulation and real-robot experiments on long-horizon bimanual tasks show that the two priors are complementary across different deployment settings. The full model excels in in-distribution deployment, while the distilled query branch is preferable under strong visual randomization.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action models have made significant progress in general robot manipulation, with models such as π0.5\pi_{0.5}, OpenVLA, and LingBot-VLA 2.0 [1, 2, 3] demonstrating strong manipulation capabilities. Flow-based policies such as π0\pi_{0} generate continuous action sequences through conditional flow matching [4, 5]. Such models either predict the End-Effector Pose (EEP) in task space, requiring a real-time Inverse Kinematics (IK) solver that may yield unreachable poses and discontinuous trajectories due to the one-to-many mapping [6], or directly regress the joint configuration, which avoids these issues but may misalign the normalized joint-space loss with physical-space task success. Specifically, standard joint-space regression losses do not explicitly account for the configuration-dependent effects of joint errors on end-effector motion. As a result, similar errors in joint space can lead to substantially different task-space deviations after forward-kinematic propagation. Meanwhile, visual conditioning in VLA models is often learned indirectly from the action objective, which may limit consistent attention to fine-grained hand-object interaction regions.

To address these issues, this paper proposes a training-phase prior injection framework for fine-grained bimanual manipulation, along two dimensions: action supervision and visual conditioning.

First, rather than applying kinematic regularization to final actions, we supervise the implicit clean-action estimate throughout the flow trajectory: the estimated clean actions at each noise level are mapped through differentiable forward kinematics, and a geometric loss over TCP pose and inter-arm relative pose ties each penalty to its physical consequence. This loss is training-only, and the policy still outputs joint commands directly at inference.

Second, we append a global query group QGQ_{G} and a local interaction query QPQ_{P} to the input sequence, supervised respectively by predicting the dense future-frame features of a frozen DINOv3 teacher [7] and by attention-level KL divergence distillation using interaction regions derived from Grounding DINO [8], explicitly guiding the model toward hand-object interaction regions. Both teachers are removed at inference.

In our evaluation, we conduct both simulation and real-robot experiments, and show that the proposed framework exhibits a number of desirable properties for fine-grained bimanual manipulation:

Simulation benchmark: on 50 bimanual tasks from the RoboTwin 2.0 [9] benchmark, our full model improves the average success rate over the π0.5\pi_{0.5}-SFT baseline by 15.1 percentage points in clean settings, while the π0.5\pi_{0.5}-Global+Local Query variant improves it by 29.0 percentage points under domain randomization.

Real-robot evaluation: on four long-horizon real-world tasks, including make watermelon juice, soda bottle opening, beverage mixing, and clothes folding, our method improves the average success rate by 14.2 percentage points over the baseline.

Physically accurate execution: supervision in physical space reduces TCP position error compared with joint-space-only training, confirming that the geometric loss better aligns the optimization objective with physical execution.

Interaction-aware perception: the decoupled global–local queries improve manipulation performance under randomized scenes and unseen-language instructions by guiding the policy toward task-relevant interaction regions.

In summary, our core idea is to compress task-space physical constraints and visual-teacher spatial priors into the training phase. Experiments in both simulation and real-world settings on long-horizon bimanual tasks show consistent improvements in accuracy and robustness.

1. Simulation benchmark: on 50 bimanual tasks from the RoboTwin 2.0 [9] benchmark, our full model improves the average success rate over the π0.5\pi_{0.5}-SFT baseline by 15.1 percentage points in clean settings, while the π0.5\pi_{0.5}-Global+Local Query variant improves it by 29.0 percentage points under domain randomization.

2. Real-robot evaluation: on four long-horizon real-world tasks, including make watermelon juice, soda bottle opening, beverage mixing, and clothes folding, our method improves the average success rate by 14.2 percentage points over the baseline.

3. Physically accurate execution: supervision in physical space reduces TCP position error compared with joint-space-only training, confirming that the geometric loss better aligns the optimization objective with physical execution.

4. Interaction-aware perception: the decoupled global–local queries improve manipulation performance under randomized scenes and unseen-language instructions by guiding the policy toward task-relevant interaction regions.

title: InstAgent: A Recursively Self-Improving Agent Operating System for Heterogeneous Robot Collaboration
authors: Haoyang Luo,Junhao Qin,Jingyan Cao,Yi Huang,Guangjie Yang,Xiaoyu Chen,Haotao Lu,Tianxiang Gui,Ye Shi,Jingya Wang
abstract: Heterogeneous robot teams enable complex, long-horizon tasks by combining complementary sensing, mobility, and manipulation capabilities across multiple embodiments. Yet existing systems struggle to retain execution-time corrections as reusable experience, maintain task-relevant context memory across space and time for reliable handoffs, and explicitly represent the inter-robot dependencies required for structured collaboration. In order to address these challenges, we present InstAgent, a recursively self-improving (RSI) Agent Operating System for heterogeneous robot collaboration. InstAgent organizes team behaviors as agentic behavior trees(BTs) that explicitly model capability assignment, inter-robot dependencies and handoff checks. The RSI mechanism updates these collaboration programs from execution feedback and preserves successful revisions for reuse in future tasks, while shared multimodal spatio-temporal memory provides context for planning and handoff validation. Experiments on 20 real-world multi-robot tasks with three high-level models show consistent gains in task success, first-attempt completion, and execution efficiency.
introduction:
Heterogeneous robot teams combine complementary capabilities in perception,
mobility and manipulation, enabling long-horizon tasks which are
difficult for a single embodiment to complete. Such tasks, however, require much more than assigning individual skills to different robots. Robots operate
across different locations and stages, and the outcome of one robot may
determine whether another can proceed. Recent large-language-model-based agentic
systems provide a promising abstraction for this setting by connecting
high-level reasoning, heterogeneous skill invocation, multimodal perception,
and execution feedback in a closed loop. This makes them particularly suitable
for long-horizon heterogeneous collaboration, where task procedures cannot
always be fully specified in advance.

Despite this promise, three challenges remain. First, complex physical tasks
rarely succeed from an initial plan alone, yet execution corrections are often
task-specific rather than accumulated as reusable executable experience. Existing
work has explored reflection, skill reuse, and feedback-driven adaptation
 [1, 2, 3, 4], but collaboration procedures corrected during execution
are not always retained in a form that later tasks can inherit and further
improve. Second, long-horizon collaboration requires persistent
spatio-temporal context beyond current local observations, which helps heterogeneous robots plan and act accordingly. Existing memory
systems support spatial and temporal retrieval
 [5, 6, 7, 8], but
historical observations must still be connected to current physical checks
before inter-robot handoffs. Third, treating heterogeneous robots as a flat
collection of callable skills under-specifies collaboration structure.
Reliable execution requires explicit inter-robot dependencies, handoff
conditions, and recovery logic, rather than isolated skill invocation alone
 [9, 10].

To address the aforementioned challenges, we present InstAgent, a recursively self-improving Agent Operating System designed to enable instant adaptation and deployment of heterogeneous robot teams across diverse and complex scenarios. As shown in Fig. , InstAgent represents
collaboration as an executable behavior-tree (BT) program that can be grounded
in shared environmental context, verified during physical execution, and
improved through accumulated experience. Its BT-based recursive
self-improvement (RSI) revises failed collaboration structures from execution
feedback and retains validated revisions for inheritance and further
adaptation. Shared Multimodal Spatio-Temporal Memory with Agent-Driven
Retrieval (SMAR-T) provides task-relevant observations with spatial,
temporal, and source information, while current observations verify physical
handoff conditions. InstAgent further composes heterogeneous capabilities into
BTs that explicitly encode inter-robot dependencies, handoff conditions, and
recovery branches. Together, these components form a closed loop of
composition, execution, verification, revision, and reuse.

We evaluate InstAgent on real-world embodiments across 20 heterogeneous
multi-robot tasks and three high-level models. Compared with BT execution without cross-task procedural
experience, feedback-updated experience improves task success by 15–25
percentage points across the three models, while increasing first-attempt
success and reducing recoveries. In the meanwhile, RAVEN-QA independently evaluates task-relevant
environmental observation retrieval.

Our main contributions are:

An agentic OS for heterogeneous multi-robot collaboration that
organizes robot capabilities and inter-robot dependencies
into executable BTs for structured coordination and execution.

An RSI mechanism that revises collaboration programs from
execution feedback and retains validated revisions for reuse, supported
by shared multimodal spatio-temporal memory (SMAR-T).

Extensive real-robot evaluations across heterogeneous platforms,
tasks, and high-level models, demonstrating consistent improvements in
task success and execution performance.

1. An agentic OS for heterogeneous multi-robot collaboration that
organizes robot capabilities and inter-robot dependencies
into executable BTs for structured coordination and execution.

2. An RSI mechanism that revises collaboration programs from
execution feedback and retains validated revisions for reuse, supported
by shared multimodal spatio-temporal memory (SMAR-T).

3. Extensive real-robot evaluations across heterogeneous platforms,
tasks, and high-level models, demonstrating consistent improvements in
task success and execution performance.

title: Bio-Inspired Magnetic Navigation Using Gradient Descent With Rao-Blackwellized Particle Filtering
authors: Zayed Herma,Andrea Vassilev,Philippe Cardin,Jean-Michel Leger
abstract: Navigation in GPS-denied environments is commonly based on magnetic maps, which are used to correct trajectory drift and enable relocalization. However, such navigation systems suffer from a strong dependence on magnetic maps that are complex, heavy, and costly to construct. Bio-inspired magnetic navigation (BIMN) does not rely on magnetic maps, making it simpler and more frugal. In this paper, we present a gradient descent BIMN method based on the Rao-Blackwellized particle filter (RBPF) for local gradient estimation. We show that magnetic navigation can be performed without magnetic maps, as gradient descent naturally attracts the system toward the destination, resulting in a simple and memory-efficient approach.
introduction:
Modern low-cost, passive navigation methods for GPS-denied environments typically rely on high-precision, pre-constructed magnetic maps. These methods use map matching, in which the measured magnetic parameters are compared with the map to estimate the most probable measurement location and reconstruct the navigation path [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].

The main challenge of this magnetic map–based approach is the requirement for a pre-constructed magnetic map. Such a map must be constructed a priori using a dedicated mapping method [7, 8]. Once constructed, the map must be stored and continuously accessed by the navigation system, which results in significant memory consumption. In addition, magnetic maps must be regularly maintained and updated to preserve localization accuracy, further increasing system complexity and operational cost.

These issues become especially pronounced in large-scale environments, where building, storing, and processing high-resolution magnetic maps is computationally intensive and expensive. As a result, the practical utility of magnetic map–based methods is generally limited to relatively small areas, making this approach unsuitable for large-scale navigation, for which constructing and maintaining such maps
would be extremely challenging.

This is why drawing inspiration from animals that navigate long distances using the Earth’s magnetic field could help overcome the complexity of using such magnetic maps. These animals have been demonstrated to navigate without relying on pre-constructed maps or external infrastructure, using mechanisms that are robust, efficient, and probably simple [9, 10, 11, 12]. For example, the long-distance migration of sea turtles across vast expanses of seemingly featureless ocean suggests that these animals rely on the Earth’s magnetic field for navigation [13, 14]. It has been shown that these animals memorize and store only the magnetic parameters of their destination, not an entire magnetic map. As they travel, they continuously measure local magnetic parameters and compare them with stored destination parameters to determine the correct direction toward the destination, as illustrated in Fig. 1 [15, 16].

This has led to the development of many bio-inspired magnetic navigation (BIMN) methods [17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22]. In these studies, the gradient (representing the first-order variation of magnetic parameters) is explicitly and manually estimated to guide the agent. This estimation typically requires executing multiple maneuvers in different directions to acquire the necessary gradient information. To compensate for inaccurate or delayed gradient estimates, complex techniques (such as evolutionary optimization, predictive control, and data-driven approaches) are often employed, leading to oversized and computationally expensive solutions.

In this paper, we propose a navigation method that is fusion-based in the sense of performing online joint estimation of the local magnetic gradient and the agent’s position during navigation toward the destination. The proposed approach formulates gradient and position as coupled states and estimates them using the Rao-Blackwellized particle filter (RBPF). The estimated local gradient is then exploited to compute the direction of motion via a gradient-descent strategy. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

Formulating the BIMN problem as a gradient-descent optimization approach (see Section II).

Jointly estimating the local gradient and the agent’s position using the RBPF (see Section III).

The proposed approach is compared with a representative state-of-the-art method [23], which assumes a constant gradient. This baseline method is selected for its conceptual simplicity and bio-inspired nature. The proposed method introduces only minimal additional estimation to handle a spatially varying gradient.

The comparison highlights the limitations of constant-gradient assumptions and demonstrates the benefits of online local gradient estimation, particularly in long-range navigation scenarios where magnetic gradients vary spatially. The results show that the local gradient is estimated along the navigation path, with uncertainty that is smaller in the direction of motion, which is the direction of attraction governed by gradient descent. Consequently, estimating the gradient in all directions is unnecessary: only the component of the gradient projected onto the direction of motion matters for effective descent (see Section IV). We also show that the developed method uses the same locally estimated gradient to correct the position and attenuate drift in the integrated trajectory, as if a local map were available.

1. Formulating the BIMN problem as a gradient-descent optimization approach (see Section II).

2. Jointly estimating the local gradient and the agent’s position using the RBPF (see Section III).

title: Foundation Models for Autonomous Space Robotics: Architectures, Physical Adaptation, and Validation
authors: Zizhe Wang,Jia Deng,Xin Lu,Zehao Jia,Yi Huang,Yao Zhu,Jianing Li
comment: . Critical review. Ancillary files include source inventory and evidence documentation
abstract: Space robots must interpret tasks and act despite unfamiliar dynamics, difficult sensing conditions, and limited opportunities for human intervention. Foundation models offer reusable perceptual and behavioral knowledge, but their value depends on how that knowledge reaches physical execution. This critical review follows space-specific requirements through perception, prediction, planning, and action to deployment and validation, emphasizing orbital manipulation and proximity operations. Terrestrial comparisons establish benefits of particular pretraining stages and model interfaces; their transfer to space dynamics and constrained onboard operation remains insufficiently tested. Event cameras offer timely motion observations across strong illumination contrasts, while spiking neural networks provide possible routes to sparse local computation. We examine how sensor degradation, state estimation and computing choices affect feedback and recovery. Higher action throughput need not yield fresher feedback; lower processor power can also coexist with higher energy per inference. We organize validation as an iterative sim-to-ground-to-space pathway, connecting physical tests with telemetry-based diagnosis and closed-loop revalidation. A satellite-capture example links observations to approach, contact and recovery, while a corresponding protocol separates generalization from adaptation with limited target-domain interaction. These comparisons identify what models already contribute and the physical evidence needed to support autonomous space operation.
introduction:
Space robots must interpret tasks and act with limited human intervention. Tracking or control errors can cause collisions; repair may be impossible. Satellite capture couples tracking, approach, contact, and stabilization; surface sampling connects terrain assessment to tool–material interaction; cabin maintenance requires manipulation in confined, shared workspaces. These operations rely on established dynamics, estimation, planning and supervisory autonomy [1, 2]. Foundation models offer reusable knowledge and behavior when task-specific interaction data are scarce. Can reuse remain useful under changed dynamics, sensing and computation?

We define a foundation model by broad pretraining and downstream reuse through a shared model or backbone. Size or architecture alone does not establish this status [3, 4, 5]. We include space applications reusing identifiable foundation models and robot models with documented pretraining and reuse, assessing transfer to held-out tasks separately.

Vision–language models (VLMs) connect visual observations to linguistic or structured outputs; vision–language–action models (VLAs) extend this interface to actions. World models predict action consequences and qualify as foundation models when their pretraining and reuse support that description. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) use spikes for computation; their generality depends on training and reuse. SNNs, event cameras, task-specific reinforcement learning and conventional control inform adaptation, deployment and evaluation of pretrained components.

We emphasize orbital manipulation and proximity operations, using intravehicular and selected planetary studies to compare shared problems and physical requirements. Remote sensing and scientific question answering enter only when relevant to robot operation. We distinguish stabilized spacecraft, free-floating manipulators, pressurized cabins and lunar rovers.

Existing surveys frame this discussion (Table 1). AI-SRO connects physics, model/control interfaces, simulators, deployment resources and progressive validation [6]. The multimodal space-robot review organizes work by task planning and end-to-end control; our comparison is limited to its original abstract [7]. The closed loop is a shared organizing principle.

We examine how experiments distinguish reused components’ contributions from task-specific adaptation and surrounding control, including timing, energy demands, new tasks and physical conditions. Within-study comparisons trace reused components, target-domain updates and tested conditions. Event cameras and SNNs receive particular attention because observation timing and sustained local computation connect model capability to physical feedback [8, 9, 10]. We organize validation into a sim-to-ground-to-space pathway and propose a capture protocol separating held-out generalization from adaptation under a fixed interaction budget.

This critical narrative review considers works available by 14 October 2026. Initial searches were followed by targeted retrieval and source checks on 15 October, retaining the original eligibility cutoff. Surveys seeded citation tracing, and web searches led to primary sources through arXiv, publishers, proceedings, institutions, and space agencies. Selection favored distinct operational interfaces, physical mechanisms, or validation settings; terrestrial studies explain transferable methods. Titles, DOIs, and versions supported deduplication.

The ancillary inventory records the search history, versions, and reading scope of all cited works. Mechanism comparisons use methodological passages; abstract-only sources support only their stated claims. Unresolved candidates and a local unpublished survey were excluded. Purposive selection limits completeness, and differences between tasks preclude pooled performance rankings.

The review proceeds from space requirements through the embodied closed loop to adaptation, validation and cross-study conclusions.

title: Unifying Embodied Foundation Models via a Model-to-Policy Formulation
authors: Xinyi Hong,Mingyang Ren
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as promising approaches to robot learning and control. These models integrate multimodal perception and action generation, but differ in their architectures, output representations, and learning objectives. In this paper, we present a unified, architecture-agnostic probabilistic formulation for embodied foundation models based on stochastic kernels. Our formulation has two key components: (i) we characterize embodied foundation models through conditional output distributions and action-realization kernels, which together induce task-conditioned robot policies; and (ii) we connect pretraining and post-training to policy deployment, accommodating model-specific pretraining objectives and offline or online post-training strategies. We instantiate the formulation for OpenVLA and DreamZero, covering autoregressive action-token prediction and joint video-action generation.
introduction:
Robot learning is moving from task-specific controllers toward embodied AI systems that learn reusable perception-to-action policies across tasks and embodiments (O’Neill et al., 2024; Team et al., 2024b). At its current stage, embodied AI largely adapts the broader foundation-model development pipeline to physical interaction (Driess et al., 2023). This pipeline combines a shared architectural core with three stages: pre-training, post-training, and deployment. The shared architectural core is typically based on the Transformer family, with modality-specific encoders, tokenizers, or output heads added (if needed) (Vaswani et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2020; Team et al., 2024a; Xu et al., 2025; Team, 2026). First, pre-training learns general representations from large-scale corpora and multimodal collections through model-specific objectives (Brown et al., 2020; Team et al., 2024a; Team, 2026). Specifically for LLMs, the resulting next-token loss follows predictable power-law relations in model size, data, and compute (similarly rigorous scaling laws are less established for other foundation models) (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2025). Second, post-training adapts the pretrained model to follow instructions, align with human or verifiable preferences, and improve downstream task performance (Wei et al., 2021; Ouyang et al., 2022). Common approaches include supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference optimization (e.g., DPO and KTO) (Ouyang et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023; Ethayarajh et al., 2024). Other routes use reinforcement learning (e.g., RLHF and RLVR, often implemented with PPO or GRPO) or on-policy distillation (OPD) (Ouyang et al., 2022; Schulman et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Agarwal et al., 2024). Finally, deployment turns the trained model into a reusable inference and reasoning core. The above foundation-model pipeline has shown broad effectiveness across scales and modalities, underpinning recent language and reasoning models (e.g., GPT-5.6 and DeepSeek-V4), multimodal or omnimodal models such as MiniMax M3 and Qwen3.5-Omni, and generative models including FLUX.2 (Achiam et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2026; Team, 2026). The resulting models can also serve as reasoning and perception cores for agents (Hong et al., 2026a). Such agents support tool use, coding, digital-environment interaction, and multi-agent coordination (Yao et al., 2022; Schick et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2023). Can the success of large foundation models be carried into the physical world? The above non-embodied foundation models generally learn a mapping fθ:𝒳→𝒴f_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} from input data to predictions or generated content (Hong et al., 2026b). However, for robot learning, embodied foundation models aim to induce a task-conditioned policy πθ:𝒯×𝒞→𝒫⁡(𝒜)\pi_{\theta}:\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}) that maps the available interaction history and task condition to a probability distribution over robot actions. Fitting a fixed data distribution is insufficient, since a policy must also perform well on the trajectories induced by its own actions (Kaelbling et al., 1998; Ross et al., 2011; Brohan et al., 2023).
Vision-language-action (VLA) models pursue this policy-learning objective by combining visual observations and language instructions to generate robot actions. The Robotics Transformer (RT) series develops this approach from RT-1’s discretized action prediction to RT-2’s transfer of internet-scale visual-semantic knowledge through autoregressive action-token prediction (Brohan et al., 2022; Brohan et al., 2023). OpenVLA likewise adapts a pretrained vision-language backbone with an action-token cross-entropy objective, while π0\pi_{0} couples such a backbone to a flow-matching action expert that generates continuous action chunks (Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024). Scaling their robot pre-training is constrained by the difficulty of collecting real robot trajectories across diverse tasks, environments, and embodiments (O’Neill et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024). Video pre-training offers a complementary route to learning motion and scene dynamics from internet-scale data without robot action labels, reducing reliance on embodiment-specific trajectories for acquiring these priors (Assran et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026). For control, the value of this pre-training lies in acquiring transferable regularities of physical interaction that support action, rather than visual realism alone (Assran et al., 2025). Such priors support control through predictive world models, as in UniPi, which uses inverse dynamics to extract robot actions from generated video plans (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Du et al., 2023). World-action models (WAMs) couple these visual predictions with action generation under language conditioning, as in DreamZero, which adapts a pretrained video diffusion backbone to jointly generate future video and robot actions (Ye et al., 2026). Conditioned on visual history and proprioception, DreamZero uses flow matching within chunks and autoregressive generation across chunks (Ye et al., 2026). Real robot trajectories ground these pretrained representations in embodiment-specific commands and physical transitions, supporting transfer across tasks, environments, and embodiments (O’Neill et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025). Adapting these representations to downstream control can also change the model’s outputs, as π0.5\pi_{0.5} adds a continuous action expert during post-training after discrete-token pre-training (Intelligence et al., 2025). The resulting outputs must then be converted into executable actions through decoding and action selection or scheduling (Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2026). These actions change the observations conditioning subsequent predictions, so the deployed policy depends on both the learned output distribution and its realization in closed-loop interaction. A common description must therefore connect these two components with the objectives and data used in pre-training and post-training.

Motivated by this connection, we develop an architecture-agnostic probabilistic formulation based on stochastic kernels. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first formulation that explicitly connects model output distributions and action realization with pre-training, post-training, and closed-loop robot interaction for both VLAs and WAMs. We instantiate it for OpenVLA and DreamZero.

title: PASS: A Trustworthy Precision Approach Simulation System for CAT III Integrity Algorithm Development
authors: Lang Zhu(1),Xin Zhang(1),Yulong Sun(1),Nan Liu(2),Jiahe Shen(2),Xiaodong Zhang(2),Xingqun Zhan(1) ((1) Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China, (2) Flight Automatic Control Research Institute, Xi'an, China)
abstract: For fixed-wing aircraft, reliable localization during approach and landing is critical to flight safety. Visual–inertial navigation is promising, but aircraft navigation also requires integrity: trustworthy outputs and timely warnings when they should not be used. Real approach data are costly to collect, while many visual errors and failures required for integrity algorithm development are difficult to reproduce safely. We present PASS, a trustworthy Precision Approach Simulation System for CAT III integrity algorithm development. In a unified temporal and geometric framework, PASS integrates configurable airport environments, prescribed trajectories, inertial simulation, calibrated stereo images, and continuous runway-relative ground truth. It supports navigation and integrity research through controllable sensor errors and environmental variations, computable visual projection errors, deterministic runway geometry priors, and condition-labeled data for statistical error modeling. We further propose Sim-to-Real Scene Trustworthiness (SRST), a measure based on DINOv2 feature distributions and UMAP, to quantify sim-to-real closeness. Experiments with representative stereo–inertial estimators demonstrate the usability of the generated sequences and quantify localization errors across algorithms and environments. PASS provides a controllable foundation for developing and evaluating visual–inertial navigation and integrity algorithms for fixed-wing precision approaches up to CAT III requirements.
introduction:
Reliable runway-relative localization is essential for autonomous fixed-wing approach and landing, particularly when conventional landing aids or Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals are unavailable, degraded, or unreliable. Cameras and inertial sensors provide complementary geometric and motion information, making visual–inertial navigation a promising solution for runway perception, aircraft pose estimation, and approach navigation Marianandam and Ghose (2014); Tsapparellas et al. (2024); Ferreira et al. (2025). In safety-critical aircraft navigation, however, positioning accuracy alone is insufficient. Navigation integrity is also required to determine whether an estimated state can be trusted and to identify misleading information before it compromises the operation. As visual measurements become increasingly involved in aircraft localization, integrity monitoring for vision-aided navigation is therefore receiving growing attention Sun et al. (2026).

Developing visual–inertial navigation and integrity algorithms requires more than synchronized sensor measurements. Navigation algorithms depend on continuous imagery, inertial measurements, calibration parameters, and reliable trajectory references, whereas integrity algorithms additionally require controllable error excitation, truth-referenced visual errors (differences between detected runway features and their projections from independent pose and runway geometry truth), deterministic geometric priors, and condition-labeled observations for uncertainty modeling and error bounding. These reference errors are needed to characterize and bound visual-measurement uncertainty for downstream computation of navigation integrity risk; PASS provides the requisite data rather than calculating that risk itself. Acquiring this information from real fixed-wing approaches is costly and constrained by operational and safety requirements. In particular, adverse visual conditions, sensor disturbances, prior information inconsistencies, and rare failure events cannot be introduced freely or reproduced systematically during flight tests. Existing runway-oriented datasets such as LARD and BARS improve access to labeled approach imagery, but primarily provide individual images and two-dimensional annotations rather than continuous calibrated visual–inertial sequences Ducoffe et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2023). They also lack the controlled disturbances, independent error references, runway priors, and condition labels needed to model measurement covariance, assess residual consistency, construct conservative error bounds, and determine the operating conditions under which a visual error model remains trustworthy. Existing resources are therefore insufficient for reproducible research that connects runway perception with visual–inertial navigation and integrity evaluation throughout fixed-wing precision approaches.

Simulation provides a practical means of generating repeatable sensor observations and exact geometric references under controllable airport, environmental, and sensor conditions. Nevertheless, two related questions must be addressed before simulated data can support downstream integrity analysis. First, fully simulated system must expose the information needed to construct and evaluate integrity models rather than merely reproduce nominal visual–inertial measurements. Second, the generated observations must be sufficiently trustworthy with respect to real approach imagery, because visually plausible rendering alone does not establish the applicability of an error model developed in simulation. The rendered stereo images, inertial measurements, calibration parameters, coordinate transformations, runway geometry, and trajectory ground truth must therefore remain mutually consistent, while the remaining sim-to-real discrepancy must be quantified explicitly.

To address these requirements, we present PASS: A Trustworthy Precision Approach Simulation System designed to support CAT III integrity algorithm development. PASS couples prescribed approach trajectories and inertial simulation based on the Precise Strapdown Inertial Navigation System (PSINS) toolbox Yan (2024) with configurable multi-airport environments and calibrated stereo imaging in Unreal Engine. A shared time base and an explicit transformation chain connect the global, runway, aircraft, inertial, camera, and image frames, allowing the system to generate continuous visual–inertial observations together with traceable runway-relative ground truth. PASS is not itself an integrity monitoring or navigation algorithm and does not directly output a protection level. Instead, it provides a controlled simulation and data interface through which navigation algorithms can be exercised and the information required by downstream integrity models can be generated, measured, and statistically characterized.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We develop PASS: A Trustworthy Precision Approach Simulation System that integrates PSINS-based trajectory and inertial simulation, configurable airport environments, and calibrated stereo-image generation. Its modular architecture, shared temporal basis, traceable sensor configuration, and explicit coordinate transformation chain maintain consistency across the generated multimodal data while allowing airport, trajectory, environment, and sensor parameters to be configured independently.

We develop PASS: A Trustworthy Precision Approach Simulation System that integrates PSINS-based trajectory and inertial simulation, configurable airport environments, and calibrated stereo-image generation. Its modular architecture, shared temporal basis, traceable sensor configuration, and explicit coordinate transformation chain maintain consistency across the generated multimodal data while allowing airport, trajectory, environment, and sensor parameters to be configured independently.

We enable PASS to provide structured support information for the development and evaluation of visual–inertial navigation integrity algorithms. This information comprises controllable sensor error excitation and environmental variation, computable visual projection errors referenced to ground truth, deterministic runway geometry priors, and condition-labeled data for statistical error modeling. Together, these capabilities support visual error distribution modeling, dynamic covariance estimation, residual construction, conservative error bounding, and integrity analysis across operating conditions while keeping the downstream integrity algorithm independent of the simulation framework.

We introduce Sim-to-Real Scene Trustworthiness (SRST), a stage-conditioned measure for small samples of real and simulated images acquired during airport approach. The measure is designed to mirror a human comparative scene judgment: a simulated image is assessed against both the corresponding category in the real-image set and competing categories. Using frozen DINOv2 features and a joint two-dimensional UMAP representation constructed separately for each approach stage, SRST quantifies category-relative scene correspondence across coastal, mountainous, desert, and urban airports without requiring image-level pairs.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews datasets and simulation resources relevant to fixed-wing runway perception, visual–inertial navigation, and downstream integrity algorithm development. Section 3 presents the PASS architecture, its modular simulation subsystems, and the integrity support information provided by the framework. Section 4 evaluates the functional usability of the generated sequences using representative stereo–inertial estimators. Section 5 concludes the paper.

The PASS dataset will be made publicly available upon publication at https://github.com/zhulang195/PASS_dataset.

title: VLA-Fabric: Learning Interaction for Composable Multi-Arm VLA Agents
authors: Chenglong Zhang,Shuaijun Liu,Feiyang You,Shuyang Hao,Chengyu Wu,Ningxin Su
comment: including references and appendices. Project website:this https URL
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are rapidly expanding what individual
robots can accomplish, yet many real-world manipulation settings require
multiple arms to operate as a coordinated system. Existing approaches organize
multi-arm coordination in different ways, including centralized joint policies,
high-level task or role assignment, and locally executed policies that react
to teammates. However, how complete action-producing VLAs should explicitly
interact with one another during action generation remains largely unexplored.
We introduce VLA-Fabric, which organizes one complete VLA per arm while
preserving local perception and action ownership, and enables coordination
through learned interaction across policy boundaries. We first systematically
study where such interaction should occur, how peer information should be
aggregated, and how the interaction should be learned, revealing complementary
coordination functions spanning shared context, peer-specific latent
information, and action-stage interaction. We then re-instantiate these
functions in a structurally different VLA architecture, showing that the
coordination principle is not tied to a particular tensor layout or backbone
implementation. Finally, we compose teams of three and four arms
and evaluate them in simulation and physical experiments.
On all four physical tasks, Full interaction improves success over
independently trained local policies by 16–40 percentage points.
Together, these results suggest that explicit interaction among complete VLA
policies offers a scalable path toward networked embodied intelligence.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are advancing the capabilities of individual
robots by connecting visual and language understanding with learned action
generation (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025). Many important robotic applications,
however, require several manipulators to contribute to a common physical
objective. Cooperative manufacturing, multi-part assembly, shared-load handling,
and flexible robotic workcells motivate systems in which multiple arms work
together (Dio et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2025). As pretrained VLAs become more
capable, their progress creates an opportunity beyond improving a single robot:
organizing multiple action-producing policies into a collaborative system.
The ability of each constituent model to perceive and act does not, by itself,
specify how those models should work together.

Recent multi-arm VLAs pursue this goal through different organizations.
RDT-1B, ET-VLA, TwinVLA, and Dexora place cross-arm dependencies within a joint
policy (Liu et al., 2025; Li and Peng, 2025; Im et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b).
Other approaches coordinate at different levels: MA-VLA assigns
atomic behaviors to individual arms (Zhang et al., 2026a), while CHORUS demonstrates
implicit decentralized coordination through locally executed policies that
observe and react to teammates without runtime messages (Doshi et al., 2026).
These approaches establish effective collaboration, with coordination inside a
joint policy, above the action policy through behavior assignment, or indirectly
through observations of teammates. This raises an organizational challenge as
the number and roles of manipulators grow. How can a multi-arm system remain
modular at the level of individual manipulators while still supporting tightly
coupled collaboration?

A natural way to obtain such modularity is to organize the system around
complete arm-local policies rather than a growing joint policy. We therefore
treat each manipulator and its complete VLA as a self-contained execution unit
that perceives its local context and produces its own actions.
Local information can remain with the policy that uses it,
and larger teams can be formed by composing additional execution units.
Crucially, local does not mean isolated. Policies participating in the
same physical task still need to adapt their actions to one another. The key
challenge is to connect these local policies through explicit interaction
without giving up their local action ownership.

To realize this local-but-connected organization, we introduce
VLA-Fabric11

https://nebulis-lab.com/VLA-Fabric/.,
a multi-VLA coordination architecture connecting complete arm-local policies
through learned internal representation interaction
(Figure 1). Each VLA retains local perception and action
generation while selected peer representations condition its computation
through explicit policy interaction. VLA-Fabric thus makes coordination
among complete policies an explicit learning and architecture problem instead
of absorbing all cross-arm dependencies into a joint policy.

First, we establish an effective VLA-Fabric interaction architecture through a
broad controlled study. Starting from a decomposable bimanual VLA with
pretrained single-arm streams (Im et al., 2026), we separate its original cross-arm
dependencies. We systematically explore a combinatorial design space covering
interaction entry points, aggregation operators, and fine-tuning strategies.
The study shows that exposing more peer information does not by itself ensure
coordination; interaction structure and adaptation determine how effectively
local policies use one another’s information. This exploration identifies
complementary interaction at shared-context, peer-specific intermediate, and
action-generation stages.

Second, we demonstrate that the same VLA-Fabric interaction paradigm can be
re-instantiated in substantially different VLA architectures. We use π0.5\pi_{0.5}
(Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) as a second realization, whose multimodal processing and action
generation differ markedly from the Eagle2 VLM-based SingleVLA used in our
initial study. Accordingly, the same coordination functions are realized at
architecture-appropriate computational boundaries while preserving complete
local policies with explicit policy interaction. The resulting
π0.5\pi_{0.5}-Fabric system enables multiple complete π0.5\pi_{0.5} policies to
interact and achieves strong performance across several
bimanual tasks. Its stronger results suggest that advances in the constituent
VLA may translate into stronger collaborative systems. This observation is
consistent with the value of pretrained single-arm capabilities demonstrated
by TwinVLA (Im et al., 2026).

Third, we establish the extensibility of VLA-Fabric from bimanual coordination
to larger teams of complete VLA policies. Additional manipulators are
incorporated by composing additional local policies and extending their
interaction. We instantiate three- and four-arm VLA-Fabric teams and evaluate
them on simulation tasks with different coordination demands.
We further validate the same organization on four physical
three- and four-arm tasks, where Full interaction consistently improves over
independently trained local policies.
Our contributions are:

VLA-Fabric interaction architecture.
We introduce VLA-Fabric, which organizes complete arm-local VLAs as the execution
units of multi-arm collaboration and connects them through learned
representation interaction. A broad controlled architecture study establishes
effective interaction structure, aggregation, and adaptation for coordinated
action generation.

Cross-architecture transfer of VLA-Fabric.
We re-instantiate the same interaction paradigm in Eagle2 VLM-based SingleVLA
and π0.5\pi_{0.5} despite their substantially different policy computations.
The resulting systems demonstrate a common coordination organization across
distinct VLA architectures.

Composable multi-arm scalability.
We scale VLA-Fabric from two complete VLA policies to teams of three and four
while preserving local action generation and explicit policy interaction.
We validate the resulting organization across simulation and physical
multi-arm tasks with differing coordination demands.

title: What Makes a Good Symbol for Hybrid Discrete-Continuous Planning?
authors: Yiyuan Pan,Changliu Liu,Jiayuan Mao
abstract: The physical world has continuous state and action spaces, yet robot planning often benefits from hybrid discrete-continuous formulations that explicitly expose combinatorial structure, such as contact modes or discrete primitive actions. Existing methods typically rely on human-defined symbol sets or symbols derived from language supervision, without asking what makes a symbol computationally useful. In this paper, we take an inference-algorithm–centric view to define usefulness: a good symbol should expose the discrete commitments that simplify solving the original planning problem. We first introduce the concept of solver-sufficient symbolization by studying finite-horizon piecewise-affine systems, for which solver sufficiency can be precisely characterized, and develop a counterexample-guided algorithm for symbol invention. We then extend this principle to invent symbols for optimization objectives parameterized by general neural networks as energy functions, showing that solver-sufficient symbols can nevertheless be induced from their continuous optimization landscapes. Experiments on simulated and real-robot tasks show that the resulting symbols reduce solving cost while preserving solution quality, while also improving interpretability and steerability. Furthermore, our theoretical and algorithmic insights help explain why certain human-defined symbols are computationally useful.
introduction:
The physical world has continuous state and action spaces, yet planning often benefits from hybrid discrete–continuous formulations that explicitly expose combinatorial structure, such as contact modes in manipulation (e.g., fixed and sliding contacts) [Posa et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2022] and symbolic relational states (e.g., holding, in) [Garrett et al., 2021]. From a resource-rational perspective in cognitive science, a useful symbol can expose key commitments and abstract away details to support efficient planning under bounded computation [Lieder and Griffiths, 2020; Ho et al., 2022]: When a person wants to go to the office with a bag, the motion of the person and the bag must initially be considered jointly. Once “the bag is being carried” is established as a symbolic commitment, the bag’s motion can be abstracted away when planning the person’s path.

While humans can invent symbols to reduce the complexity of decision-making, deep learning–based solutions to decision-making often choose to encode the full decision landscape within a single continuous-space model [Chi et al., 2025; Janner et al., 2022]. They remove the need to declare discrete modes and dependencies a priori, but fundamentally cannot remove the underlying combinatorial structure of the problem. For example, for neural-network–parameterized dynamics models, basins and barriers appear in the optimization landscape. This makes planning or optimization hard as tasks and horizons grow [Florence et al., 2022].
To this end, researchers have considered exposing symbol commitments explicitly as state variables, such as the object relation of person-carrying-bag, to break much of the global coupling in planning.
The symbol invention problem studies inducing these symbols from data, but typically from predefined grammars and labels [Silver et al., 2023; Athalye et al., 2025]. Such symbols are often interpretable and descriptive, yet their construction typically relies on heuristics about the problem structure, such as sparsity and locality. As a result, they may hinder rather than simplify planning. In this paper, we address this fundamental question:

Our definition of a useful symbol comes from the perspective of inference-time solving. We consider a general family of hybrid discrete-continuous planning algorithms based on search-then-optimize [Geoffrion, 1972; Dechter, 1990]: symbols partition the entire decision space into conditioned subproblems, within which continuous-space optimization is performed. Let x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} denote all decision variables and hh the planning objective. Our goal is to solve the hybrid optimization problem:

To put these in practice, we begin with simple piecewise affine (PWA) systems [Rodrigues and How, 2003], where the solver sufficiency and complexity can be studied exactly using TU-dimension tools [Hoffman and Kruskal, 2010]. We then extend this perspective to general settings involving neural networks, focusing on energy-based formulations which include frameworks such as diffusion and flow-matching policies [Chi et al., 2025; Lipman et al., 2022]. In both settings, we develop algorithms for
both symbol invention and symbol-guided planning. Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce solver-sufficient symbolization, in which symbolic commitments preserve optimality while reducing grounded solving cost. This formalizes the symbolic invention problem as an optimization problem rather than a purely descriptive interface.

We introduce solver-sufficient symbolization, in which symbolic commitments preserve optimality while reducing grounded solving cost. This formalizes the symbolic invention problem as an optimization problem rather than a purely descriptive interface.

We provide a mathematical foundation for analyzing why certain human-defined concepts are useful in robotic planning, and characterize task hardness by the amount of irreducible discrete structure that must remain explicit for faithful solving.

We develop and evaluate a symbol invention and hybrid planning framework that retains key advantages of symbolic planning, including interpretability and behavior steerability.

In search-then-optimize planning [Geoffrion, 1972; Audet et al., 2026], the key step is to choose a conditioned subproblem, such as mode assignments in MILPs [Marcucci and Tedrake, 2020; Cauligi et al., 2021] and energy-based model inference with multi-seed initialization [Florence et al., 2022; Chi et al., 2025]. This choice is hard because decisions are coupled. Researchers have formalized such coupling in AI planning problems [Chen and Giménez, 2007; Mao et al., 2023]. Hybrid discrete-continuous planners aim to address this by introducing symbols [Konidaris et al., 2018; Garrett et al., 2020], but their symbols come from labels or simple algebraic combinations of state variables [Silver et al., 2023; Athalye et al., 2025]. We instead derive symbols from the solver itself: the commitments required before make the conditioned problem cheap to solve, and the commitment number measures the problem’s coupling and irreducible combinatorial hardness. We include a more comprehensive discussion of related work in Appendix A.

1. We introduce solver-sufficient symbolization, in which symbolic commitments preserve optimality while reducing grounded solving cost. This formalizes the symbolic invention problem as an optimization problem rather than a purely descriptive interface.

2. We provide a mathematical foundation for analyzing why certain human-defined concepts are useful in robotic planning, and characterize task hardness by the amount of irreducible discrete structure that must remain explicit for faithful solving.

3. We develop and evaluate a symbol invention and hybrid planning framework that retains key advantages of symbolic planning, including interpretability and behavior steerability.
