title: Robotic Spatiotemporal Editing: A Unified Interface for Controllable Action Generation via Masked Action Reconstruction
authors: Yanbang Li,Bu He,Yi Tian,Yu-Chiao Huang,Chenyu Zhang,Ruoqu Chen,Yuanzhe Liu,Yuxiang Gao,Mengdi Xu
abstract:
Generative policies can synthesize robot behaviors, yet controlling and editing them through diverse spatiotemporal references remains challenging.
Real-world manipulation requires robots to satisfy user-specified constraints on where, when, and how actions are executed.
Our key insight is that spatiotemporal control references, such as keypoints, flows, orientations, and keyposes, can be viewed as partial specifications of the same temporal Cartesian action space.
We introduce the MAP (Masked Action Space) interface to unify these action references and formulate controllable manipulation as an action inpainting problem.
Our Inpainting Policy (IP) reconstructs missing action dimensions of the end-effector, combining progress-guided alignment with multi-mask training to support unseen action constraint combinations.
We further adopt a training-free RePaint variant that iteratively inpaints the action during denoising to reduce control error.
On ManiSkill and LIBERO-10, our policy achieves average task success rates of 92.67%92.67\% and 64.67%64.67\%, respectively.
Real-world experiments demonstrate spatiotemporal control with average positional and rotational errors of 44.3​mm44.3\,\mathrm{mm} and 7.8∘7.8^{\circ}, respectively.
Project page: https://robotic-spatiotemporal-editing.github.io/rose.github.io/.
introduction:
Generative models have recently demonstrated remarkable progress in robotic manipulation, enabling policies to synthesize complex robot behaviors from visual observations and task descriptions (Chi et al., 2025; Black et al., 2026; Brohan et al., 2023).
However, generating plausible behaviors alone is insufficient for deploying robots in the physical world.
Real-world tasks require robots not only to decide what to do but also to satisfy constraints on where, when, and how to execute an action  (Rempe et al., 2026).
Moreover, humans and intelligent systems often need to refine, modify, and compose robot behaviors by adding spatiotemporal constraints.
For example, when tidying a table, a user may use a hand gesture or a sketch instruction (Li et al., 2025b) to specify where an object should be placed, rather than merely asking the robot to tidy the table.
While generative models can create robot behaviors, the next challenge is enabling humans and intelligent systems to control and edit them.

Meanwhile, robotics is gaining access to diverse spatiotemporal references from world models, 3D/4D videos, advanced agents, grasp models, and human demonstrations (Jang et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Murali et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2025b), including keypoints (Huang et al., 2024), flow (Xu et al., 2024), keyposes (Yu et al., 2024), and grasp proposals (Fang et al., 2023; Hao et al., 2025) (see Figure 1(A)).
These representations are physically grounded and low-dimensional, but they only provide partial information on future robot motion rather than complete executable actions.
Existing approaches typically address this gap with signal-specific policies or conditioning mechanisms.
This motivates the need for a unified action interface that can transform diverse spatiotemporal references into controllable robot behaviors.

Our key insight is that heterogeneous spatiotemporal control are not different control problems, but partial action tokens of the same underlying Temporal Cartesian Action Space.
We design Masked Action Space (MAP) as a shared interface that represents these references through partially specified action tokens and a binary mask (see Figure 1(B,C)).
We formulate controllable action generation as a masked action inpainting problem, and we propose Inpainting Policy (IP) to reconstruct masked components in MAP and turn them into a complete executable trajectory (see Section 3.3).

To enable this formulation, we design three components.
(1) A progress-guided sliding window aligns control references with the current task stage using estimated progress value (Chen et al., 2026a) rather than raw execution timesteps (Section 3.2).
(2) A two-stage joint-training strategy uses random masks in the first stage and structured masks in the second stage to learn robust control over diverse and unseen control references (Section 3.4).
(3) As a training-free alternative, we also adopt a RePaint-style inpainting strategy that can be applied during the inference-time denoising process of an off-the-shelf policy.
We conduct experiments on 15 tasks across the ManiSkill, LIBERO-10, and real-world environments, covering six standard control references and randomly structured references.
In sum, our method demonstrates several capabilities:

Versatile controllability.
Inpainting Policy supports diverse spatiotemporal references, including keypoints, flows, orientations, poses, and combinations of these reference types.
In real-world experiments, it attains mean position and rotation errors of 44.3​mm44.3\,\mathrm{mm} and 7.8∘7.8^{\circ}, respectively.
Meanwhile, our method improves the success rate on LIBERO-10 by 4.67 percentage points compared with the baseline.
This proves that our policy enables arbitrary spatiotemporal controllability without compromising task completion.

Versatile controllability.
Inpainting Policy supports diverse spatiotemporal references, including keypoints, flows, orientations, poses, and combinations of these reference types.
In real-world experiments, it attains mean position and rotation errors of 44.3​mm44.3\,\mathrm{mm} and 7.8∘7.8^{\circ}, respectively.
Meanwhile, our method improves the success rate on LIBERO-10 by 4.67 percentage points compared with the baseline.
This proves that our policy enables arbitrary spatiotemporal controllability without compromising task completion.

Interpretability.
MAP (Masked Action Space) provides a human-readable and editable interface that bridges multi-dimensional spatiotemporal information from the physical world with robotic manipulation actions via the masked temporal Cartesian space.
It explicitly indicates which timesteps and action dimensions are constrained.

Practicality.
Our method can be directly applied to diffusion- or flow matching-based policies in simulated or real-world environments.
Built on a lightweight 49​M49\mathrm{M}-parameter DiT model, it achieves a 92.67%92.67\% success rate and a control error of 0.0230.023 (Table 1) in ManiSkill experiments.
In real-world experiments, a 118​M118\mathrm{M}-parameter diffusion model achieves a success rate above 90%90\%.

title: GR-VIP: Geometric representation conditioning for precise visuomotor policy
authors: Chanhwi Lee,Jiwon Seong,Eunje Choi,Hohyung Lee,Jongsoo Lee,Junyeong Bae,Inveom Kwak,Woosang Shin,Soohee Han
comment: Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). . This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
abstract: Achieving precise terminal position and heading alignment remains a significant challenge for learning-based mobile robot control. Recent vision-based learning methods have shown promise for precise target-relative control and generalization to unseen environments with pretrained visual encoders, but general-purpose visual representations are not specifically designed to capture the fine-grained spatial differences between current and goal views required for precise control, and real-world demonstrations combining millimeter-scale terminal accuracy with zero-shot transfer across environments remain limited. To address these challenges, we propose Geometric Representation Conditioning for Precise Visuomotor Policy (GR-VIP), a goal-conditioned visuomotor policy that leverages a visual encoder pretrained for relative camera pose estimation. Rather than using the final relative-pose estimate, GR-VIP conditions action prediction on the dense relational features produced before pose regression, preserving fine-grained cross-view information for learning corrective actions from demonstrations. We evaluate GR-VIP on a real-world docking task and demonstrate high docking success rates and millimeter-scale terminal accuracy in both the training and unseen environments, without additional training for transfer. Furthermore, supplementary experiments illustrate the policy’s ability to align with non-docking targets and complete docking under a tested low-light condition.
introduction:
Learning-based methods enable mobile robot behaviors to be learned directly from data, rather than relying on manually designed control strategies [1, 2].
These approaches have been applied to a wide range of mobile robot tasks, including navigation [3, 4], trajectory tracking [5, 6], and visual servoing [7, 8]. However, achieving precise terminal alignment remains challenging in applications such as docking, inspection, and manipulation-ready base positioning, where successful operation requires accurate positioning and orientation relative to a target [9, 10, 11].

Recent vision-based learning methods have explored precise target-relative positioning for mobile robots [10, 12]. These approaches have demonstrated promising performance in precise positioning and generalization to unseen objects or conditions. However, precise control requires the policy to distinguish fine-grained spatial differences between the current and desired configurations and translate them into appropriate corrective actions. General-purpose visual representations are not explicitly pretrained to encode goal-relative geometric relationships, and existing approaches often introduce additional geometric or target-specific processing to support precise control.
Despite these advances, real-world demonstrations that combine millimeter-scale terminal accuracy with zero-shot transfer across environments remain limited.

To address these challenges, we propose Geometric Representation Conditioning for Precise Visuomotor Policy (GR-VIP), a goal-conditioned visuomotor policy that uses a visual encoder pretrained for relative camera pose estimation. We hypothesize that geometry-aware cross-view representations provide a suitable prior for precise goal-relative control, rather than relying on the final relative-pose estimate. GR-VIP therefore retains dense relational features before pose regression and uses them for policy conditioning. This allows the policy to exploit fine-grained geometric information while learning appropriate corrective actions from demonstrations.

We evaluate GR-VIP on a real-world mobile robot docking task requiring precise terminal position and heading alignment. We compare our method with baselines using alternative visual representations in the training environment and under unseen background and target conditions.
Our experiments show that GR-VIP achieves millimeter-scale terminal accuracy and a high docking success rate in the training environment, while maintaining high success rates and millimeter-scale accuracy in unseen environments without additional training.
Furthermore, additional experiments illustrate alignment to configurations specified by non-docking goal images and successful docking under a low-light condition. Fig. 1 provides an overview of GR-VIP’s capabilities.

title: Hardware-as-Regularization: Enhancing Data Consistency in Imitation Learning via an Adjustable Passive Compliant Leader Arm
authors: Hideyuki Ichiwara,Yushi Kaida,Hirokazu Ishida
abstract:
Low-cost passive leader arms enable scalable data collection for imitation learning, but their lack of restoring forces leaves redundant joints unconstrained, yielding highly inconsistent joint-space trajectories.
We address this with a low-cost passive joint module (an adjustable mechanical clutch and a 3D-printed spiral spring) that pulls each joint toward a user-defined neutral posture.
This passive restoring force acts as a physical prior equivalent to joint-space L2L_{2} regularization (“Hardware-as-Regularization”), improving kinematic consistency with shorter completion time than an unregularized arm and preserved movement smoothness.
Experiments show substantial variance reduction over a naive passive arm, trajectory consistency on par with an active virtual spring of the same actuator class, and substantially higher downstream success rates (e.g., 73.3% vs. 36.7% on Block Stacking); a stiffness sweep shows consistency degrading monotonically as stiffness decreases, confirming that mechanical stiffness behaves like a regularization weight.
introduction:
Modern robot manipulation research is increasingly driven by large-scale imitation learning and deep visuomotor policies [17, 18, 6].
To acquire the necessary demonstration data at scale, the community has rapidly adopted low-cost, 3D-printable passive leader arms (e.g., ALOHA [24, 13] and GELLO [21]).
However, this architectural simplification introduces a severe mechanical vulnerability: the complete absence of restoring forces leaves redundant degrees of freedom (DoFs) unconstrained.
Operators naturally allow their posture to drift arbitrarily in the null-space, inducing severe kinematic inconsistency: highly multimodal joint-space trajectories that degrade the optimization landscape and sample efficiency of downstream imitation learning [5, 11].

In classical robotics, kinematic redundancy is resolved via active impedance control.
While utilizing high-end, expensive actuators can easily yield high-fidelity virtual stiffness, this fundamentally contradicts the community’s core objective of scalable, democratized data collection.
Conversely, synthesizing active virtual stiffness on modern, low-cost telemetry rigs inherently risks high-frequency instability due to control loop latency [8], requiring heavy artificial damping that degrades operational transparency.
To bridge the gap between the necessity for kinematic consistency and the physical limits of low-cost hardware, we introduce the paradigm of Hardware-as-Regularization (Fig. 1). Drawing inspiration from passive haptics [1], we propose a novel, purely mechanical compliant joint module featuring a Hirth coupling and a 3D-printed spiral spring. Operating in continuous time with zero latency, this spring is passive: it injects no active energy into the system.
Mathematically, it acts as a physical structural prior, applying L2L_{2} regularization directly in the joint space to continuously guide the operator’s posture toward a user-defined neutral point.

The main contributions of this paper are threefold: (1) a low-cost, passive (no active energy injection) joint mechanism using a 3D-printed spiral spring and an adjustable clutch; (2) the concept of Hardware-as-Regularization, showing that physical compliance naturally resolves kinematic inconsistency in redundant teleoperation; and (3) empirical evidence that our hardware reduces joint-space variance in demonstrations, yielding downstream success rates substantially higher than a naive passive arm and comparable to an active virtual spring system of the same actuator class. title: MambaAct: Efficient Mamba Action Experts for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Khuyen Pham,Tran Nguyen Le,Edoardo Fazzari,Cesare Stefanini
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise for generalist robotic manipulation, but their inference cost remains a major bottleneck for real-time control. This limitation is especially pronounced in flow-matching VLAs such as π0.5\pi_{0.5}, where the action expert is evaluated repeatedly during iterative denoising. We introduce MambaAct, an efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained visual-language prefix encoder of π0.5\pi_{0.5}, while replacing its transformer-based action expert with a compact Mamba-based action expert. Within this expert, Mamba serves as the action mixer that models dependencies across the noisy continuous-action sequence. To preserve visual-language conditioning without repeated token-level cross-attention, MambaAct uses a lightweight Context Compressor to map Vision-language model (VLM) prefix tokens into a compact conditioning signal that gates and modulates each Mamba action block. MambaAct uses a 10×10\times smaller action expert and reduces flow-matching denoising latency by 64.8%64.8\% on LIBERO and 58.8%58.8\% in real-world deployment, while improving mean LIBERO success by 1.081.08 percentage points across three independent fine-tuning seeds and maintaining gains on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks. Our code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/giakhuyendihoc/MambaAct.
introduction:
Recent flow-matching VLAs such as π0\pi_{0} [1] and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [2] achieve strong manipulation performance, but their iterative action-generation process introduces substantial inference cost. At every policy query, the visual-language prefix can be computed once, whereas the action expert must be evaluated repeatedly across multiple flow-matching denoising steps. As a result, action generation can become the dominant source of latency even when the visual-language backbone itself is relatively compact.

Recent efforts to improve VLA efficiency have largely reduced this cost by decreasing the number of sampling steps, compressing or pruning pretrained networks, reducing visual-token processing, or redesigning the policy around smaller architectures. While effective, these approaches primarily accelerate inference by reducing how often existing components are evaluated or by simplifying the visual-language pathway and overall model. In contrast, the architecture of the repeatedly evaluated action expert itself remains comparatively underexplored as an efficiency axis. This motivates us to ask whether flow-matching inference can instead be accelerated by replacing the action-generation module while preserving the pretrained visual-language representations and standard flow-matching formulation.

We address this question with MambaAct, a compact Mamba [3] action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained π0.5\pi_{0.5} visual-language encoder and replaces its large Transformer-based action expert with a lightweight Mamba sequence mixer. Mamba is attractive in this setting because its selective state-space formulation provides a compact inductive bias for modeling ordered, strongly correlated action sequences. As we show empirically, this design enables aggressive action-expert compression while preserving policy performance. To efficiently condition the newly initialized expert on the pretrained VLM, we introduce a Context Compressor and gated FiLM [4] interface that transform the visual-language prefix into a compact representation reused throughout flow-matching denoising. The resulting expert contains only 29.729.7M parameters, compared with 311.5311.5M for the original π0.5\pi_{0.5} action expert.

Our main contributions are:

We introduce MambaAct, establishing action-expert replacement as a complementary efficiency axis for flow-matching VLAs. MambaAct replaces the repeatedly evaluated Transformer action expert with a compact Mamba expert while retaining the pretrained visual-language backbone and standard flow-matching formulation, without additional pretraining or distillation.

We show that Mamba enables aggressive action-expert compression: MambaAct uses over 10×10\times fewer action-expert parameters than π0.5\pi_{0.5} while improving mean LIBERO [5] success by 1.081.08 percentage points across three fine-tuning seeds.

Through controlled ablations, we examine the contributions of the Mamba action mixer and conditioning interface to the efficiency-performance trade-off. We further demonstrate that MambaAct composes with VLM-depth reduction and transfers to SmolVLA [6], indicating that action-expert replacement generalizes across flow-matching VLA backbones.

title: Ego2Contact: Predicting Touch from Egocentric Human Video for Contact-Rich Robot Manipulation
authors: Qianqian Yang,Dayou Li,Bangya Liu,Zihao Zhu,Nuo Chen,Siyuan Xu,Hezhen Hu,Chen Yu,Rebecca Friesen,Minghui Zheng,Cynthia Hipwell,Xiaoning Qian,Kenji Shimada,Zhiwen Fan
abstract: Contact locations and interaction forces are critical for contact-rich robot manipulation but are often ambiguous from vision alone. Measuring them on robots requires specialized tactile hardware and platform-specific data collection, which keeps robot tactile data scarce. Human egocentric video is far easier to scale but lacks touch. Recent predictors trained on egocentric recordings paired with tactile-glove measurements can predict this missing signal from video alone. These predictors, however, remain confined to human hands, which differ from robot hands in appearance and tactile layout. We present Ego2Contact, which learns a visual-tactile prior from human interactions and transfers it to robot hands. Its predictor fuses temporal scene context with hand-local visual features to infer bimanual tactile fields from the RGB video. Anatomical region correspondences align varying robot tactile layouts with the predictor’s canonical grid, turning robot measurements into fine-tuning targets and predictions into policy inputs. Ego2Contact outperforms prior tactile predictors on human data, including unseen objects, and on robot data after adaptation. The adapted predictor provides tactile inputs for both simulated reinforcement learning and real-robot policy post-training. In simulation, policies using predicted touch outperform non-tactile baselines and recover part of the benefit of ground-truth tactile sensing. These results show that human-learned tactile priors can supply touch when direct tactile sensing is limited.
introduction:
Reliable contact-rich robot manipulation depends on understanding where physical contact occurs and how interaction forces evolve. Dexterous behaviors, from regulating grip force against slip to detecting contact onset under occlusion, rely on contact information that is often ambiguous from visual observations alone [1, 2]. Tactile sensors provide direct measurements of these interactions, yet collecting large-scale visual-tactile data on robots remains challenging. Tactile skins and optical sensors require specialized hardware that is difficult to integrate and tightly coupled to specific end-effector geometries [3, 4]. Consequently, tactile recordings are costly to collect and difficult to reuse across platforms, leaving tactile measurements largely absent from large-scale cross-embodiment datasets [5].

Human egocentric video, by contrast, is far easier to collect at scale [6, 7, 8] but lacks touch. Recent datasets recorded with sensing gloves pair egocentric RGB video with dense full-hand pressure measurements [9, 10, 11]. Training a predictor on such data makes it possible to recover this missing signal directly from visual observations, without a tactile sensor at inference time. However, existing visual-tactile predictors are developed and evaluated exclusively within the human domain [12, 10, 11], and they do not show that inferred touch can drive robot policies. In contrast, robot-centric approaches that imagine or predict tactile signals learn entirely within a single robot’s native sensor space and do not draw on human interaction data [13, 14]. Methods that do transfer human tactile priors to robots entangle tactile estimation with a specific policy architecture or action space [15, 16]. What remains missing is a unified mechanism that extracts a generalizable visual-tactile prior from human interactions and delivers it to heterogeneous robots as explicit tactile observations that their policies can consume.

Establishing this human-to-robot bridge involves two fundamental challenges. The first is to resolve the visual ambiguity during contact inference. Since the interacting surfaces are routinely occluded by the hand, a static image or an estimated 3D hand pose does not uniquely determine the underlying pressure distribution. Identical hand configurations can exert vastly different forces depending on the task phase. Therefore, reliable inference demands integrating the temporal dynamics of the scene with fine-grained local hand appearance. The second challenge is to overcome the morphological and sensory discrepancy between human and robot hands. Robot hands differ visibly from gloved human hands, which shifts the visual input away from the human training distribution. A predictor trained on human gloves also produces pressure on a human-centric layout, whereas the downstream robots may rely on sparse rigid-link force readings in simulation or high-density taxel arrays in the real world. Without a structured interface, predictions in human space cannot be supervised by robot measurements or consumed by robot control policies.

We introduce Ego2Contact, a framework that learns a visual-tactile prior from human egocentric video and transfers it to robot hands, where it provides tactile observations for robot learning (Figure 1). Ego2Contact formulates tactile estimation as conditional flow-matching generation over a canonical 2D hand-grid representation [10]. To address the visual ambiguity, our diffusion transformer is conditioned on a cross-attentive fusion of temporally aggregated scene tokens and hand-local visual features. The canonical grid organizes tactile signals into explicit anatomical regions, so it naturally serves as a cross-embodiment interface. By establishing region-level correspondences between this grid and a target robot’s physical sensing zones, we map distinct robot tactile recordings into the canonical space for fine-tuning and decode the generated grid predictions into policy-compatible tactile inputs. Fine-tuning on paired robot video also adapts the predictor to the robot’s visual appearance. Because the predictor outputs explicit tactile observations, it remains decoupled from the downstream policy and serves both reinforcement learning and vision-language-action (VLA) post-training.

We validate Ego2Contact across the perception-to-action loop. In tactile prediction, our method outperforms regression and pose-conditioned baselines across seen and unseen objects on human data, as well as after adaptation to collected robot data. More importantly, the adapted predictor functions as a virtual tactile sensor that provides link-level contact features for reinforcement learning in simulation, and it generates dense tactile images from demonstration videos to post-train a VLA policy on a real dexterous hand. In simulation, policies consuming predicted touch improve over non-tactile baselines and recover part of the benefit of ground-truth tactile sensing.

In summary, this work has the following contributions.

We propose Ego2Contact, a conditional flow-matching visual-tactile generator that fuses temporal scene context with hand-local visual features to synthesize accurate bimanual pressure fields from egocentric video.

We establish an anatomical adaptation interface that aligns human tactile priors with different robot sensor topologies, turning robot measurements into fine-tuning targets and canonical predictions into policy-compatible inputs.

We evaluate Ego2Contact from human tactile prediction to simulated reinforcement learning and real-robot VLA post-training, showing in simulation that vision-inferred touch improves the success rate of contact-rich manipulation over non-tactile baselines and recovers part of the benefit of real tactile sensing.

2. We establish an anatomical adaptation interface that aligns human tactile priors with different robot sensor topologies, turning robot measurements into fine-tuning targets and canonical predictions into policy-compatible inputs.

title: SenseSwarm: Swarm Exploration via Neural Structure Estimation with Shared World-Anticipation for Rapid Mapping
authors: Haohua Que,Haojia Gao,Mingkai Liu,Hoiian Au,Qian Zhang,Jiayue Xie,Yule Cai,Bokui Chen,Xueqian Wang,Fei Qiao
abstract: A robot swarm covers a building faster with more robots, but the map is only as complete as the space the robots have physically visited. We target the amount of an unknown building a decentralized swarm knows at each instant, ahead of physical coverage. SenseSwarm serves a lightweight learned map predictor on the swarm’s shared occupancy map and folds the predicted structure back into a stigmergic guidance field. Its 709K-parameter predictor is fine-tuned on the swarm’s own multi-front observations, which we show is necessary: a single-robot predictor collapses on such views. We build a benchmark of twelve real building floors from HouseExpo, HKUST, and KTH, up to 24,000 square meters, and run 1,620 simulations across nine coordination methods, swarm sizes 32 to 512, and three seeds. On physical coverage the swarm is near parity with a greedy frontier planner, as expected. On map reconstruction, every non-predictive baseline needs 1.3 to 1.9 times longer to reach an 80 percent known map, and SenseSwarm holds an equal-time area lead of about 670 square meters, up to 1,359. Folding the prediction into the shared field matters: the same predictor applied per robot matches our speed but suffers a 6.9 times higher inter-robot contact rate at 512 robots. The prediction is computed once per shared map, so its cost stayed flat from 32 to 512 robots.
introduction:
Multi-robot exploration of an unknown building is a core capability for search and rescue, inspection, and mapping [1]. A larger team explores faster, yet the useful output is the map, and the map is only as complete as the space the robots have physically sensed: every unentered room stays blank until a robot walks up to it. We target this ceiling and ask how much of the building a swarm can know at each instant, ahead of physical coverage, rather than how fast it can walk every cell.

Prior work optimizes traversal. Frontier methods drive robots to the known-unknown boundary [2, 3, 4], next-best-view planners select informative viewpoints [7], decentralized systems such as RACER and TARE coordinate teams to high efficiency [8, 9], and benchmarks standardize the metrics [10]. All report how fast the robots cover the space; to our knowledge, none reports how fast a decentralized swarm reconstructs the map when unseen structure is predicted rather than visited.

Map prediction closes exactly this gap, but for single robots: generative networks predict unknown structure and planners act on it [11, 12, 13], MapEx inpaints the global grid [17], PIPE Planner adds pathwise information gain [18], and SenseMapNet with SenseExpo distill a lightweight local predictor [19, 20]. For multiple robots, 4CNet runs a per-robot diffusion predictor conditioned on teammate trajectories, demonstrated on three robots [21]. No method reports a map-reconstruction speedup for a decentralized swarm. That slot is empty, and it is the one we fill.11
1
            
            
            
          Videos of every run, the benchmark maps, and the construction scripts: https://que121.github.io/senseswarm-site/

Reaching it requires a predictor that runs at swarm scale, stays accurate on what a swarm actually observes (thin multi-front strips of a shared map, not a single robot’s connected blob), and guides the swarm without central control. SenseSwarm answers with one predictor served on the shared map, tiled so the cost tracks the frontier and not the robot count, fine-tuned on the swarm’s own observations, and deposited as a stigmergic field that each robot reads only locally.

We evaluate in ARGoS [22] on twelve real floors [23, 24] with 32 to 512 robots, against seven baselines covering every non-predictive decentralized family [25, 26, 27, 28] plus an integration ablation that runs the same predictor per robot, standing in for the 4CNet mechanism at swarm scale.
Our contributions are threefold.

The first swarm-scale exploration benchmark on real super-large buildings, to our knowledge. Twelve real floors up to 24,000 square meters, in a 1,620-run matrix [10].

Predictive stigmergy. One predictor serves the shared map and becomes a stigmergic field read only locally, so the cost tracks the frontier, not the robot count. It must match the swarm’s observation distribution: trained for a single robot, the same architecture drops from 0.85 to 0.34 IoU.

Reconstruction is where prediction pays. Every non-predictive baseline needs 1.3 to 1.9 times longer to reach an 80 percent known map, and folding the prediction per robot costs 6.9 times the contacts at 512 robots.

title: Structured Perception Representations for Off-road Dynamics Learning
authors: Micah Nye,Samuel Triest,Matthew Sivaprakasam,Isaiah Adu,Sebastian Scherer,Wenshan Wang
comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026.
abstract: Autonomously navigating off-road terrain at high speed demands accurate control, which often relies on dynamics models that capture complex interactions between the robot and terrain. In off-road regimes, terrain interaction is a major component of the vehicle’s dynamics. Prior work attempts to capture this effect by training learned models of the vehicle’s dynamics, conditioned on its perception of the local environment. However, said conditioning is often overly simplistic, ignoring the spatial structure of the dynamics problem. Our approach, SpatialBEV, exploits this spatial structure. At each step, we query the bird’s-eye-view (BEV) features around the predicted state, conditioning the next prediction on current geometric and semantic cues. We additionally present a benchmarking approach that mines a dataset’s most difficult scenarios. On datasets collected across seasons, SpatialBEV reduces prediction error by 17.1%, compared to physics-based and learned baselines. We further evaluate on hardware on high-speed (≥\geq10m/s) and geometrically challenging courses with a 25.3% reduction in maximum cross-track error. More details can be found at https://theairlab.org/spatial-bev-dynamics.
introduction:
Autonomous navigation in unstructured, off-road environments at high speeds remains a significant challenge for model-predictive control (MPC) frameworks. MPC is a well-established method in control theory; however, its success depends on accurate dynamics models for forward prediction. Traditional methods rely on simplified physics models [18, 50, 20, 15, 25] that struggle to capture complex terradynamics induced by challenging terrains like loose gravel, deep snow, or standing water. High speeds exacerbate these unmodeled interactions which may lead to task failure.

While learned dynamics models have emerged as a potential solution due to their expressivity, they often neglect environment observation [41, 7]. When a robot commands identical actions under identical initial conditions on different surfaces with differing geometry or friction, the resulting trajectory varies significantly [12, 5]. In state-only models, this variance is captured as an unmodeled disturbance term or stochastic noise term. However, this uncertainty is largely epistemic; it is a direct consequence of the model’s inability to observe the environmental physics imposed on the robot during interaction.

Motivated by this shortcoming, we propose a dynamics representation that conditions its prediction on environment geometry and visual semantics. We use birds-eye-view (BEV) representations which provide a spatially-aligned structure for environment attributes such as terrain elevation and Visual Foundation Model (VFM) features. While prior works encode BEV features as a fixed contextual prior at the beginning of a prediction pass [47, 30, 35], this leaves the spatial representation underutilized. Instead of treating the BEV information as a single prior, we make full use of its spatial structure by treating it as a continuous source for incremental feedback and state correction at every prediction step. This explicit architecture ensures the most relevant BEV features are queried at each step. This is especially important at high speed, where a robot traverses large distances and fixed-prior approaches condition every prediction step on the same initial encoding, rather than the features local to the robot’s current position.

We demonstrate the efficacy of this representation through extensive evaluation. We also introduce a systematic testing methodology that clusters similar actions to isolate high-variance regimes, specifically targeting the scenarios where current models are likely to fail and where environment context is necessary for accurate dynamics prediction. Our results span both offline evaluation on aggressive driving data around multiple test sites as well as online hardware deployment on high speed (≥\geq10m/s) and geometrically challenging courses. Through all experiments, we show that our spatial representation for incremental conditioning reduces forward prediction error and improves closed-loop tracking. Specifically our work provides three key contributions:

A new method for leveraging structured perception representations for environment context in dynamics modeling

A benchmarking approach to mine the most challenging sequences of dynamics datasets

Extensive offline experiments and online hardware experiments at high speeds (≥\geq10 m/s), demonstrating the efficacy of our approach

title: Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Policy Improvement via Flow-Reversed Action Anchors
authors: Carl Qi,Weijun Dong,Xiaojie Wang,Peiyi Chen,Rahul Sajnani,Mingyuan Zhang,Amy Zhang,Jose Barreiros,Manikatan Nambi,Lillian J. Ratliff,Dylan Randle
abstract:
Generalist robot policies offer strong behavioral priors, but achieving deployment-level reliability and throughput remains difficult. Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve these policies, yet its effectiveness is constrained by the cost of online interaction. Existing methods adapt frozen flow-matching policies by treating noise space as a continuous action space. We show that this behaviorally unstructured space makes exploration inefficient, often preventing these methods from extracting meaningful learning signals on challenging tasks. We introduce AnchorQ, which enables coarse-to-fine policy improvement through a structured, refinable latent action representation. At each decision step, AnchorQ uses flow reversal to map reference behaviors to state-conditioned latent anchors, samples local particles around those anchors, and applies value-guided sampling to explore promising refinements. Our analysis shows that anchors reduce identification complexity at the cost of support bias; particle refinement trades this bias against action-class complexity; and critic accuracy determines the reliability of KL-regularized, value-guided selection. Across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, AnchorQ outperforms state-of-the-art post-training baselines in sample efficiency, delivering a 37% improvement in real-world success rate and 97% higher simulated task throughput under the same interaction budget. Additional visualizations are available on our website 11

introduction:
Generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a powerful starting
point for robotic manipulation. Through extensive pretraining, these policies
can follow language instructions and transfer to objects, scenes, and tasks
beyond the training set
(Black et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025a; Kim et al., 2025; TRI LBM Team et al., 2025).
Yet deployment demands more than broad competence: robots must achieve high
success rates and throughput in their target environments, while adaptation
itself must remain inexpensive. Pretrained VLAs remain imperfect under changes
in geometry, clutter, object placement, and task execution, while collecting
demonstrations that densely cover these variations is costly.
Reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training offers a natural route to
deployment-specific improvement, but fine-tuning a large VLA is computationally
expensive and can degrade useful pretrained behaviors. An appealing alternative
is therefore to keep the generalist policy frozen and learn how to select and
refine its actions.

Prior methods adapts pretrained VLA policies by learning lightweight action corrections, steering latent inputs, or selecting among candidate actions (Yuan et al., 2025; Wagenmaker et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026; Nakamoto et al., 2024).
Flow-matching policies provide an additional adaptation interface through the
noise that initializes action generation. For a fixed state ss and numerical
sampler, an initial latent zz is deterministically mapped to an action
chunk, a=π0​(s,z)a=\pi_{0}(s,z). The latent can therefore serve directly as the action for RL: changing how zz is selected changes the executed behavior without modifying the VLA. For example, diffusion steering via reinforcement learning (DSRL) learns directly
in the latent noise space of a frozen policy (Wagenmaker et al., 2025).

This raises a more fundamental question: what action representation should be used for RL to adapt pretrained VLA policies?
At one extreme, a handful of behaviorally meaningful actions, such as moving left or right, can make online learning much easier, but only by restricting the behaviors the policy can express.
At the other extreme, existing approaches (Wagenmaker et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2025) search expressive but behaviorally unstructured continuous action or latent spaces. The learner must discover which action corrections or latent vectors produce useful behaviors in each state, without an explicit set of behavioral alternatives to guide this search. This makes efficient exploration extremely difficult: as we demonstrate in our experiments, DSRL and action-space residual RL baselines fail to learn effective policies on challenging tasks within the interaction budget.
What is missing is an online action representation that is both structured and refinable: compact when coarse behaviors suffice, but able to expose richer behavior when needed.

To address this gap, we construct a structured and refinable action representation around state-conditioned noise-space anchors, which we generate at every decision by applying flow reversal (Tang et al., 2026) to a small library of semantically meaningful reference actions.
Building on this representation, we introduce AnchorQ, a coarse-to-fine RL method for adapting frozen flow-matching policies directly in their latent noise space.
AnchorQ first samples local particles around each anchor and applies exponential value tilting to bias sampling toward high-value particles. It then selects an anchor and samples a refined noise latent from its tilted particle distribution, which the frozen flow policy decodes into an action. We train the critic QQ using temporal-difference (TD) learning from online experience to guide both particle tilting and anchor selection.

The main contributions are summarized as follows:

A structured and refinable action representation for online RL. We propose a new online action representation and a coarse-to-fine RL method that turn continuous-space exploration into selection and refinement of behaviorally meaningful actions.

Guarantees for coarse-to-fine latent search. We show that the flow-reversed noise anchors reduces identification complexity
(Theorem 1), while particle refinement
trades support bias against the complexity of the local action class
(Theorem 2). We further show that value tilting reliably amplifies high-value refinements under critic error (Theorem 3), while epistemic uncertainty adaptation calibrates exploitation to critic confidence (Theorem 9, Appendix I).

Consistent empirical gains in simulation and on real robots.
Across three benchmarks in LIBERO 
(Liu et al., 2023a) and RoboTwin (Chen et al., 2025), AnchorQ outperforms the state-of-the-art steering baselines, which include continuous noise space RL and residual-based RL, with 97% higher throughput than the closest baseline. We also deploy AnchorQ to solve three challenging real robot manipulation tasks, where it outperforms both the frozen base policy and the RL baseline under the same interaction budget.

1. A structured and refinable action representation for online RL. We propose a new online action representation and a coarse-to-fine RL method that turn continuous-space exploration into selection and refinement of behaviorally meaningful actions.

2. Guarantees for coarse-to-fine latent search. We show that the flow-reversed noise anchors reduces identification complexity
(Theorem 1), while particle refinement
trades support bias against the complexity of the local action class
(Theorem 2). We further show that value tilting reliably amplifies high-value refinements under critic error (Theorem 3), while epistemic uncertainty adaptation calibrates exploitation to critic confidence (Theorem 9, Appendix I).

3. Consistent empirical gains in simulation and on real robots.

title: DefFlow: Goal-Conditioned Deformable Object Manipulation using 3D Point Flows
authors: Gaurav Singh,Sergio Orozco,Ryan Duong,Mete Tuluhan Akbulut,George Konidaris,Srinath Sridhar
abstract:
Manipulating deformable objects toward desired 3D configurations is a fundamental capability for robots operating in unstructured physical environments.
However, as the range of possible initial and target configurations grows, goal-conditioned deformable manipulation requires a robot to infer increasingly diverse manipulation behaviors in addition to precise continuous actions.
We introduce DefFlow, a framework for goal-conditioned manipulation of deformable objects toward a broad range of 3D configurations. DefFlow learns from demonstrations by jointly predicting the goal-conditioned 3D point flow of the robot and deformable object.
We show that this formulation better captures both the manipulation decisions, such as when and where to grasp, release, or re-grasp, and the precise continuous motions required for goal reaching, rather than predicting only the robot flow.
Across rope, granular-media, and cloth manipulation settings with diverse initial and target configurations, DefFlow substantially outperforms goal-conditioned action-prediction and robot-flow-only baselines on success rates and goal-distance metrics.
We further demonstrate deployment of our framework on a real robot using real point-cloud observations and unseen goal configurations. Project Page:
https://def-flow.github.io.
introduction:
Deformable-object manipulation often involves reaching a desired target shape or configuration, such as routing cables or ropes into curved shapes, wrapping or draping cloth, or shaping granular material.
Enabling robots to achieve a diverse range of such goals is central to developing more general and versatile deformable-object manipulation systems [1].

However, developing goal-conditioned policies that can reliably reach a broad range of such goal configurations remains challenging for several reasons.
First, unlike rigid objects, whose configurations can be described by 6-DoF poses, deformable objects can undergo a wide range of 3D shape changes governed by complex dynamics.
Second, reaching a specific goal requires modeling the coupled dynamics of the robot and deformable object, capturing how their configurations evolve together toward the target [2].
Finally, as the space of possible initial and target configurations becomes broader, the behaviors required to connect them become increasingly diverse, and can be completely different for different goals or starting configurations even for the same object within the same setting.
For example, reaching one rope configuration may require a single grasp and drag, while another may require twisting, releasing, and re-grasping at a different location.

Prior works have explored learning goal-conditioned deformable object policies from 3D pointclouds [3, 4, 5].
However, these approaches typically show settings with relatively narrower distributions of object configurations and isolated behavior primitives, such as a single grasping action followed by servoing [3] or only pinching/squeezing behaviors [4, 5].
Using dense 3D flows as the underlying representation has been shown to improve policy learning from pointclouds for deformable tasks [6], however it is limited to only predicting rigid tool flows [6].

In this work, we introduce DefFlow, a goal-conditioned policy for manipulating deformable objects toward a broad range of 3D configurations using dense 3D point flows.
Our key insight is to use goal-conditioned joint robot-deformable object 3D point flow as the underlying representation learning objective and repurpose that as the robot policy using the robot flows.
This formulation, combined with our data curation recipe enables better goal-conditioned representation learning by associating robot behaviors with their corresponding object deformations, helping distinguish behaviors through their effects on the scene and generalizing to a diverse set of goal shapes that require completely different action trajectories and decisions to reach.
We find that compared to only predicting the robot motion [6], the goal-conditioned 3D flows of the full scene together can improve goal-reaching performance and better predict the manipulation behaviors such as grasping, releasing, and re-grasping, together with the precise continuous actions that the robot must execute to make the objects reach diverse goal configurations.

This recipe has been explored in 2D image space [7, 8]: models that learn the coupled scene prediction in the same output space, e.g. video models, can be repurposed as better policies as the robot motion predicted maps to better action priors.
This has been explored mostly for settings with defined tasks (usually using language conditioning) [7, 8].
For goal-conditioned manipulation, while a similar recipe has been explored with 3D pointclouds, it is limited to rigid objects whose motion is predicted using 6-DoF poses [9]. In contrast, we explore this recipe in goal-conditioned deformable manipulation using dense 3D point flow prediction as the underlying objective.
We test DefFlow on a large number of varied configurations across rope, granular-media, and cloth manipulation with broad start and goal distributions, showcasing the ability of our approach to generalize to diverse configurations and outperform baselines that predict only robot actions or robot flow.

To summarize, our contributions are:

We introduce DefFlow, a goal-conditioned policy for manipulating deformable objects toward a broad range of 3D configurations requiring diverse manipulation behaviors.

We show that learning to predict the goal-conditioned 3D flows for the full scene in addition to robot-flow improves generalization to diverse goal-shapes, decisions and continuous actions for goal reaching.

We show the effectiveness of our approach in various complex goal-reaching environments with a large number of target configurations. We also further validate our approach by deploying it on a real robot with unseen goal shapes.

1. We introduce DefFlow, a goal-conditioned policy for manipulating deformable objects toward a broad range of 3D configurations requiring diverse manipulation behaviors.

2. We show that learning to predict the goal-conditioned 3D flows for the full scene in addition to robot-flow improves generalization to diverse goal-shapes, decisions and continuous actions for goal reaching.

3. We show the effectiveness of our approach in various complex goal-reaching environments with a large number of target configurations. We also further validate our approach by deploying it on a real robot with unseen goal shapes.

title: Simultaneous Force and Motion Control in Generalised Coordinates
authors: Jon Woolfrey
comment: submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2027
abstract: Robot manipulators often come into contact with rigid objects when performing work. This imposes physical constraints on their motion. Simultaneous force & motion control was developed to regulate contact forces commensurate with these constraints, whilst projecting motion control in to the orthogonal, unconstrained directions. This is typically formulated in the task coordinates, i.e. operational space, then mapped to joint torques to command the robot. However, most constraints on the robot control, such as joint limits, collision avoidance, singularity avoidance, etc. are naturally expressed in generalised coordinates (joint space). Thus, formulating the control problem in task space makes it difficult to guarantee control feasibility. In this paper Gauss’ principle of least constraint is used to solve the control as a quadratic programming (QP) problem in generalised coordinates. It is shown that the theoretical solution to this problem produces the correct constrained dynamics for accurate contact force control. Moreover, inequality constraints may be appended to ensure feasibility and safety. Simulation results were conducted in MuJoCo and compared to the operational space formulation. The proposed method is able to simultaneously maintain a desired contact force, minimise trajectory tracking error, and adhere to practical inequality constraints.
introduction:
Robots are rapidly advancing out of the factory and into the wider world. In doing so they are expected to perform work in unstructured environments. This often requires them to make contact with physical objects. For example, many robotic systems are being developed to perform manual labour such as:

Polishing hard surfaces [1],

Washing dishes [2] ,

Lifting and moving boxes [3], and

Manual machining [4].

In all these examples the objects impose physical constraints on the robot’s dynamics. The robot must carefully regulate the ensuing interaction forces as it moves to prevent damage to the object, or itself.

Forces at the endpoint of a robot arm 𝐟e∈ℝm\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{e}}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathrm{m}} are expressed in task space (Cartesian coordinates). But they are mapped to the joint torques 𝝉∈ℝn\boldsymbol{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathrm{n}} via the Jacobian matrix 𝐉e​(𝐪)∈ℝm×n\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{e}}(\mathbf{q})\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathrm{m\times n}} [5]:

Conversely, it is difficult, if not impossible, to reason about complex manipulation tasks in generalised coordinates. As such, operational space control (in task space) was proposed [6] and has become a canonical control method reiterated through numerous textbooks [7, 8, 9]. The premise is straightforward:

Model the force and motion in task coordinates,

Devise a controller in the task space to meet requirements, then

Use (1) to obtain the required joint torques.

If robots are expected to complete increasingly sophisticated manipulation tasks in unstructured environments, then the controller must be robust to numerous operational demands. In particular there are 3 hurdles that simultaneous force and motion control must satisfy:

The decoupling of 𝐟e\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{e}} into the motion and interaction forces ought to be preserved when projected into generalised coordinates,

It ought to account for kinematic redundancy, and

It must adhere to practical constraints such as joint limits, singularity avoidance, collision avoidance, etc.

Problem 1 has been addressed in the literature via the “dynamically consistent” projection [10]. Still, some literature hence promoted kinematic projection [8, 11, 12].

Problem 2 was addressed in [6]. If the task space dimensions are fewer than the configuration space (m<n\mathrm{m<n}) then we may simply append the null space projection of the Jacobian:

𝝉1\boldsymbol{\tau}_{1} now represents the primary control input,

𝐍e∈ℝn×n\mathbf{N}_{\mathrm{e}}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathrm{n\times n}} is the null space projection matrix such that

𝐍eT𝐉eT=𝟎\mathbf{N}\mathrm{{}_{e}^{T}}\mathbf{J}\mathrm{{}_{e}^{T}}=\mathbf{0}, and

𝝉2\boldsymbol{\tau}_{2} represents a secondary task.

Problem 3 is the crux of the matter. In the past, when robots were confined to the factory performing prescribed tasks, both the environment and motion could be planned to ensure safe, feasible execution. This can no longer be guaranteed in the wider world. Kinematic redundancy may be used to abet the controller but it cannot guarantee satisfaction of the numerous, hierarchical tasks in addition to feasibility. This also leads to a fourth problem:

How can 1), 2), and 3) be resolved simultaneously?

The literature on dynamic, legged robots have made some headway in this regard. Initially, the control paradigm for walking was borrowed directly from the operational space formulation. Contact forces on the ground were synthesised into the operational space dynamics and projected to the joint torques [13, 14].

At some point there was a pivot to using quadratic programming (QP), which permits inequality constraints on the solution. This was driven by practical necessity whereby the controller must respect joint limits, contact friction cones, and balancing requirements [15, 16, 17]. The objective functions are typically heuristic, usually minimising (unweighted) task errors, or slack variables. The control design had become less physically meaningful. Adherence to dynamics was imposed through constraint equations.

This article synthesises the physical coherence of the operational space formulation with the practicality of QP methods (Fig. 2). Gauss’ principle is used to construct a dynamically-consistent objective function for the QP problem [18]. Then, by imposing the Pfaffian constraints commensurate with the rigid contact, it is shown that the theoretical solution gives the complete inverse dynamics for force and motion control. Specifically, a centripetal-like constraint term precipitates from this derivation which is often missing from other methods. Its absence adversely affects the contact force [1].

Kinematic redundancy is resolved by stacking multiple, dynamically-consistent QPs: the solution of each lower-priority QP is embedded in the objective of the QP above it, so the highest priority task is enforced exactly. Importantly, inequality constraints are also readily appended to the QP to account for practical considerations such as joint limits [19], singularities, or obstacle avoidance [20].

Section II reviews the task space formulation whose solution is used to compare and contrast the proposed method.

Section III covers the generalised coordinates, including derivation of the inverse dynamics, and control formulation.

Section IV provides details for implementation.

Section V validates the method through simulation using ROS2 and MuJoCo.

title: PASS-VLN: Passability-Aware Local-Command Vision-and-Language Navigation
authors: Cong Zou,Xiangsheng Shi,Xuanhui Wang,Fubin Wang,Guangjun Ge,Chao Wang,Yu Wang
abstract: Reliable vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires not only understanding instructions but also determining whether and how a robot can physically execute them. However, existing VLN benchmarks typically assume executable instructions and focus on long-horizon tasks. This leaves body-dependent local execution, including passability and collision-free execution, largely unexamined. Evaluating these factors within long-horizon tasks would entangle local physical execution with task planning and long-term spatial memory, making navigation failures difficult to attribute. We therefore focus on grounding local navigation commands in executable motion under environmental and robot body constraints. We present PASS-VLN, a passability-aware local-command VLN benchmark and model. The benchmark holds the scene, instruction, start pose, and reference route fixed while varying robot body width, requiring target completion when the instructed passage is feasible and stopping before blockage otherwise. Our model encodes body width through obstacle inflation in a depth-derived local bird’s-eye view, fuses geometry with visual and linguistic context, and predicts discrete latent action codes for continuous closed-loop execution. Experiments show that PASS-VLN improves collision-free success by approximately 1212 percentage points over a strong VLN model fine-tuned on our benchmark, while adapting reach-versus-stop behavior to body constraints and generalizing to unseen body widths. When integrated with a high-level planner, PASS-VLN achieves higher success with fewer local commands, while real-world deployment further demonstrates its effectiveness as a low-level executor. The benchmark and model will be released.
introduction:
Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow natural-language instructions and navigate to a target in visual environments. R2R established the standard indoor VLN setting [1], followed by benchmarks for more complex multilingual instructions [2], continuous control [3], remote object grounding [4], persistent navigation [5], and physics-aware unified evaluation [6].

Most existing VLN benchmarks provide a complete route instruction per episode and assume that the instructed motion is physically executable. Directly incorporating body-dependent physical execution, including passability and collision-free execution, would couple local execution with planning, progress tracking, spatial memory, and route-level reasoning, making navigation failures difficult to attribute. Many recent VLN methods emphasize stronger reasoning, memory, and planning [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14], whose gains do not necessarily translate into improved local physical execution. Conventional navigation methods based on local mapping and motion planning account for traversability and collision constraints, but typically take geometric goals or reference paths as input without a natural-language interface for interpreting spatially grounded commands [15, 16, 17].

These considerations motivate focusing on local physical execution as a capability that complements high-level reasoning and memory. A human or a high-level agent, including one based on a VLM, can issue local commands, while a low-level executor grounds each command in current observations and converts it into physical motion. The local command serves as their semantic interface, specifying an immediate local objective and the spatial cues needed to interpret it. For example, “move forward and stop between the sofa and the table” specifies landmarks, spatial relations, and a stopping condition while leaving broader task planning to the command issuer.

Such a local executor must reason about not only where to go, but also whether and how the motion can be physically executed. Most existing VLN research emphasizes semantic spatial reasoning, such as left/right relations, object ordering, relative positions, and path structure [18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23], without explicitly considering physical spatial feasibility under body constraints. In practice, a correctly grounded passage may still be too narrow for the robot, and traversable passages may require body-dependent clearance and alignment. A local executor should therefore consider the instructed motion and its physical feasibility under the current embodiment.

To address these requirements, we introduce PASS-VLN, a PASSability-aware local-command VLN framework comprising a controlled benchmark and a body-width-conditioned model for planar physical execution. The benchmark holds the scene, instruction, start pose, and reference route fixed while varying robot body width. For paired configurations where passage feasibility changes under the same command, the narrower robot is expected to reach the target, whereas the wider robot is expected to stop before the blockage, directly testing whether execution adapts to the interaction between instructed motion, environmental geometry, and robot embodiment. The benchmark covers commands based on local observations and commonsense spatial knowledge for visible-target navigation or bounded exploration, as well as commands requiring broader scene or route knowledge.

To connect language understanding with body-dependent geometry and motion execution, PASS-VLN projects depth into a local bird’s-eye view (BEV) and incorporates body width through obstacle inflation, making the geometric representation reflect robot-specific clearance. Fusing this representation with language, current vision, and visual history allows the policy to interpret the instructed motion in relation to its physical feasibility. To translate this understanding into continuous execution, the model predicts discrete latent action codes learned from short trajectory windows, which are decoded into planar relative motions for closed-loop control. The main contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce a controlled VLN benchmark that isolates local execution from long-horizon navigation and explicitly evaluates body-width-dependent physical feasibility. title: Pedicel-Targeted Strawberry Harvesting via Imitation Learning on a Low-Cost Teleoperated Robotic Arm
authors: Nitin Rai,Won Suk Lee,Hongyoung Leon,Heping Zhu
comment: . This paper was peer-reviewed and accepted in the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), "From Innovation to Adoption: Hardware, AI, Policy, and Funding Challenges in Agricultural Robotics Workshop, " Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, 2026
abstract: Precise pedicel-targeted grasping in strawberry harvesting remains a critical bottleneck due to the pedicel’s small diameter (1.3-3 mm), color similarity with surrounding foliage, and precise force control required for clean abscission zone detachment. As a market-grade crop, strawberry aesthetic value makes bruise-free pedicel detachment essential over direct fruit grasping. Classical approaches struggle to unify vision models, motion planning, and contact manipulation into a robust framework, particularly in occluded canopy environments. Therefore, this work presents a visuomotor imitation learning pipeline for pedicel-targeted strawberry harvesting that unifies perception, motion planning, and contact manipulation from collecting human teleoperation demonstrations, training an Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy with a ResNet-50 visual backbone, and deploying the learned policy autonomously on a Jetson AGX Orin edge platform at 15 Hz. The trained policy achieved consistent loss convergence from 2.84 to 0.091 over 100K gradient steps on 130 demonstrations. We have also established a reproducible open-source pipeline with publicly released dataset and model weights for the agricultural robotics community. Full dataset is available at nitindominicrai/strawberry_pedicel_grasp_teleoperation and trained policy at nitindominicrai/act_strawberry_pedicel. To replicate this work, all code, configurations, and deployment instructions are publicly available at autonomous_strawberry_pedicel_harvesting.
introduction:
Strawberries (Fragaria ×\times ananassa) are widely grown across Florida during the winter season, typically from October to mid-March. In 2024, Florida planted 16,200 acres (6,556 ha) of strawberries and produced over 332M lbs (150.6M kg) of fruit [1]. Maintaining this level of production and fruit quality requires timely harvesting by February-March, placing significant demand on the available labor force. During peak harvesting season (Feb-March), an average of 110 workers per 100 acres are required, underscoring the urgent need for ground-based robotic harvesting robots in strawberry production [2].

Over the past decade, significant research has focused on vision-guided robotic end-effectors for direct strawberry fruit grasping [3, 4]. However, direct fruit contact can introduce bruising risks that degrade aesthetic quality and market value under uncontrolled grasping force [5]. Pedicel-targeted grasping offers a less damaging alternative, yet presents its own challenges, the pedicel measures only 1.3-3 mm in diameter, shares spectral similarity with surrounding foliage and calyx, and must be localized within a densely occluded canopy. Classical CV pipelines struggle with such slender structure detection, and coupling detection with downstream motion planning introduces compounding error in unstructured field conditions.

Therefore, in this work, we present an end-to-end imitation learning approach for pedicel-targeted strawberry harvesting that bypasses explicit intermediate perception
and planning stages entirely. Using a low-cost teleoperation platform, we collect human demonstrations of the full reach-grasp-twist-pull sequence and train an Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy directly from synchronized wrist-camera observations and joint-space actions [6]. The trained policy is deployed autonomously on a Jetson AGX Orin edge device, providing a fully self-contained harvesting system. The contributions of this work are as follows:

A teleoperation protocol and open-access dataset for strawberry pedicel grasping, comprising episodes of the complete reach-grasp-twist-pull sequences recorded at 30 FPS.

Training and evaluation of an ACT visuomotor policy with ResNet-50 as a backbone on the collected dataset, demonstrating convergent learning behavior required for pedicel detachment.

Deployment and benchmarking of the trained policy on a Jetson AGX Orin, assessing the inference constraints and failure modes of edge-deployment.

title: Shape-Aware Neural Time Fields for Rigid-Body Motion and Manipulation Planning
authors: Yanming Zhou,Yuchen Liu,Ahmed H. Qureshi
abstract: Rigid-body motion planning is fundamental to robotic transport and manipulation, where both object position and orientation determine whether a body can move through cluttered environments. This coupling makes planning challenging because translation and rotation can be constrained very differently by surrounding geometry. We propose Shape-Aware Neural Time Fields, a physics-informed neural motion planning framework that learns a reusable travel-time, or cost-to-go, representation for rigid-body motion while explicitly accounting for these distinct geometric restrictions. The learned field captures local motion difficulty in translation and rotation and is paired with a sampling-based planner that balances progress toward the goal with the cost of reaching nearby poses. We evaluate the framework across 2D and 3D rigid-body planning tasks and non-prehensile manipulation through object pushing in diverse environments. Results show substantial improvements in planning success and inference efficiency over physics-informed neural planning baselines, while remaining competitive with classical sampling-based planners at significantly lower planning times. Ablation studies further validate the contributions of both the learned representation and the proposed planning strategy. Finally, closed-loop pushing experiments under execution deviations and external disturbances demonstrate that fast replanning enables reactive and adaptive task execution. Video demo can be found here: https://youtu.be/5rUwvolPAgE. Code implementation can be found here: https://github.com/Ymz2006/Shape-NTFields
introduction:
The piano movers’ problem asks how to move a rigid body between two poses without colliding with obstacles [1]. In object transport and manipulation, both position and orientation determine whether a body can pass through openings and clutter. Rigid-body planning must therefore account for translation and rotation, which geometry can constrain differently.

Classical planners use search, sampling, or trajectory optimization [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Many solve each start-goal query separately. PRM and LazyPRM reuse roadmaps but still require online connections and graph search [7, 8], and the resulting paths may require further optimization [9]. These recurring costs motivate reusable planning representations with efficient inference.

Learning-based planners shift part of this computation offline by reusing trained models to predict paths or planning costs for new start-goal queries [10, 11]. Physics-informed approaches such as Neural Time Fields (NTFields) instead learn continuous goal-conditioned travel-time representations directly from geometry without requiring expert trajectories [12, 13]. Geometry sets a scalar propagation speed that measures local motion difficulty, rather than physical execution velocity: greater clearance gives higher speed, while proximity to obstacles lowers it. The learned field provides reusable goal-dependent costs for motion generation. Recent work extends this approach through metric learning and planning in large or unknown environments [14, 15, 16].

For rigid bodies, however, a single geometric notion of local motion difficulty may be insufficient because translation and rotation are restricted differently by obstacles. An elongated object may translate along a narrow corridor yet collide with a wall when attempting to turn. Reaching the next opening may therefore require first moving into free space, reorienting, and then approaching the passage. Existing shape-aware and object-pose neural time fields account for body geometry and orientation [17, 18], but their speed supervision does not separately specify translational and angular clearance. We therefore introduce separate translation and rotation representations and geometry-derived propagation targets, with both targets depending on the complete pose to retain their geometric coupling.

Reliable path extraction must also account for local motion difficulty. A candidate with low remaining travel time may still be difficult to reach through a constrained translation or rotation. We therefore score both its remaining time to the goal and the local cost of reaching it. Variations in field-derived speed across sampled motions then guide a steering correction, connecting geometric supervision to path generation.

We introduce Shape-Aware Neural Time Fields (Shape-NTFields), combining distinct translation and rotation supervision with sampling-based path extraction. For each fixed body and environment, the field serves new start-goal queries and closed-loop replanning from updated poses.

Our contributions are as follows:

Translation and rotation supervision. Separate representations and geometric speed targets capture the two motion components within one pose-dependent field. Inverse-speed weighting emphasizes constrained poses, and Relative Normal Loss supervises speed decrease toward reduced clearance.

Planning with local and global travel-time costs. Our sampling-based planner balances remaining travel time against local motion cost. Speed variation across candidates supplies a steering direction for the next pose update.

We evaluate the framework on 2D and 3D rigid-body planning tasks spanning seven shapes and four environments per dimension, together with closed-loop non-prehensile pushing experiments. In 3D, our method achieves 92.9% success with 0.055 s mean inference time, compared with 63.7% success for TDM [14], while the 2D planner achieves 94.3% success at 0.048 s mean inference time. Qualitative real-world UR5e demonstrations further show repeated replanning after execution deviations and external perturbations.

1. Translation and rotation supervision. Separate representations and geometric speed targets capture the two motion components within one pose-dependent field. Inverse-speed weighting emphasizes constrained poses, and Relative Normal Loss supervises speed decrease toward reduced clearance.

2. Planning with local and global travel-time costs. Our sampling-based planner balances remaining travel time against local motion cost. Speed variation across candidates supplies a steering direction for the next pose update.
