title: Task Structure and Scalability in Multi-Robot Authoring
authors: Christian Marowski,Byung-Cheol Min
abstract: Multi-robot authoring can reduce completion time by distributing drawing work, but the resulting speedup depends on task structure and the allocation-routing pipeline. We investigate these relationships by representing drawings as geometric stroke graphs and comparing component-level (single-token) allocation with shared-token (decomposed) allocation, which permits multiple robots to work within a connected component. A simulation study of 385 drawings and teams of one to eight robots shows diminishing speedup gains under single-token allocation and larger mean speedups under the shared-token pipeline, each normalized by its own single-robot completion time. Shared-token execution also exhibits lower idle-time shares at larger team sizes, although it does not reduce completion time for every drawing. Comparisons across structural attribute groups reveal associations between structural descriptors and differences in scaling behavior, with greater separation between several attribute groups at larger team sizes. These findings characterize empirical scaling in the evaluated pipelines and highlight the importance of considering within-component workload and graph structure alongside component count. Additional materials are available at https://sites.google.com/view/multirobotauthoring/home.
introduction:
Multi-robot authoring uses teams of robots to reproduce user-specified geometry through drawing, printing, and related fabrication processes [1, 2, 3]. Additional robots create opportunities for parallel execution, but do not guarantee proportional reductions in completion time. Limits on parallel work are a familiar concern in parallel computing [4], while multi-robot execution also involves travel, workload imbalance, and interference [5]. For authoring, the central question is therefore: How do task structure and allocation strategy affect the benefit of increasing team size?

A geometric stroke graph makes this question explicit (Fig. 1). Edges represent drawable segments, and vertices represent stroke waypoints and detected intersections. Under component-level (single-token) allocation, each connected component is assigned as an indivisible task to one robot. Under shared-token allocation, work within a component can be distributed among robots. This distinction changes the available concurrency, but the resulting completion time also depends on route construction, non-drawing transit, and local robot interactions.

We evaluate 385 user-generated drawings with one, two, three, four, six, and eight robots in a shared simulator. We report completion time, speedup relative to each pipeline’s own single-robot baseline, and robot-time composition. The shared-token pipeline exhibits larger mean speedups and lower idle-time shares at larger team sizes, but is not faster for every drawing. Comparisons across structural attribute groups describe variation in scaling differences. Because routing procedures also differ, the study characterizes complete allocation-routing pipelines rather than isolating the causal effect of allocation granularity. Our focus is to characterize how the relative performance of two implemented allocation-routing pipelines varies across such inputs, rather than to introduce a new printing platform or claim that decomposition alone determines performance.

The key contributions of this work are as follows:

An empirical scaling comparison of component-level and shared-token allocation-routing pipelines across 385 stroke graphs and six robot-team sizes.

A paired completion-time analysis and robot-time accounting that characterize performance differences across the two pipelines.

A descriptive analysis of associations between six structural descriptors and differences in the pipelines’ speedup relative to their respective single-robot baselines.

1. An empirical scaling comparison of component-level and shared-token allocation-routing pipelines across 385 stroke graphs and six robot-team sizes.

2. A paired completion-time analysis and robot-time accounting that characterize performance differences across the two pipelines.

3. A descriptive analysis of associations between six structural descriptors and differences in the pipelines’ speedup relative to their respective single-robot baselines.

title: FCTS: Failure-Guided Curriculum Tree Search Over Generated Terrain for Legged Parkour
authors: Narayanan Palghat Parameswaran(1),Dong-Ki Kim(2),Jay Patrikar(2),Santiago Gutierrez(2),Harshad Zade(2),Shayegan Omidshafiei(2),Harmish Khambhaita(2) ((1) Carnegie Mellon University, (2) FieldAI)
comment: . Under review. Project page with videos:this https URL
abstract:
Quadruped parkour policies handle canonical obstacles well, but their training curricula often miss the irregular, compound geometry of industrial and disaster-response sites, where agile locomotion matters most. Such environments pose a hard generalization problem: even training directly on reconstructed geometry from the target site does not reliably yield policies that traverse it.
Hand-designed curricula span only a few terrain families, and recent LLM-generated curricula offer little control over which policy weaknesses they target.
We propose FCTS, a failure-conditioned terrain curriculum framework that uses localized traversal failures to automatically generate the terrains a policy should train on next. Each failure’s location, termination mode, robot state, and surrounding terrain geometry condition this generation, and Monte Carlo Tree Search explores alternative curriculum trajectories under a fixed training budget.
On terrains built from scanned real-world construction sites, FCTS raises success rate from 28.4% to 85.8% on a medium-difficulty course and from 14.9% to 44.7% on a hard course relative to the strongest parkour or LLM-curriculum baselines, and maintains higher progress on extreme terrains where full traversal is rare.
Hardware experiments on a quadruped robot confirm that the learned FCTS policies transfer to the real world. Please see our Project Page for additional videos.
introduction:
Learning-based quadruped locomotion has enabled robots to traverse gaps, stairs, hurdles, and elevated platforms with remarkable agility [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].
However, these capabilities are typically learned from a pre-defined training distribution of terrain with carefully controlled obstacle variations.
Such policies often break down on real-world environments like those in Figure 1.
Irregular surfaces, discontinuities, and narrow supports are each familiar in isolation, but they co-occur in arrangements that fall outside this distribution.
The training distribution, not the policy, is the binding constraint.

Traditional legged-robot training relies on manually designed terrain families
that define the obstacle structures encountered during learning.
Methods such as Extreme Parkour (EP) [4],
Robot Parkour Learning [2], and
ANYmal Parkour [3] construct such terrain families and use a
difficulty scheduler to increase terrain difficulty as the policy improves.
However, the underlying terrain families themselves remain fixed throughout
training. Extending this terrain library by hand is difficult, time-consuming, and can be sub-optimal. This motivates generating new training terrains
automatically from the policy’s observed failures.

Recent work has begun to use Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate the design of
executable components for reinforcement learning. Eureka [6]
demonstrated that an LLM can generate and iteratively improve reward code, often
outperforming expert-designed rewards across a broad set of tasks.
Building on this idea, Eurekaverse [7] applies LLM-based
generation directly to legged-robot training terrains and synthesizes executable
terrain programs and revises them based on policy performance.

What signal drives generation?
Eurekaverse evaluates the policies trained on its generated
terrains and uses the best-performing policy and its associated terrain set to
guide the next round of generation. The feedback is therefore an aggregate
performance signal: it indicates how the policy performed on average on the generated terrain set,
but not where traversal failed or which local geometry caused the failure.
Without this localized information, subsequent terrain generation follows the LLM’s prior over
plausible terrain rather than the policy’s weaknesses. What is missing is feedback that identifies where the
policy fails and why.

Our key insight is that a failed traversal provides a rich diagnostic signal: it localizes where the policy’s competence breaks down and characterizes the conditions at that point using cues such as failure coordinates, robot state at termination, local terrain geometry, and visual context.
These specify what terrain to train on next, so that each expansion measures that boundary and moves it toward the target domain.

We formulate curriculum discovery in a principled way by building on the
Monte Carlo Tree Search framework [8]: checkpoints form nodes,
while edges correspond to RL training runs on LLM-generated terrains conditioned
on failure feedback of the parent checkpoint.
Each node in the search tree rehearses terrain from its own ancestor nodes in the branch to limit forgetting.
Under a fixed wall-clock budget, the search returns a portfolio of policy
checkpoints.

We refer to this method as FCTS, for Failure-Guided Curriculum Tree Search.
Our contributions are:

Failure-Conditioned Terrain Curriculum Generation.
We close the generation loop on observed failures rather than on an aggregate
score, conditioning each new terrain on the failure location, termination
condition, robot state, and surrounding geometry.

An MCTS Formulation of Automated Terrain Curriculum Generation.
We cast curriculum discovery as a tree search over policy checkpoints and
terrain-conditioned training runs, with branch-history rehearsal and anytime
search under a fixed wall-clock budget.

Evaluation on Reconstructed Real-World Sites.
We evaluate on held-out courses constructed from scanned industrial and
disaster-response geometry, and demonstrate transfer to a physical quadruped.

1. Failure-Conditioned Terrain Curriculum Generation.
We close the generation loop on observed failures rather than on an aggregate
score, conditioning each new terrain on the failure location, termination
condition, robot state, and surrounding geometry.

2. An MCTS Formulation of Automated Terrain Curriculum Generation.
We cast curriculum discovery as a tree search over policy checkpoints and
terrain-conditioned training runs, with branch-history rehearsal and anytime
search under a fixed wall-clock budget.

3. Evaluation on Reconstructed Real-World Sites.
We evaluate on held-out courses constructed from scanned industrial and
disaster-response geometry, and demonstrate transfer to a physical quadruped.

title: Embodiment-Classifier Guidance: Transferring Frozen VLAs Across Robot Dynamics without Demonstrations
authors: Devin Han,Hershraj Niranjani
abstract:
Flow-based policies such as π0\pi_{0} are trained on a fixed set of embodiments, and transferring them to new ones is an open problem.
To adapt a frozen π0\pi_{0} to a new embodiment without additional demonstrations or parameter updates, we train a lightweight embodiment classifier to distinguish successful action chunks on the source body from those on the target body, using a few calibration tasks.
On transfer tasks that π0\pi_{0} saw on its source body but the classifier was never trained on, we nudge each denoising step of π0\pi_{0} with the classifier’s gradient, which estimates the direction from the distribution of successful actions on the source body toward that on the target body.
On the LIBERO simulation benchmark with four modified controllers, embodiment-classifier guidance raises π0\pi_{0}’s average success on the target bodies from 72% to 80% across 12 suite–controller pairs, with a 31% relative reduction in failures (11 of 12 gain; 5 significant after Holm correction).
In simulation, guidance is data-efficient, needing few target-body rollouts per task, which makes it promising for sim-to-real transfer, where rollouts are costly.
Guidance is mixed on weak wrists and harmful on a locked wrist, when the classifier lacks data or favors infeasible motions.
Collecting more target-body data with guided π0\pi_{0} can fill such gaps: on one weak-wrist arm, guided π0\pi_{0} solved a task on which unguided π0\pi_{0} had zero successes in the original data, and retraining the classifier on the guided successes raised success from 52.5% to 70.7%.
introduction:
Flow-based VLA policies such as π0\pi_{0} [2] are trained on a fixed set of robot bodies (an arm together with its low-level controller), and deploying them on new ones remains an open challenge.
On a body with different dynamics (a softer controller, command latency, a weaker wrist motor, another arm), the same policy can fail even when the scene and the task are unchanged (Fig. 1).
Such gaps separate simulation from the lab and the lab from the field; closing them usually takes target-body demonstrations and fine-tuning [11] or a per-task steering policy learned from reward [24].

Background. π0\pi_{0} maps an observation (camera images, robot state and a language instruction) to an action chunk: the next 50 actions of 7 numbers each, which together form a single point in a 350-dimensional space.
Like an image diffusion model, it generates this point by sampling: starting from Gaussian noise, a learned velocity field moves it toward a plausible chunk over 10 denoising steps (Fig. 1, middle).
The robot executes only the first 5 actions of each chunk, discards the rest, and samples a new chunk from the next observation.

Approach. We instead change only how a frozen flow policy samples.
π0\pi_{0} has no input that says which body it controls, so it samples chunks that suit its source body.
We train a small embodiment classifier to tell π0\pi_{0}’s successful action chunks on the source body from those on the target body, and add its gradient to π0\pi_{0}’s velocity at every denoising step.
Intuitively, the classifier scores how much a noisy chunk looks like a target-body success, so its gradient points toward chunks that work on the target body, while π0\pi_{0}’s velocity field still provides the task-level plan, such as which object to reach and where to place it.
As we derive in Eq. (2), with an exact classifier this gradient, suitably scaled, is exactly the velocity difference between the two bodies’ distributions of successful chunks; under the assumptions in App. B, guided sampling would then draw from the target body’s successes, and we hypothesize that these assumptions hold approximately in practice.

Relation to prior work. Similar classifier guidance has been used to refine image diffusion models [14] and to adapt pretrained diffusion models to data-scarce target domains [21]; we apply it to robot embodiment transfer, with the body as the classifier’s label. Unlike embodiment-aware guidance from a known controller’s tracking cost [9], our guidance is learned from successful rollouts.
Because the classifier sees no images, instruction or task label, only noisy action chunks (which implicitly carry the end-effector pose; Sec. 2), guidance with a classifier trained on a few calibration tasks can improve π0\pi_{0}’s target-body success on other transfer tasks, which the classifier was never trained on. π0\pi_{0} itself was trained on these tasks with its source body, so our tests measure transfer across robot dynamics, not generalization to new tasks.

LIBERO [18] is a simulated benchmark of tabletop manipulation tasks in four suites. Our contributions, evaluated on it with one π0\pi_{0} checkpoint and paired, pre-registered tests, are:

Embodiment-classifier guidance: a way to steer a frozen flow VLA to a new body with a classifier learned from successful rollouts, with no demonstrations or fine-tuning (Sec. 2).

Guidance improves frozen π0\pi_{0} on most controller changes: with four modified controllers, it raises average success from 72% to 80% over 12 suite–body pairs, with a 31% relative reduction in failures (gains in 11 of 12; Sec. 4.1).

Embodiment-classifier guidance is data-efficient in simulation: the classifier trains on the successful episodes among about 23 target-body rollouts per calibration task on LIBERO-Object (pick-and-place), with no demonstrations, reward model or updates to π0\pi_{0}. In a preliminary check on one body, an untuned LoRA fine-tune with the same collection budget lowered success (Sec. 4.3).

It is not a universal fix: it is mixed on weak-wrist arms and hurts where the body cannot execute π0\pi_{0}’s plans (Sec. 4.2).

Guided rollouts fill data gaps: collecting more target-body data with guided π0\pi_{0} finds successes on a task where unguided π0\pi_{0} had none, and retraining the classifier on the guided successes lifts a weak-wrist KUKA arm from 52.5% to 70.7%, while the same amount of extra data from unguided π0\pi_{0} reaches only 57.8% (Sec. 4.3).

1. Embodiment-classifier guidance: a way to steer a frozen flow VLA to a new body with a classifier learned from successful rollouts, with no demonstrations or fine-tuning (Sec. 2).

2. Guidance improves frozen π0\pi_{0} on most controller changes: with four modified controllers, it raises average success from 72% to 80% over 12 suite–body pairs, with a 31% relative reduction in failures (gains in 11 of 12; Sec. 4.1).

3. In a preliminary check on one body, an untuned LoRA fine-tune with the same collection budget lowered success (Sec. 4.3).

4. It is not a universal fix: it is mixed on weak-wrist arms and hurts where the body cannot execute π0\pi_{0}’s plans (Sec. 4.2).

5. title: Micro-Localization: High-Precision Mobile Robot Localization Using Microscopic Ground Texture
authors: Aaron Wilhelm,Marina de Albuquerque Marcon,Emith Uyanwatte,Nils Napp
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
We demonstrate high-precision global localization using natural ground texture viewed through microscope optics, achieving localization in the tens-of-micrometers regime.
For the planar ground texture localization problem considered here, we relate optical magnification and image-space localization uncertainty to physical localization precision.
Leveraging this relationship, we then develop a microscope-based localization system that addresses the calibration, camera-modeling, and focus challenges introduced by high-magnification imaging.
We evaluate this system across several surface textures using a calibrated precision gantry.
Across 1,007 held-out queries per surface, the system localizes every query and achieves translation RMSEs of 28–73 μ\mum.
Independent photometric registration agrees with the feature-based localization estimates to within approximately 9 μ\mum RMSE.
We further demonstrate localization on a low-cost mobile robot using the gantry-collected maps, and also show that the system can resolve micrometer-scale
displacement caused by thermal expansion.
These results show that microscopic natural surface texture can bring mobile localization into a precision regime typically associated with fixed positioning systems.
introduction:
Mobile robots offer a compelling way to bring inspection, manipulation, and fabrication capabilities to large or reconfigurable workspaces.
However, many of these tasks require positioning accuracy far finer than that needed for navigation.
Precision manufacturing systems such as CNC machines can achieve micrometer-scale positioning, but their rigid mechanical structure confines them to a fixed work envelope.
In many mobile applications, such precision may only be needed near the task, motivating localization methods that provide high accuracy locally while preserving the flexibility of a mobile platform.

Ground texture localization provides a promising basis for this capability.
Rather than relying on sparse landmarks or installed fiducials, these methods use the natural surface texture beneath a robot as a global reference.
Because the surface is viewed at close range, a given planar displacement produces a larger displacement of the texture in the native sensor image than it would under a more distant viewing geometry, helping enable high physical localization precision.
We refer to this relationship between physical displacement and the resulting image displacement as the geometric sensitivity of the imaging system.
Building on this principle, we use microscope optics to substantially increase optical magnification to target globally referenced localization in the tens-of-micrometers regime.

High optical magnification provides a second benefit beyond increased geometric sensitivity: it can reveal natural surface structure that is not readily visible or distinctive at conventional imaging scales.
Surfaces that appear weakly textured at the macro scale can expose rich microstructure, while surfaces with visible macroscopic patterns can reveal additional fine-scale structure under microscopic observation.
Figure 2 illustrates this change in appearance for the surfaces considered in this work.
We use this naturally occurring microtexture as a visual reference for localization without modifying the surface with artificial landmarks.

Using this sensing configuration, we show that natural microscopic surface texture supports globally referenced planar localization in the tens-of-micrometers regime across multiple surfaces.
At this scale, localization errors are a fraction of the diameter of a human hair.
This precision is achieved with a localization pipeline built on an established ground texture localization method, without requiring a localization algorithm specialized for micrometer-scale operation.

We envision this level of precision for localized high-precision work regions, where such accuracy is needed near the task rather than throughout the broader environment.
The system is therefore not intended to replace general-purpose navigation across an entire factory or building.

The primary contributions of this work are:

A geometric formulation relating optical magnification, image-space localization uncertainty, and physical localization precision, motivating the use of microscopic surface texture for high-precision localization

A microscope-based ground texture localization system that addresses the calibration, camera-modeling, and focus challenges introduced by high-magnification optics

A demonstration of tens-of-micrometers global localization on a low-cost mobile robot using a surface map collected independently with a precision gantry

We validate these contributions across three distinct surface types using a calibrated gantry reference system and further demonstrate our system’s ability to measure micrometer-scale displacement by observing the thermal expansion of an aluminum beam.
We will release the resulting high-resolution microscopic ground texture datasets and accompanying code.

1. A geometric formulation relating optical magnification, image-space localization uncertainty, and physical localization precision, motivating the use of microscopic surface texture for high-precision localization

2. A microscope-based ground texture localization system that addresses the calibration, camera-modeling, and focus challenges introduced by high-magnification optics

3. A demonstration of tens-of-micrometers global localization on a low-cost mobile robot using a surface map collected independently with a precision gantry

title: When Plans Change, Remember: Replanning-Guided Visual Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Victoria Smelova,Daniil Kazachkov,Georgiy Kazantsev,Iuliia Tsvetkova,Egor Cherepanov,Nikita Kachaev,Artem Latyshev,Aleksandr I. Panov,Alexey K. Kovalev
abstract:
Long-horizon, multi-stage Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies often require
visual information that is no longer present in the current observation.
Retaining the complete observation history is computationally expensive and
highly redundant, motivating selective visual memory. We introduce
RePlanMem-VLA (Replanning-Guided Keyframe Memory for VLA), which turns a policy’s own plan revisions into an online memory-write signal. Under receding-horizon execution, consecutive action chunks predict some of the same future actions. RePlanMem-VLA treats unusually large disagreement between these temporally aligned predictions as evidence of a task-relevant event. We first compare 35 disagreement measures across single-task autoregressive decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformers trained from scratch, then validate the selected signals on pretrained OpenVLA-OFT and π0.5\pi_{0.5} policies over MIKASA-Robo-VLA tasks. The resulting detectors achieve ROC-AUC of
0.981–0.997. We then use the selected signals in RePlanMem-VLA to trigger updates to a bounded visual memory, with a robot-masked write filter suppressing redundant frames. In the evaluated memory-retention experiments, RePlanMem-VLA preserves task-relevant observations until the later decision point in 100%100\% of episodes. Real-robot replay data further show that event selection and redundancy suppression extend beyond simulation. These results establish plan revision as a policy-internal signal for controlling what a VLA remembers.
Website: https://vika787.github.io/RePlanMem/.
introduction:
Long-horizon manipulation often requires Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies to use visual information
that has left the current observation, including object properties (Chen et al., 2026a; Shi et al., 2026),
earlier environment states (Chen et al., 2026a; Shi et al., 2026), and task
progress (Buamanee et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2026).
Retaining the full history preserves these cues but increases context length and
computation while adding visual redundancy (Jang et al., 2025; Qiu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026).
We therefore seek a small set of informative observations.

We call these observations keyframes: they preserve cues needed
later (Shi et al., 2026; Lei et al., 2026) or mark task-phase
transitions (Buamanee et al., 2026; Yi et al., 2026). Prior work
selects them with vision-language models (Lei et al., 2026), waypoint
heuristics (Shi et al., 2023),
learned retrieval (Sridhar et al., 2026), progress estimates (Liu et al., 2026),
or event detectors (Zeng et al., 2026b). We investigate whether the policy’s own plan revisions can provide an online signal for selecting these observations.

Under receding-horizon execution, consecutive action chunks predict some of the same future actions, while the new plan incorporates
the latest observation (Fig. 1). Comparing these temporally aligned predictions reveals how the policy revises its intended behavior after receiving new visual information.
Our central hypothesis is that task-relevant observations induce unusually large revisions in predictions for the same future
actions. This motivates using plan disagreement as a policy-internal signal to identify candidate keyframes for visual memory.

We introduce RePlanMem-VLA
(Replanning-Guided Keyframe Memory for VLA), which derives its selection
signal from revisions between overlapping action predictions already produced
during normal replanning. Selected keyframes become part of the policy’s visual context,
keeping past observations available for subsequent action prediction, while a robot-masked write filter suppresses redundant frames, reducing repeated overwrites. At deployment, the trigger requires neither keyframe annotations nor privileged simulator state.

Our experiments are conducted on MIKASA-Robo-VLA (Cherepanov et al., 2026b), an extension of MIKASA-Robo (Cherepanov et al., 2026a)
for evaluating memory-intensive manipulation with VLA policies. We first screen 35 disagreement metrics using autoregressive decoder-only and
Flow-Matching Transformers (Lipman et al., 2023)
trained from scratch. We then evaluate detectors based on the selected signals with
pretrained OpenVLA-OFT (Kim et al., 2025) and
π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) policies, obtaining ROC-AUC of
0.981–0.997.
In the evaluated memory-retention experiments, RePlanMem-VLA
preserves task-relevant observations until the later decision
point in 100%100\% of episodes, while robot-masked filtering
reduces redundant overwrites.
Real-robot replay data further support its event-selection and
redundancy-suppression behavior beyond simulation
(Fig. 2).

Our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce RePlanMem-VLA, which identifies keyframes from
policy-internal revisions of predictions for the same future actions across
consecutive replanning steps (Section 3.3).

We introduce RePlanMem-VLA, which identifies keyframes from
policy-internal revisions of predictions for the same future actions across
consecutive replanning steps (Section 3.3).

We identify disagreement measures that best align with keyframe events through systematic analysis across decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformer policies, and verify their transfer to pretrained OpenVLA-OFT and π0.5\pi_{0.5} policies
(Sections 4.1 and 4.2).

We develop a bounded visual-memory mechanism where plan disagreement determines when to write and redundancy-aware filtering, including robot-masked clustering, determines what to retain, substantially reducing redundant updates while preserving task-relevant observations (Sections 3 and 4.3).

title: RTISSLAM-3D: Full 6-DoF SLAM With an In-Air 3D Imaging Sonar
authors: Jan Steckel,Vincent Katter,Wouter Jansen
abstract: Echolocating bats navigate dense forests using sonar alone, and in-air 3D imaging sonars now capture the entire frontal hemisphere with every pulse. Sonar SLAM, however, has so far been planar: current systems estimate a 2D trajectory and discard the elevation information in the sonar images, an assumption that does not hold on rough and sloped terrain such as a forest floor. In this paper, we introduce RTISSLAM-3D, a novel 6-DoF SLAM system for a wheeled robot that carries an in-air 3D imaging sonar, an IMU and wheel encoders. A CFAR detector on the sphere reduces every sonar image to a sparse set of 3D detections, which we use for a 3D acoustic odometry that models the shape of the sonar beam, for place recognition with polar submap descriptors, and for the verification of loop closures by 3D registration, all combined in a 6-DoF pose graph with attitude factors. We evaluated RTISSLAM-3D on a 545 m545\text{\,}\mathrm{m} drive through a forest, with a 3D lidar SLAM as reference. The loop closures reduced the horizontal error of the acoustic odometry from 1.74 m1.74\text{\,}\mathrm{m} to 0.28 m0.28\text{\,}\mathrm{m}, with a height error of 0.12 m0.12\text{\,}\mathrm{m}, and 94.6 %94.6\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the resulting 3D sonar map lies within 0.3 m0.3\text{\,}\mathrm{m} of the lidar map.
introduction:
Sonar was one of the first sensors with which mobile robots built maps [1, 2, 3], and in-air sonar keeps working in exactly those conditions in which cameras and lidar struggle: in darkness, smoke, dust and fog, and next to glass [4, 5, 6]. Indeed, ultrasonic sensors are cheap, small and robust, and the embedded 3D imaging sonars of the last decade, such as the eRTIS [5, 6], turn the echoes of a single broadband pulse into an image of the reflected energy as a function of range and direction over the complete frontal hemisphere, the so-called energyscape [4]. With nonlinear beamformers such as Delay-Multiply-And-Sum (DMAS) with a coherence factor [7], these images have become sharp enough to be used for more than obstacle avoidance and reactive control [8, 9].

In two recent papers, we have shown how such sonar data can drive a modern, robust SLAM back-end. BatSLAM 2.0 [10] combined sequence-verified place recognition on the echoes of a binaural bat-like sonar with a factor-graph back-end [11, 12], and produced reliable topological maps in strongly aliased environments. RTISSLAM [13] replaced the binaural sensor by an eRTIS imaging sonar and used its energyscapes as place descriptors. Furthermore, the system extracts acoustic odometry from the sequence of the data, and anchored an occupancy grid to the nodes of the pose graph, so that a metric map is constructed, updated by every loop closure. Both systems, however, are operating in a strict 2D assumption: they estimate the position and heading of the robot on a plane, and they use the 3D imaging capability of the sensor only to build a 2D map, by suppressing the elevation dimension of the energyscape (looking at a horizontal slice). This is a reasonable choice in an office or a warehouse with flat floors, but it throws away a significant portion of what the sensor measures. Furthermore, this approach breaks down as soon as the robot leaves the flat floor, as is common in offroad scenarios, and for UAV navigation.

Outdoors, and in particular in a forest, the ground is neither flat nor level, and the robot rolls and pitches as it drives over roots and stones. The relevant structure (tree trunks, shrubs, fallen branches) is best represented in 3D, and a planar slice through it at the height of the sensor depends on the attitude of the robot. Furthermore, a forest is a notoriously difficult environment for place recognition as it can be strongly self-similar. In our own first experiments with the 2D RTISSLAM on real forest data, the recall of single-view place recognition at a useful precision was close to zero, and loop closures could only be found by restricting the search to the vicinity of the current pose estimate.

In lidar SLAM, the step from 2D to 3D has long been made: 3D point clouds are registered with point-to-point or point-to-distribution ICP variants [14, 15, 16], places are recognized with egocentric polar descriptors of the 3D structure [17], and maps are stored as 3D occupancy grids [18]. Underwater, multibeam and imaging sonars have been used to build volumetric submaps [19]. For in-air sonar, however, a full 3D SLAM system, estimating the 6-DoF trajectory of the robot and a 3D map from the sonar, has, to the best of our knowledge, not been demonstrated on a real robot. The data of an in-air imaging sonar is quite different from a lidar scan: a capture yields at most a few dozen detections within a range of a few meters, the angular resolution is a few degrees, often with anisotropy in azimuth and elevation, specular surfaces are only seen near normal incidence, and the ground returns both a direct echo and a mirror image through ground multipath. A sonar SLAM system needs to take all of these peculiarities into account when trying to succesfully build a spatial map.

In this paper, we propose RTISSLAM-3D, a novel full 6-DoF SLAM system for an in-air 3D imaging sonar on a wheeled robot, which uses the sonar’s 3D images for every part of the localization: for odometry, for place recognition and for the metric verification of loop closures. Only an IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) and the wheel encoders complement the sonar, and no learned components are used in the whole pipeline. In our approach, every capture is imaged over the full frontal hemisphere and turned into a sparse set of 3D detections by a CFAR detector that operates on the sphere, efficiently implemented through the heat kernel of a graph Laplacian, which is in effect a Gaussian blur over a set of irregular directions on a sphere. The ground echoes give the height and tilt of the sensor above the local ground and reveal the multipath mirror images, which are removed. A 3D acoustic odometry registers every detection set to a local 3D submap, with the beam-shaped uncertainty of each detection, and takes the rotation from the gyroscope. Keyframes enter a 6-DoF pose graph with IMU attitude factors, loop closures are proposed by a polar descriptor of the 3D submap and verified by a 4-DoF registration of the two submaps, and a 3D log-odds occupancy map is built on the optimized poses.

We evaluate RTISSLAM-3D on a 545 m545\text{\,}\mathrm{m} drive through a forest in Trondheim, Norway, with a gravity-aligned 3D lidar SLAM as reference, and we show that it reduces the horizontal trajectory error of the wheel and gyroscope odometry from 2.40 m2.40\text{\,}\mathrm{m} to 0.28 m0.28\text{\,}\mathrm{m}, with a height error of 0.12 m0.12\text{\,}\mathrm{m}, closes 233 loops of which none is off by more than 0.5 m0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{m}, and builds a 3D map in which 94.6 %94.6\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the occupied voxels lie within 0.3 m0.3\text{\,}\mathrm{m} of the lidar ground-truth map.

The contributions of this paper are as follows: (1) a 3D imaging and detection chain for in-air sonar over the full frontal hemisphere, with a CFAR detector on the sphere and the removal of ground multipath through a fitted ground plane, (2) a 3D acoustic odometry that registers sparse sonar detections with their beam-shaped uncertainty, (3) 3D place recognition for sonar, with candidates proposed by a polar submap descriptor and verified by submap registration, (4) the complete 6-DoF SLAM system and a 3D occupancy map with beam-shaped evidence and free-space carving, and (5) an evaluation on real data against a gravity-aligned 3D lidar reference, with ablations of every component. The complete pipeline, from the raw recording to the map and the videos, runs with a single command and will be made available as open source.

The rest of the paper is structured as follows. First, we give an overview of RTISSLAM-3D in section II. Next, we detail the imaging and detection chain, the acoustic odometry, the place recognition, the pose graph and the mapping in section III. Section IV describes the robot, the recording and the reference, after which section V presents the results. We discuss the limitations of our work in section VI and conclude the paper in section VII.

authors: Runhan Huang,Xiangcheng Zhang,Haoyu Chen,Yitong Li,Yen-Jen Wang,Bohan Lyu,Haotian Ye,Chuye Hong,Yixuan Wang,Chloe Su,Haoyu Xiong,Yangzhen Wu,Enze Xie,Travis Manderson,Stefano Ermon,Pieter Abbeel,Antonio Torralba,Dawn Song,Weirui Ye,Yilun Du

abstract: Robot learning has advanced significantly by scaling demonstration datasets and model capacity; however, deploying a new robot embodiment or task typically necessitates a dedicated teleoperation corpus. Furthermore, resulting policies remain bounded by their imitation distributions, limiting generalization and continual self-improvement. We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), an open-source framework for robot agents centered on scaling exploration: enabling agents to improve by acquiring online experience and synthesizing executable programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent generates robot control code directly, operating without action demonstration data, hand-engineered action primitives, or value-function guidance. Through online exploration, the agent identifies decision sequences that achieve task goals and compiles them into modular programs encapsulating the full perception-planning-control loop for fast inference. Using RAX, we present a systematic multi-embodiment study on scaling online exploration across fine-grained precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks using single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid systems in simulation and on real robots. Generalization performance on unseen environments improves consistently as exploration scales. In simulation, RAX outperforms top baseline models by +37.4%+37.4\% on average. On real robots, RAX autonomously learns memory-dependent, articulated, high-precision, deformable, and long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks without human demonstrations, continually improving performance by composing verified skills from prior exploration sessions. As exploration scales, we observe emergent system capabilities including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and human-robot agent collaboration. We open-source RAX as a generalist robot-agent platform that allows new robot embodiments to be integrated solely via API interfaces, bypassing teleoperated data collection and policy training entirely. More details are available on our project page at robot-agent-exploration.com.
introduction:
“We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what
we have discovered. Building in our discoveries only makes it harder to see how the
discovering process can be done.”

“We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what
we have discovered. Building in our discoveries only makes it harder to see how the
discovering process can be done.”

— Richard S. Sutton, The Bitter Lesson (2019)

Robot learning has made substantial progress by scaling demonstration data and model capacity with imitation learning, aiming to replicate the training recipe that transformed language modeling (Kaplan et al., 2020). Vision-language-action (VLA) models and World-Action models (WAMs) fine-tune pretrained VLMs and video generation models, respectively, using large teleoperation corpora (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024). However, deploying a new robot or task still requires a dedicated teleoperation corpus of its own (O’Neill et al., 2024; Team et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026e; Yuan et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Bi et al., 2026). Furthermore, the knowledge of such policy models is inherently bounded by the demonstrations they imitate. Consider a mobile robot tasked with loading a car in an unfamiliar house: while opening doors, grasping bags, and placing objects may each be familiar skills, the robot must adapt to novel scenes, visual appearances, and task compositions while discovering new approaches. This adaptation and discovery process is absent during imitation learning on static teleoperation data. Consequently, these policies struggle to generalize and self-improve, even when provided with environment interactions and test-time compute. This limitation motivates a central question: can robots self-improve and learn to discover new skills through autonomous online experience and active exploration?

Humans learn physical skills by attempting a task, observing the outcome, diagnosing failures, and practicing until their behavior becomes reliable. LLM agents exhibit a similar pattern in software domains: they explore unfamiliar systems by executing programs, inspecting outputs, and revising their work (Yang et al., 2024). Instead of training policies exclusively on teleoperated demonstration data, we let agents program robots directly (Lozano-Perez, 1983) without hand-designed action primitives. The agent explores online to discover decisions that drive task success, then automates these decision-making principles into modular robot programs that integrate perception, planning, and control. It continuously debugs and tests these programs through online execution. These programs encode the agent’s underlying principles for how to generate successful actions based on environment perception, rather than merely mimicking the actions themselves, thereby enabling more robust generalization. Furthermore, the agent can compose, modify, and update these programs when confronting increasingly complex scenes and tasks, continually improving through online experience.

We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), a cognitive architecture for robot agents. Its core organizing principle is scaling exploration: robot agents should improve by gathering their own online experience and optimizing their programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent receives a natural-language instruction, at most a few goal images or visual demonstrations, and a budget of exploration episodes. It interacts directly through the robot’s perception and control interfaces without requiring human teleoperation or value function guidance. The underlying language model parameters remain fixed and no policies are trained; instead, learning updates a persistent workspace of programs, notes, and verified skills. The agent converts successful interactions into autonomous code programs and stores reusable knowledge for subsequent episodes and tasks.

As exploration scales, we observe several emergent system capabilities: the agent constructs task-relevant 3D perception models, plans actions via pose search in 3D joint space, generates fully automated programs with closed-loop visual and force feedback, and adapts its programs when encountering novel task conditions. Furthermore, we observe agentic behaviors on real robots, including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and active human-robot interaction. For example, the robot executes end-effector contact probing for precise localization when depth measurements are inaccurate. In mobile manipulation experiments, following an initial collision with a cabinet, the agent automatically instantiates a safety check to verify workspace clearance before every base rotation. To test code robustness, the agent actively requests the human operator to vary object layouts, systematically testing the spatial generalization of the autonomous program.

In RAX, we equip the agent with rich multimodal sensing by exposing metric depth and force signals through the robot interface. A unified architecture supports tabletop bimanual arms, dexterous hands, mobile household robots, and humanoids through interfaces to each robot’s sensors, controllers, and kinematic models (Section 4). Unlike standard VLAs or WAMs operating on RGB images alone, the agent autonomously leverages these rich sensing signals to construct 3D point clouds and fit object models directly from perception. It then searches for actions to manipulate these 3D models while accounting for their unique shapes and affordances. Force feedback further enables the agent to resolve spatial uncertainty through contact and enable close-loop control on force signals in insertion tasks. Such multimodal world modeling have been largely absent from generalist policy models, yet naturally align with human cognitive processes.

To enable high-frequency closed-loop control, the agent compiles its decision-making process into executable Python programs that generate actions directly from sensor signals. Unlike prior approaches that rely on human-designed action primitives or policies trained on demonstrations (Lu et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026), our approach directly generates robot control programs that encapsulate the full perception-planning-control loop, whereas standard policies discard the underlying decision-making process essential for generalization. In practice, we observe the agent writing programs that automatically segment and identify objects in 3D using point-cloud fitting and hue-based identification, then plan actions grounded in this 3D world model, with retry loops and exception handling naturally incorporated into the code. Because actions are planned directly on perceived 3D objects rather than learned through imitation, this approach generalizes to far more diverse object layouts and domain variations than standard VLAs or WAMs. For semantically rich perception in open-world environments, the agent can program direct API calls to LLMs (such as Gemini) within the code to assist with object identification, while incorporating checkpoints and exception handling to step in and verify progress. Over the course of exploration, both action inference latency and token counts decrease as an increasing fraction of decisions becomes automated through code.

As experience scales with exploration, RAX maintains an intra-task memory file system across episodes to record failure lessons and successful strategies, allowing the agent to continually refine its programs. Across multiple tasks and sessions, we maintain a repository of modular programs as verified skills for various tasks and manipulation primitives. Each skill includes the executable code for a specific task, accompanied by execution logs from successful runs, clear preconditions, and verification checkpoints, allowing skills to be composed and reused for complex downstream tasks. In real-world mobile manipulation experiments in household settings, the agent practices individual tasks, each in its own exploration session, such as picking and placing boxes or tucking in office chairs, and commits them as verified skills. When subsequently evaluated on a composite, long-horizon task involving more than six sequential object manipulations, the agent achieves substantial automation and efficiency gains by reusing these stored skills. We envision agents practicing skills in a distributed, parallel fashion to build a rich repository of diverse capabilities, thereby enabling continual lifelong learning.

Using RAX, we conduct the first large-scale, multi-embodiment, systematic study of
scaling exploration for robot agents, spanning fine-grained precision and long-horizon tasks
across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, RoboDojo, DexJoCo, BEHAVIOR-1K, and HumanoidArena in simulation and
on two real robots. We evaluate the resulting policies on unseen scenes, separating
exploration from evaluation. Performance grows steadily with exploration, and on
fine-grained and long-horizon tasks on which state-of-the-art methods rarely succeed, RAX achieves high success rates, surpassing the strongest prior models by +37.4 on average over
five benchmarks (1, Section 13). Without any expert action trajectories, RAX sets a new
state of the art on RoboDojo (+53.4), BEHAVIOR-1K (+38.3), DexJoCo (+31.4), and
LIBERO-Pro (+21.2). On HumanoidArena, it sets a new state of the art (+7.9) with three
teleoperated demonstrations per task, where every baseline uses 100. On real Franka and Rainbow RB-Y1
robots, RAX masters five complex tabletop manipulation tasks and a long-horizon mobile
manipulation task with zero demonstrations, and verified skills accumulated across sessions let
later sessions build on earlier ones.

We summarize our contributions below:

We introduce RAX and establish scaling online exploration as a foundational principle for agentic robotics. In RAX, the agent operates directly through perception and robot control interfaces without policy training, compiling successful decision sequences into executable code programs that run autonomous execution loops.

Using RAX, we conduct the first systematic, multi-embodiment study of scaling online exploration across simulation and real robot environments. RAX acquires diverse manipulation capabilities solely through autonomous exploration, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by +37.4+37.4 points on average across five simulation benchmarks, while solving high-precision, deformable, articulated, and long-horizon manipulation tasks on real robots without human demonstrations.

We demonstrate rapid adaptation and continual learning on real robots, showing that generated programs can be selectively updated in response to environmental and task shifts while retaining verified skills in a persistent repository for composition and reuse in complex tasks.

title: Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence?
authors: SenseNova,Joint Research Team:Zhongang Cai,Ziang Cao,Tailai Chen,Han Chong Chua,Linjun Dai,Hanming Deng,Hokin Deng,Haiwen Diao,Chenjing Ding,Weichen Fan,Xiao Fu,Zerui Gong,Chenyang Gu,Zexin He,Zhi Hou,Bo Li,Qinyue Li,Quanzhou Li,Xiaowan Li,Zhichao Liao,Dahua Lin,Zilong Lin,Bo Liu,Chunxiao Liu,Pengfei Liu,Tianqi Liu,Ziwei Liu,Chen Change Loy,Lewei Lu,Jiapeng Luo,Yuexiao Ma,Liang Pan,Xingang Pan,Oscar Qian,Ziyi Shang,Yuyao Shao,Dawei Su,Dacheng Tao,Qingyi Tao,Quan Wang,Ruisi Wang,Xiaogang Wang,Ziyi Wang,Beichen Wen,Donghao Wu,Jiaxu Wu,Silei Wu,Xiaoming Wu,Zhonghua Wu,Hongcan Xiao,Weiye Xu,Atsushi Yamashita,Lei Yang,Zhe Yang,Baiqiao Yin,Wanqi Yin,Hanfei Zhao,Tianbo Zhong,Long Zhuo,Jing Zuo
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Multimedia (cs.MM)

abstract:
GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field.
First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra. We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance (Fig. 1). Our analysis suggests that future research should increasingly focus on improving
1) the generality of in-context learning
2) cost and execution time,
3) physical-state verification,
4) recovery from irreversible failures, and
5) long-horizon preservation of progress.
Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control. Besides exploring the ideal action representation and chucking parameters, we identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller (e.g., π0.5\pi_{0.5}) is costly but effective.
Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment. Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for in-context learning are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints.
Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks. We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs rather than current robot capabilities, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate.
Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence. The key remaining challenge is to translate benchmark success into reliable, efficient, and scalable real-world deployment.
introduction:
The advent of GPT-6-Astra marks a major shift in embodied intelligence: a general-purpose model can now tackle robotic manipulation and navigation tasks that have traditionally been dominated by specialized models, such as VLAs and WAMs, while exhibiting capabilities including zero-shot generalization, in-context learning, and failure recovery.
In this technical report, we use GPT-6-Astra as a lens to examine a broader question: what does this new level of embodied capability mean for the research community, and where should the field go next? We first conduct a large-scale evaluation across diverse embodied tasks to characterize the extent of its capabilities and identify which problems are already approaching saturation. We then study harness design to understand the performance–cost trade-offs involved in translating these capabilities into effective control. Next, we validate our findings on real robots, asking how far benchmark success carries over to physical deployment and what gaps remain.Finally, we revisit benchmark design and envision what the next generation of embodied benchmarks should look like.

First, we probe the upper bound of GPT-6-Astra’s embodied capabilities under a unified protocol. We conduct a large-scale study across 12 representative benchmarks, covering tabletop robotic arms, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under this protocol, GPT-6-Astra outperforms existing methods by substantial margins, including recent agentic approaches that also build on GPT-6-Astra. Notably, as shown in Fig. 1, it approaches saturation on the LIBERO series and SIMPLE, while achieving 81.9% on RoboDojo and 87.3% on DexJoCo. The protocol follows two simple and well-motivated principles:

1) We allow in-context learning (ICL) from the training set whenever successful demonstrations are available, which we consider reasonable since such demonstrations are conventionally accessible when training smaller task-specific policies. GPT-6-Astra studies the available training data and constructs a frozen knowledge package containing task guidance, motion and visual references, executable helpers, recovery procedures, and metadata. At test time, it retrieves and adapts these resources to the current scene. This substantially improves performance when the demonstrations closely cover the test distribution, but the benefit weakens as tasks move away from the data used to build the package.

2) We extensively increase the execution budget, allowing up to 10×\times more interaction steps than the official setting. We find that standard step limits can significantly underestimate GPT-6-Astra’s capabilities. Additional interaction yields large gains on tasks that benefit from repeated correction, such as RoboDojo and Bench2Dex, because GPT-6-Astra can detect failed actions, revise its strategy, and recover through further interaction. This emerging failure-recovery capability is the key mechanism that allows a larger execution budget to translate into higher success rates.

Our strong empirical results put us in a position to identify the remaining limitations of GPT-6-Astra more clearly. Specifically, we find that:
i) in-context learning transfer poorly beyond the tasks from which the demonstrations are drawn;
ii) even simple tasks incur inference cost and execution time far beyond what would be practical for commercial deployment;
iii) GPT-6-Astra often struggles to verify physical success and identify which task condition remains unmet;
iv) GPT-6-Astra often struggles to identify the cause of task failure;
v) it cannot reliably recover from consequential or irreversible failures; and
vi) long-horizon execution remains difficult, as the model struggles to preserve and track progress across many subtasks.

Second, we ablate the harness design and find that effectively unleashing GPT-6-Astra’s embodied performance depends critically on both the collaboration protocol and the action interface. We first study the interaction between “System 2” (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and “System 1” (e.g., π0.5\pi_{0.5} [13]). Closed-loop collaboration, where GPT-6-Astra reviews and refines VLA-proposed actions before execution, substantially improves performance over standalone or open-loop execution, but frequent System-2 supervision incurs significant token cost. Reviewing longer action sequences improves this trade-off, while combining closed-loop collaboration with ICL yields the strongest performance at the highest cost.
We further study action representation and chunking, and identify a representation gap between multimodal reasoning and low-level robot control. Direct joint-angle control underperforms, while more semantically aligned end-effector commands work better; adaptive action chunking further improves performance while reducing unnecessary model calls. Together, these findings suggest that harness design should expose action spaces aligned with the model’s reasoning capabilities while delegating precise execution to lower-level controllers, with adaptive interaction to balance performance and inference cost.

Third, we validate GPT-6-Astra on real-world robots spanning single and dual robotic arms, grippers, dexterous hands, a wheeled mobile manipulator, and a humanoid. Our study reveals three key findings.
1) GPT-6-Astra operates effectively across a wide range of embodiments, but its success rate remains highly task-dependent. It performs particularly well on tasks such as tabletop grasping, while deformable-object manipulation, precise contact, and long-horizon tasks remain challenging.
2) GPT-6-Astra demonstrates surprising active-vision capabilities, intentionally repositioning the camera to obtain observations needed for subsequent actions.
3) GPT-6-Astra shows that a slow “System 2” model can directly collaborate with a high-frequency “System 0” locomotion controller to perform humanoid manipulation that requires high-frequency local control.
At the same time, real-world deployment introduces challenges that are largely absent from simulation.
GPT-6-Astra can no longer easily trade additional execution steps for higher success rates, due to safety constraints, mechanical limits, and real-time requirements.
Moreover, successful trajectory demonstrations, which are central to our ICL setup in simulation, are often expensive or unavailable in real-world applications.

Fourth, we showcase a prototype of what we envision as the next generation of benchmarks for embodied intelligence.
We propose three principles.
1) Tasks should be derived from human needs and expressed as people would naturally state them, with evaluation based on the utility of the outcome rather than a fixed goal state.
2) No in-domain training episodes or scene-specific demonstrations should be provided; instead, agents should acquire experience during deployment.
3) The world should continue to evolve while the agent deliberates, making reasoning time and its physical consequences part of the evaluation.
The prototype makes several remaining limitations more apparent in a deployment-oriented setting:
i) GPT-6-Astra focuses on the current step but can lose track of other changes it has caused in the environment, such as leaving a refrigerator open;
ii) without demonstrations, it struggles to figure out how unfamiliar objects and mechanisms work, or how to position its own body to interact with them; and
iii) because the world continues to change while it reasons, its observations can become outdated before the resulting action is executed.
Building such benchmarks also raises practical challenges in reliable judging, simulation fidelity, real-time evaluation, and evaluation cost.

In summary, by pushing GPT-6-Astra toward its capability limits, dissecting the harness that enables this performance, validating its behavior on real robots, and rethinking how embodied intelligence should be evaluated, we aim to clarify both what has changed and what remains fundamentally unsolved.

title: StopWatch: Goal Grounding for Object-goal Navigation
authors: Xinhao Liu,Yunsheng Tian,Yuheng Qiu,Pieter Abbeel,Xi Chen,Guanya Shi,Chen Feng
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: Project websitethis https URL
abstract: Pretrained VLMs bring rich world knowledge and semantic priors to object-goal navigation, and fine-tuning a VLM into a navigation policy has become a common recipe. Despite this progress, success rates remain low, and it is unclear which capability these fine-tuned policies lack. Our diagnosis identifies goal grounding as the dominant failure. These policies explore well, yet often fail to notice that the goal is already in view or to estimate how far away it is. To address this failure, we ground the goal explicitly. Explicit grounding substantially improves success and reaches state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks across three scene collections. We also correct annotation defects in these benchmarks, so that future methods are evaluated more faithfully. Our analysis on the clean benchmarks shows that, with ground-truth grounding, our policy nearly matches the expert that generated its demonstrations, leaving the headroom in perception rather than policy learning. Our work points to goal grounding as a missing piece of object-goal navigation and offers a simple and effective solution to the task.
introduction:
Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) bring web-scale visual and semantic knowledge to embodied navigation.
In object-goal navigation, where an agent must find an instance of a named object category in a novel scene, fine-tuning them on expert demonstrations has become a common recipe (Zhang et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2025; Chu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). Progress has come from larger demonstration sets (Zhang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b; Chu et al., 2026) and better modeling of the observation history (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b), yet these policies still generalize poorly to unseen goal categories. Further scaling brings diminishing returns (Zhang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026), and some observe that perception and grounding, rather than the navigation policy, limit performance (Xue et al., 2026; Chu et al., 2026). What is missing is a diagnosis of which capability these policies lack. In this paper we give that diagnosis and build an object-goal navigation system around it.

Our diagnosis indicates these policies fail at goal grounding: determining whether the goal is in view and how far it is. These policies learn search well from demonstrations. They actually reach the goal far more often than they succeed (StopWatch: 
Goal Grounding for Object-goal Navigatione). An end-to-end policy can come within 0.25 m of the goal in 76% of episodes yet succeed in only 52% (Fig. 2). In contrast, given the ground-truth semantics in view and distance to the goal, the same policy can have a success rate of 89%. Stopping at the right place thus turns out to be harder than reaching it.

The diagnosis suggests a direct remedy. We make goal grounding explicit, so that before each action the agent states which objects are in view and how far the goal is, much like chain-of-thought reasoning in language models and embodied agents (Wei et al., 2022; Zawalski et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025). Unlike free-form reasoning traces, which are generated by large VLMs and prone to noise (Zawalski et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026), our goal grounding is derived from the semantic and geometric labels of the training scenes. Every demonstration frame comes with its own ground-truth goal grounding at no extra labeling cost.

At test time, the grounding text must be predicted, so we build a pipeline of two models with this text as their interface. A perception model predicts the grounding from RGB observations, and a policy model reads it alongside the observations to choose the next action. The two are trained separately, the policy on ground-truth grounding and the perception model on the same annotations. Goal grounding could also be learned inside a single end-to-end model as an additional output, but such a model navigates worse in our experiments. The pipeline reaches state-of-the-art success on six object-goal navigation benchmarks, 8.8 points above the strongest baseline on HM3D-OVON val_unseen with corrected annotations (Tab. 1). These results reduce a long-standing failure of object-goal navigation to a concrete perception problem.

Our contributions are threefold:

We identify goal grounding as a missing piece for object-goal navigation. Policies often reach the goal but fail to stop, which can be mostly fixed by correct grounding.

Guided by this, we build a two-model pipeline that makes goal grounding explicit, reaching state-of-the-art results on all benchmarked object-goal navigation tasks.

We guide future work from two perspectives. We remedy annotation defects in existing benchmarks, so future methods are evaluated more faithfully. On the clean benchmarks, we show that the policy is already strong and the remaining headroom lies in perception.

1. We identify goal grounding as a missing piece for object-goal navigation. Policies often reach the goal but fail to stop, which can be mostly fixed by correct grounding.

2. Guided by this, we build a two-model pipeline that makes goal grounding explicit, reaching state-of-the-art results on all benchmarked object-goal navigation tasks.

3. We guide future work from two perspectives. We remedy annotation defects in existing benchmarks, so future methods are evaluated more faithfully. On the clean benchmarks, we show that the policy is already strong and the remaining headroom lies in perception.

title: SparseMax-dSTL: Sound Robustness with Horizon-Independent Gradient Allocation for Temporal Logic Trajectory Optimization
authors: Sai Sandeep Damera,Ryan Matheu,John S. Baras,Calin Belta
subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY); Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: . This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
abstract: A gradient-based solver that enforces a Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specification uses a smooth approximation of its quantitative semantics, the robustness. In safety-critical trajectory optimization, this approximation must have two properties. First, it must be sound, that is, nonnegative only on trajectories that satisfy the specification. Second, at each temporal operator, the weight of its gradient on the violating samples must stay bounded away from zero, however long the horizon. The approximations in use, including the log-sum-exp, its sound variant, and the generalized-mean robustness, do not have both. We introduce lower approximations of the minimum and the maximum whose gradients are sparsemax projections, and we prove that the robustness built from them has both. It lies below the exact robustness and is therefore sound, and its error has a bound that is independent of the number of samples and known before optimization. The gradient of each approximation is exactly zero on every sample beyond a data-dependent threshold, so the weight on violating samples a gap beyond the others has a positive lower bound at every horizon. On a planar unicycle and on a seven-joint manipulator beside a person in simulation, the log-sum-exp approximation is positive on a violating trajectory. As the horizon of the manipulator’s task grows from 10 to 80 s, the gradient weight of the sound variant on the violating samples falls from 0.22 to 0.04, while that of sparsemax stays at 1. In a constrained trajectory optimization of the unicycle, the constraint on the log-sum-exp robustness returns a violating trajectory, whereas the constraint on the sparsemax robustness returns a trajectory that satisfies the specification with the required margin.
introduction:
A gradient-based solver that enforces a signal temporal logic (STL) specification as a constraint does not evaluate the specification itself. STL assigns trajectories a scalar robustness, a nesting of minima and maxima over predicates and time samples whose sign determines satisfaction [1, 2]. The nesting is nonsmooth, so the solver differentiates a smooth surrogate of every extremum [3, 4] and accepts a trajectory as feasible when the resulting smoothed robustness is nonnegative. The surrogate therefore determines which trajectories the solver accepts as feasible and how its gradient is allocated among the time samples.

Consider a robot manipulator that hands a part to a person. Its STL specification requires that it stay out of the zone into which the person reaches until it has picked the part, keep a minimum separation from the person, and move slowly near the person. The first requirement is an until operator, whose left operand (stay out of the zone) must hold until its right operand (the pick) holds at some sample of a time window. Each sample of the window is a witness, and the robustness of the operator is a maximum over its witnesses. A trajectory that crosses the zone for a third of a second before the pick violates the specification at fewer than twenty of the hundreds or thousands of samples in the horizon, while the manipulator waits at the zone boundary for the rest. Figure 1(a) sketches such a trajectory with nine samples. A smoothed robustness that constrains such a trajectory must have two properties. First, it must be sound, that is, negative on every violating trajectory. Second, its gradient allocation, the weight that its gradient places on each sample, must not vanish on the violating samples as the waiting time grows. A policy gradient or a gradient-based safety filter that differentiates the robustness needs the same two properties.

The smoothing techniques in use today provide at most the first. The log-sum-exp (LSE) robustness [5] replaces the maximum of mm sample values z=(z1,…,zm)z=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}) by β−1​log​∑ieβ​zi\beta^{-1}\log\sum_{i}e^{\beta z_{i}} with a parameter β>0\beta>0. It exceeds the maximum by up to log⁡m/β\log m/\beta [6], attained when all values are equal, and it can be nonnegative on a violating trajectory [7]. We call this smoothing the plain LSE. We show that an until operator produces such ties when the deepest violation of its left operand precedes the window, so the plain LSE robustness is positive on a shallow violation. Sound measures remove that defect. The softmax-mean measure under-approximates both extrema [7], and the arithmetic-geometric mean and the generalized-mean robustness (GMR) preserve the sign of the exact robustness [8, 9]. We ask how much weight a temporal operator keeps on its violating samples under each sound measure as the horizon adds samples. Subtracting from the LSE its largest excess, log⁡m/β\log m/\beta, gives the sound LSE, which never exceeds the maximum and whose gradient, the softmax of β​z\beta z, gives every sample a positive weight. At a worst-case error ε\varepsilon per operator, its weight on the violating samples tends to zero as the horizon adds samples whose values lie within ε\varepsilon of theirs. By eq. (12) of [9], GMR averages the violating samples over all dd samples of the operator, so its weight on kk of them is of order (k/d)1/q(k/d)^{1/q} for the exponent qq of its power mean.

We replace every extremum by a lower approximation derived from the maximum regularized by a quadratic penalty of weight γ>0\gamma>0, whose gradient is the sparsemax projection onto the simplex [10, 11]. Figure 1 shows the construction on these nine samples. The value lies below the exact extremum by at most γ/2\gamma/2 for any number of samples, and every sample farther than a data-dependent threshold from the extremum receives a derivative of exactly zero. To our knowledge, the resulting robustness is the first smooth one that is a lower bound of the exact robustness and whose weight on the violating samples, for every gap by which they lie beyond the others, has a lower bound that does not depend on the horizon. Our contributions are the following.

1) Sound robustness from sparsemax lower extrema. We construct lower approximations of both extrema from the regularized maximum of [11] and prove that the robustness built from them, until included, is a lower bound of the exact one with an error known before optimization (Propositions 1 and 1, composed as in [6]). We also bound the excess of the plain LSE at an until operator from below and obtain the depth of violation up to which its robustness is positive (Proposition 2).

2) Horizon-independent gradient allocation. We prove that the sparsemax weight on kk violating samples that lie a gap Δ\Delta beyond the NN others is at least min⁡{1,k​Δ/γ}\min\{1,k\Delta/\gamma\} for every NN. At equal worst-case error ε\varepsilon, the weight of the sound LSE tends to zero as NN grows if Δ<ε\Delta<\varepsilon (Theorems 2 and 1).

3) Numerical examples. We show on violating trajectories of a planar unicycle and a manipulator that the plain LSE robustness is positive and that the measured weights follow the closed forms. The optimizations demonstrate the two properties with a first-order solver, where the gradient’s allocation sets the update; the immediate update advantage is claimed for first-order methods only (Section V).
